teile.einleitung: For more than two decades Walter Ulbricht was the most powerful politician in the GDR. As party leader of the SED he built up the state on the Soviet model. In 1971 he was replaced by Erich Honecker.
wichtigste: Ulbricht was born in Leipzig in 1893 and trained as a cabinetmaker.
From 1938 he lived in exile in Moscow.
On 30 April 1945 he returned to Berlin with the Ulbricht Group.
From 1950 he led the SED, and from 1960 the Council of State as well.
In 1971 Erich Honecker took over the party leadership.
Ulbricht died on 1 August 1973.

abschnitte.text: Walter Ulbricht was born in **Leipzig** on **30 June 1893**. All his life he spoke with a **Saxon accent**. From 1907 to 1911 he did an apprenticeship as a **cabinetmaker**. After that he became active in the **labour movement** and later in the Communist Party. After the Nazis came to power he fled via Prague and Paris and from 1938 lived in **Moscow**.

On **30 April 1945**, even before the end of the war, the **Ulbricht Group** returned from Moscow to Berlin. Its task was to build up a new administration under Soviet supervision. **Wolfgang Leonhard** was also a member. He later passed on Ulbricht’s sentence: “It has to look democratic, but we must have everything in our hands.” It shows that the communists only pretended to want to share power.

abschnitte.titel: The most powerful man in the GDR
abschnitte.text: In 1950 Ulbricht became **General Secretary** of the Central Committee of the **SED**; from 1953 the post was called First Secretary. This made him the most powerful politician in the GDR. After Wilhelm Pieck’s death in 1960 the office of president was abolished. Ulbricht became **Chairman of the Council of State**. In June 1961 he said: “Nobody has any intention of building a wall.” Two months later the **construction of the Berlin Wall** began.

From 1963 Ulbricht introduced the **New Economic System** of Planning and Management, **NÖS** for short. Businesses were to be given more responsibility of their own and incentives to make a profit. At the end of the 1960s the reform was watered down. On **3 May 1971** Ulbricht officially resigned “for health reasons”. With Soviet consent, **Erich Honecker** took over the party leadership. Ulbricht died after a stroke on **1 August 1973**.

gewusst: Ulbricht remained Chairman of the Council of State until his death, even after resigning as party leader.
Wolfgang Leonhard described his time in the Ulbricht Group in his book “Die Revolution entlässt ihre Kinder”, published in English as “Child of the Revolution”.

teile.einleitung: The Socialist Unity Party of Germany, SED for short, was the ruling party of the GDR. It came into being in 1946 in the Soviet occupation zone. Until the end of 1989 it decided almost everything in the state and in society.
wichtigste: The SED was founded in April 1946.
It came about through the forced merger of the KPD and the SPD.
Its party badge showed two hands in a handshake.
The real centre of power was the Politburo.
In December 1989 the People’s Chamber removed the SED’s claim to leadership from the constitution.
From February 1990 the successor party was called the PDS.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided into occupation zones. In April 1946, in the **Soviet occupation zone**, the **KPD** and the **SPD** were merged to form the SED. Many Social Democrats were put under pressure in the process, which is why people speak of a **forced merger**. In the West the SPD rejected this merger. The party badge showed **two hands in a handshake** as a sign of the union.

Formally the **Party Congress** elected the **Central Committee**, and the Central Committee elected the **Politburo**. In fact it was the small Politburo under the **General Secretary** that took the important decisions. The party was organised according to **democratic centralism**. This means that decisions of the higher bodies were binding on all the lower ones. In practice the party was strictly controlled from the top. Well-known party leaders were Walter Ulbricht and Erich Honecker.

In the GDR there were other parties besides the SED, the **bloc parties**. But together with mass organisations they were united in the **National Front** under the leadership of the SED. In elections there was only one joint **single list**. So there was no real choice. In addition, the constitution laid down the **leading role of the SED**.

In the autumn of 1989 many people in the GDR protested, and on 9 November the **Berlin Wall** fell. On **1 December 1989** the **People’s Chamber**, the GDR parliament, deleted the sentence about the leading role of the SED from Article 1 of the constitution. As a result the party lost its guaranteed **monopoly on power**. It first called itself **SED-PDS** and from February 1990 just **PDS**, Party of Democratic Socialism. Later the party **Die Linke** (The Left) grew out of it.

gewusst: The GDR’s state coat of arms, with a hammer and compasses in a wreath of ears of grain, was not the same as the SED’s party badge with the handshake.
Erich Honecker led the SED from 1971 until October 1989.

teile.einleitung: Laos is a country in Southeast Asia with no access to the sea. Since 1975 it has been ruled by a communist party, which is still the case today. Laos is known for the Mekong River, Buddhist temples and the old royal city of Luang Prabang.
wichtigste: Laos lies in Southeast Asia and has no coast.
The capital is Vientiane.
Since 1975 the Lao People's Revolutionary Party has ruled as the only party.
The Mekong is the country's most important river.
Most people are Buddhists.
During the Vietnam War a great many bombs fell on Laos, and many unexploded bombs are still in the ground today.
About 7.5 million people live in Laos (as of 2023).

abschnitte.text: Laos borders China, Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Myanmar. It is the only country in Southeast Asia **without a coastline**. Large parts of it are mountainous and covered in forest. The **Mekong** flows through the country and forms the border with Thailand for long stretches.

In the 14th century the kingdom of **Lan Xang**, the “Land of a Million Elephants”, was founded. From the late 19th century Laos was part of French Indochina. In 1953 it became independent, and after that there was a long civil war. In 1975 the communists of the Pathet Lao took power and abolished the monarchy.

During the Vietnam War, from 1964 to 1973, the USA dropped more than two million tonnes of bombs on Laos. Measured by population, Laos is regarded as the most heavily bombed country in the world. Many **cluster bombs** did not explode and still lie in fields and forests today. Again and again they injure farmers and children, which is why they are painstakingly cleared.

Many different ethnic groups live in Laos; the largest is the Lao. The official language is **Lao**. Most people follow **Theravada Buddhism**, and in many places you can see monks in orange robes. Many families live from farming, especially growing rice.

Laos is a one-party state, and there are no free elections and no freedom of the press. Since the 1980s private companies and trade have been allowed, similar to China. In 2021 a railway from China to Vientiane was opened. The city of **Luang Prabang** with its temples and the mysterious **Plain of Jars** are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country with no access to the sea.
A bomb that has not exploded and can still be dangerous.
One of the longest rivers in Asia; it flows through six countries.
An old form of Buddhism that is widespread in Southeast Asia.

gewusst: In Luang Prabang, monks walk through the streets every morning at sunrise and are given sticky rice by the people.
Some of the stone jars on the Plain of Jars are more than 2,000 years old, and nobody knows exactly what they were used for.

teile.einleitung: The “Mao Bible” is a collection of quotations from the Chinese leader Mao Zedong. Because of its red cover it is also called “The Little Red Book”. During the Cultural Revolution it became a symbol, and it is one of the most printed books in the world.
wichtigste: Its actual title is “Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung”.
It contains short quotations from Mao Zedong's speeches and writings.
It was first published by the Chinese People's Liberation Army.
The first edition appeared in 1964.
The Red Guards waved it at mass rallies.
In 1979 the party stopped it being printed.

abschnitte.text: Its actual title is **“Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung”**. Mao Tse-tung is an older spelling of **Mao Zedong**. The book is a collection of **short quotations** from his speeches and writings, arranged by topic. Because of its red cover it is called **“The Little Red Book”**. In German-speaking Europe it was often called the **Mao-Bibel**, the “Mao Bible”.

The collection was put together under Defence Minister **Lin Biao** for training soldiers. It was published by the Chinese **People's Liberation Army**. The first edition appeared in **1964**. Only later was the book distributed to the whole population. From **1966**, during the **Cultural Revolution**, it was printed in huge numbers.

During the Cultural Revolution, old ideas and Mao's opponents were to be fought. Many people were persecuted. The **Red Guards**, mostly young schoolchildren and students, held the little red book up high at huge rallies in **Beijing**. Well-known quotations include the claim that opponents were only **“paper tigers”**, that is dangerous only in appearance. Another quotation says that a revolution is **not a dinner party**.

The state had the book printed in huge numbers and translated into many languages. Estimates range from more than **a billion** to several billion copies. Around **1968**, some students in **Western Europe** also carried the book as a political statement. After the end of the Cultural Revolution, it lost its importance. In **February 1979** the party **stopped it being printed**.

gewusst: The quotation “A revolution is not a dinner party” comes from a report by Mao on the peasant movement in Hunan in 1927.
The book was so small that it fitted easily into a jacket pocket.

teile.einleitung: NATO is a military alliance of countries in Europe and North America. It was founded in 1949, when the Cold War between East and West was intensifying. The members promise to defend one another.
wichtigste: NATO was founded on 4 April 1949.
It is a military alliance for joint defence.
Its headquarters are in Brussels, the capital of Belgium.
An attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
In 2026 NATO has 32 members.
Switzerland is neutral and not a member of NATO.

abschnitte.text: NATO is the abbreviation for the **North Atlantic Treaty Organization**. The treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949. Twelve countries founded the alliance, among them the USA, Canada, Great Britain and France. The members lie on both sides of the **Atlantic**. That is why the alliance is named after this ocean.

The most important principle is in **Article 5** of the treaty. If one member is attacked, this counts as an attack on all. Then the countries help one another. This is called the **duty of mutual defence**. At the time, the Western countries wanted to protect themselves against the Soviet Union in this way.

NATO came into being during the **Cold War**. That is the name for the conflict between the West, led by the USA, and the East, led by the Soviet Union. In 1955 the Soviet Union and its allies founded an alliance of their own, the **Warsaw Pact**. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in 1991. NATO continued to exist, and later many former Eastern Bloc countries joined too.

Since its founding many countries have joined. **Finland** joined in 2023 and **Sweden** in March 2024. Both countries had long been neutral. In 2026 NATO has **32 members**. The flag is dark blue with a white **compass rose** like the one on a compass. Switzerland is neutral and not a member, but it works together with NATO in certain areas.

gewusst: NATO’s headquarters are in Brussels, where many institutions of the European Union are also based.
The compass rose on the NATO flag is meant to show the members’ common path.

teile.einleitung: The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance was the economic alliance of the communist states. It existed from 1949 to 1991 and was led by the Soviet Union. In the West it was usually called Comecon.
wichtigste: Comecon was founded in Moscow in January 1949.
Its secretariat was based in Moscow.
The GDR joined in 1950.
With Mongolia, Cuba and Vietnam, countries outside Europe also joined.
Albania stopped taking part in 1961.
Comecon was dissolved on 28 June 1991.

abschnitte.text: In January 1949 the **Soviet Union** and five other states founded the council in Moscow: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. Its job was to **coordinate** the economies of the Eastern Bloc states under the leadership of the Soviet Union, in other words to bring them into line with one another. It was also a response to the **Marshall Plan**, with which the USA helped Western Europe to rebuild. The secretariat was based in **Moscow**. In the West the council was usually called **Comecon**.

On 29 September 1950 the **GDR** joined. In 1962 **Mongolia** became a member, the first state outside Europe. **Cuba**, which mainly supplied sugar, followed in 1972, and later **Vietnam**. **Albania** had fallen out with the Soviet Union and stopped taking part from 1961. After that it turned towards China.

From the 1960s the **“Druzhba”** oil pipeline, Russian for friendship, carried crude oil from the Soviet Union to other member states, including the GDR. In 1971 Comecon adopted the **Comprehensive Programme**. It was meant to bring the members’ economic plans more closely into line. Each country was to specialise in certain goods. Trade with the West, on the other hand, remained small.

In 1989 and 1990 the communist governments came to an end in many Eastern Bloc states. The countries turned towards the market economy and the West. As a result Comecon no longer had a purpose. On **28 June 1991** it was dissolved. A few months later the Soviet Union also broke apart.

gewusst: The Druzhba pipeline is one of the longest oil pipelines in the world, and parts of it are still in operation today.
Mongolia was the first member of Comecon that was not in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Eastern Bloc was the group of communist states in Eastern Europe that were under the influence of the Soviet Union after the Second World War. An “Iron Curtain” separated them from the West. Many people there suffered from the lack of freedom of opinion and freedom to travel.
wichtigste: The Eastern Bloc included the Soviet Union, Poland, the GDR, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria.
The Soviet Union largely decided the policies of these countries.
Many people criticised the lack of freedom of opinion and freedom to travel.
Militarily the states were joined together in the Warsaw Pact.
Uprisings such as those in Hungary in 1956 and in Prague in 1968 were crushed.
In 1989 the communist governments collapsed peacefully almost everywhere.
Switzerland took in many refugees from Hungary and Czechoslovakia.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Soviet troops were stationed in large parts of Eastern Europe. In the years that followed, communist parties came to power there with Soviet help. The Eastern Bloc included Poland, the GDR, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and the Soviet Union itself, and Albania until the 1960s. In 1946 the British politician Winston Churchill spoke of an **Iron Curtain** dividing Europe.

In 1949 the countries founded the **Council for Mutual Economic Assistance** to coordinate their planned economies. In 1955 the military alliance known as the **Warsaw Pact** was set up as a counterpart to NATO. The borders with the West were secured with fences, mines and watchtowers. From 1961 the Wall stood in Berlin.

Work, housing and school were usually guaranteed, but the choice in the shops was often small. For some goods, such as cars, people waited many years. Criticising the government was dangerous, and secret police forces kept watch on people. Travel to the West was forbidden for most people, which is why many criticised the lack of **freedom of opinion** and **freedom to travel**.

On 17 June 1953 workers protested in the GDR, and Soviet tanks put an end to the uprising. In 1956 the Hungarians fought for freedom in the **Hungarian Uprising**, which was also crushed. In 1968, in the **Prague Spring**, Czechoslovakia wanted “socialism with a human face”, but Warsaw Pact troops invaded. In Poland the free trade union Solidarność was founded in 1980.

In 1989 the communist governments in Eastern Europe fell one after another, mostly peacefully. In 1991 the Warsaw Pact and the Soviet Union dissolved. Today many of these countries are members of the EU and NATO. Switzerland took in about 14,000 refugees from Hungary in 1956 and about 12,000 from Czechoslovakia in 1968.

begriffe.erklaerung: Figurative expression for the heavily guarded border between Eastern and Western Europe.
The military alliance of the Eastern Bloc states from 1955 to 1991.
The long power struggle between East and West without a major direct war.
Polish for “solidarity”, a free trade union in Poland.

gewusst: Yugoslavia was communist, but did not belong to the Eastern Bloc because it fell out with the Soviet Union in 1948.
In the Eastern Bloc the Trabant was a typical car, which people in the GDR often had to wait more than ten years for.

teile.einleitung: “Soviet” is a Russian word meaning “council”. It was the name for assemblies of elected representatives of workers, soldiers and peasants. The soviets played a big part in the Russian revolutions and gave the Soviet Union its name.
wichtigste: Soviet means council.
The first soviets came into being in the Revolution of 1905.
In February 1917 the Petrograd Soviet was formed alongside the Provisional Government.
Lenin’s slogan was “All power to the soviets!”.
In November 1917 the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets confirmed the Bolsheviks’ seizure of power.
From 1936 the highest parliament of the Soviet Union was called the Supreme Soviet.

abschnitte.text: During the **Revolution of 1905**, workers in several Russian cities elected their own **councils** for the first time. In Russian, council is “**soviet**”. The soviet of **St Petersburg** became particularly well known. The councils organised strikes and represented the workers’ concerns. After the revolution they were dissolved again.

In February 1917 the **tsar** was overthrown. A **Provisional Government** was formed. At the same time workers and soldiers elected the **Petrograd Soviet of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies**. The government passed laws, but soldiers and workers often listened more to the soviet. This situation is called **dual power**. It greatly weakened the Provisional Government.

**Lenin**, the leader of the **Bolsheviks**, called for the Provisional Government to be overthrown with the slogan “**All power to the soviets!**”. Little by little the Bolsheviks won the majority in many soviets. During the **October Revolution** the **Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets** met in Petrograd. It declared the government deposed and passed decrees on peace and land.

At the end of 1917 elections were held for the **Constituent Assembly**. It was supposed to draw up a constitution for Russia. However, the Bolsheviks received only about a quarter of the votes. In **January 1918** they dissolved the assembly after a single day of sitting. From then on they ruled alone, officially in the name of the soviets.

In 1922 the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics**, the Soviet Union for short, was founded. The constitution of **1936** created the **Supreme Soviet** as the highest organ of state power. On paper it was the country’s parliament. But real power lay with the leadership of the **Communist Party**. In elections there was usually only one candidate to choose from.

gewusst: Because Russia still used a different calendar in 1917, the “October Revolution” took place in November according to our calendar.
In Germany, too, there were workers’ and soldiers’ councils on the Russian model in 1918.

teile.einleitung: Alberto Fujimori was president of Peru from 1990 to 2000. He fought the economic crisis and the terrorist group “Shining Path”, but ruled in an increasingly authoritarian way. Later he was convicted of human rights crimes and corruption.
wichtigste: In 1990 Fujimori won the presidential election against the writer Mario Vargas Llosa.
On 5 April 1992 he dissolved Congress in a self-coup.
In 1992 Abimael Guzmán, the leader of the “Shining Path”, was captured.
His intelligence adviser Vladimiro Montesinos built up a network of bribery.
In November 2000 Fujimori resigned by fax from Japan.
In 2009 he was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

abschnitte.text: **Alberto Fujimori** was a little-known **agricultural engineer** whose parents came from Japan. In 1990 he stood in the presidential election in **Peru**. In the run-off he defeated the famous writer **Mario Vargas Llosa**. He benefited from many people’s distrust of established politics. At that time Peru was in a severe economic crisis with very high inflation.

On **5 April 1992**, with the help of the army, Fujimori dissolved **Congress** and suspended the constitution. This is called a **self-coup**, in Spanish “autogolpe”: a head of state in office shuts down parliament and the courts. After that Fujimori at times ruled by **decree**. In September 1992 **Abimael Guzmán**, the leader of the terrorist organisation **“Shining Path”**, was captured in Lima. This boosted Fujimori’s reputation.

Fujimori’s influential adviser **Vladimiro Montesinos** effectively ran the intelligence service and built up a network of **bribery** and blackmail. In September 2000 a video was published showing Montesinos handing money to an opposition member of Congress. These “**Vladivideos**” exposed a huge system of corruption. Shortly afterwards Fujimori travelled to a summit and fled to **Japan**. From there he sent his resignation **by fax** in November 2000. Congress did not accept it and removed him for “moral incapacity”.

Under Fujimori a secret army unit, the **Grupo Colina**, carried out the massacres of **Barrios Altos** and **La Cantuta**, in which civilians were killed. For this Fujimori was sentenced in **2009** to **25 years in prison**. He was the first elected former president to be convicted of human rights crimes in his own country. In December 2017 President **Pedro Pablo Kuczynski** pardoned him, which sparked big protests. The pardon was later overturned, but Fujimori was nevertheless released in 2023. He died in 2024.

Some of Alberto Fujimori’s children are also active in politics. His daughter **Keiko Fujimori** leads a party of her own and has stood for president several times. She lost the run-offs of 2011, 2016 and 2021. Her brother **Kenji** was a member of Congress. To this day the name Fujimori is controversial in Peru: some people remember the fight against terror, others the corruption and human rights violations.

gewusst: Resigning by fax from abroad was a very unusual way for a head of state to step down.
Because of his Japanese origins, many Peruvians called him “El Chino”.

teile.einleitung: Lenin's Mausoleum is a tomb on Red Square in Moscow. It contains the embalmed body of Lenin, the founder of the Soviet Union. Visitors can still see him today.
wichtigste: The mausoleum stands on Red Square right in front of the Kremlin wall.
Lenin's body is embalmed and is treated regularly.
The first mausoleum, from 1924, was made of wood.
Today's stone building, from 1930, is made mainly of red and dark granite.
The architect was Alexei Shchusev.
The mausoleum has the shape of a stepped pyramid.
From 1953 to 1961 Stalin also lay in it.

abschnitte.text: Lenin died in January **1924**. His successors wanted people to be able to go on seeing him. That is why his body was **embalmed**, that is preserved with special substances. The mausoleum stands on **Red Square** in Moscow, right in front of the **Kremlin wall**. Behind it are the graves of other Soviet figures. To this day, specialists regularly treat the body with solutions.

A few days after Lenin's death, a first mausoleum was built **of wood**. From **1930** the present stone building was constructed. Both were designed by the architect **Alexei Shchusev**, one of the best-known architects of the Soviet Union. For the stone building, **red granite**, black **labradorite** and other stones were used. The colours match the red Kremlin wall.

The mausoleum is built of blocks stepped one above the other. It looks like a flat **stepped pyramid**. At the top there is a platform. During **military parades**, the party leaders stood there on the **viewing stand**. From here they gave speeches and saluted the troops marching past.

In the **Second World War**, German troops advanced on Moscow. That is why Lenin's coffin was taken to safety in **Tyumen** in western Siberia. In **1945** it returned to Moscow. After Stalin's death in **1953**, his body was also displayed in the mausoleum. In **1961** it was removed and buried by the Kremlin wall. In Russia there is still debate today about whether Lenin should be buried.

gewusst: Inside the mausoleum it is cool, and visitors may not take photos or speak loudly.
In Soviet times, people often queued for hours in long lines in front of the mausoleum.

teile.einleitung: The Soviet-Afghan War lasted from 1979 to 1989. In it the Soviet Union fought on the side of the Afghan communists against resistance fighters. The war cost a great many lives and weakened the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The People’s Democratic Party of Afghanistan took power in 1978.
During the invasion in December 1979, the ruler Hafizullah Amin was killed.
In 1986 Gorbachev called the war a “bleeding wound”.
Officially just under 15,000 Soviet soldiers died.
The last soldiers withdrew in February 1989.
President Mohammad Najibullah stayed in power until 1992.

abschnitte.text: In April 1978 the **People’s Democratic Party of Afghanistan** came to power in Afghanistan. This overthrow is called the **Saur Revolution**. The communist party carried out radical reforms. Many people, especially in the countryside, rejected them. **Uprisings** broke out all over the country. The government asked the Soviet Union for help.

There were fierce power struggles within the party. The Soviet Union distrusted the ruler **Hafizullah Amin**. In **December 1979** Soviet troops moved in. Special forces stormed the **Tajbeg Palace**, and Amin was killed. In his place Moscow installed **Babrak Karmal**. This marked the start of a long war against the resistance fighters, the **mujahideen**.

The Soviet Union could not win the war. Officially just under **15,000 Soviet soldiers** died. On the Afghan side, according to estimates, between about 600,000 and 1.5 million people died, and millions fled. At the **27th Party Congress** in 1986 **Mikhail Gorbachev** spoke openly of a “**bleeding wound**”. In this way he prepared the withdrawal. It was based on the **Geneva Accords** of 1988.

On **15 February 1989** General **Boris Gromov** was the last soldier to cross the bridge over the **Amu Darya** river. President **Mohammad Najibullah** continued to govern with Soviet help. When this help stopped after the end of the Soviet Union, his government collapsed in 1992. The veterans who came home were called **Afgantsy**. They often suffered from psychological wounds and felt forgotten, because for a long time it was hardly possible to talk openly about the war.

gewusst: The Amu Darya forms part of the border between Afghanistan and the countries of Central Asia that belonged to the Soviet Union at that time.
After the Soviets withdrew, the war in Afghanistan continued between various groups.

teile.einleitung: Human rights are rights that every person has simply because they are a human being, for example freedom and protection from torture. On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris. It is regarded as one of the most important documents in world history.
wichtigste: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948.
It consists of 30 articles.
The first article says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
It came about as a response to the terrible crimes of the Second World War.
Eleanor Roosevelt led the commission that drew up the text.
The declaration is not a law, but it has shaped many constitutions and treaties.
Today 10 December is Human Rights Day all over the world.

abschnitte.text: **Human rights** apply to all people, whatever their skin colour, religion, language or sex. Nobody has to earn them, and no state may simply take them away. They include the right to life, liberty and security as well as protection from **torture** and slavery. Freedom of opinion, freedom of religion and the right to education are also among them.

abschnitte.titel: How it came about after the war
abschnitte.text: In the Second World War and the **Holocaust** millions of people were persecuted and murdered. Afterwards the states of the world wanted to prevent anything like this from ever happening again. In 1945 they founded the **United Nations**, the UN for short. A commission led by **Eleanor Roosevelt**, the widow of US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, wrote the text of the declaration.

On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly voted on the declaration at the **Palais de Chaillot** in Paris. 48 states voted in favour, none against, and eight states abstained, among them the Soviet Union. The declaration consists of a preamble and 30 articles. It has been translated into hundreds of languages, more than almost any other text.

The declaration is really a **recommendation** and not a binding law. Even so, it became the model for many constitutions and international treaties. In 1966 the UN adopted two **human rights covenants**, which are binding on states once they sign them. In Europe the European Convention on Human Rights also protects people’s rights, including in Switzerland.

The UN Human Rights Council has its seat in **Geneva**, and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights also works there. Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002. The fundamental rights in the Swiss **Federal Constitution** largely correspond to human rights. Even so, human rights are still violated in many countries of the world today, for example in dictatorships.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right that every person has simply because they are a human being.
The United Nations, an organisation of almost all the states in the world.
When great pain is deliberately inflicted on someone, for example to force a confession.
The worth that every person has and that must be respected.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is regarded as one of the most translated texts in the world.
Children also have rights of their own: the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989 has applied in Switzerland since 1997.
Eleanor Roosevelt called the declaration a “Magna Carta for all mankind”.

teile.einleitung: On 17 June 1953 hundreds of thousands of people in the GDR took to the streets. What began as a protest against higher work quotas became an uprising against the government. Soviet tanks crushed it.
wichtigste: It was triggered by a 10 per cent increase in work quotas for the same pay.
On 16 June 1953 construction workers on the Stalinallee in East Berlin downed tools.
The West Berlin radio station RIAS spread the news throughout the GDR.
The Soviet army crushed the uprising with tanks.
At least 55 deaths are documented, and more than 15,000 people were arrested.
In West Germany 17 June was a public holiday until 1990.

abschnitte.titel: More work for the same pay
abschnitte.text: In 1953 the GDR government decided to raise the **work quotas** by **10 per cent**. A work quota lays down how much someone has to produce in a certain time. Pay was to stay the same. In effect this was a **pay cut**. The increase was to apply by 30 June 1953, the 60th birthday of **Walter Ulbricht**. Many workers were furious.

On **16 June 1953** the construction workers on the huge **Stalinallee** building site in East Berlin downed tools. They marched through the city in protest. The radio station **RIAS**, the broadcaster in the American sector of West Berlin, reported on it in detail. This is how people throughout the GDR found out about it. On **17 June** the strike spread to many towns and villages. Now many people also demanded free elections and the resignation of the government.

The **Soviet occupying power** declared a **state of emergency**. It sent in tanks and thousands of soldiers. Many people lost their lives. Historians have been able to document **at least 55** deaths for certain, and other cases remain unexplained. More than **15,000** people were arrested.

In the Federal Republic, 17 June became a public holiday from 1954 as the “**Day of German Unity**”. Since 1990, 3 October has been the national holiday. As early as 22 June 1953 the West Berlin Senate renamed a large street in the Tiergarten. Since then it has been called **Strasse des 17. Juni** (17 June Street) and runs from the Brandenburg Gate to Ernst-Reuter-Platz.

The writer **Bertolt Brecht** lived in East Berlin. He wrote a mocking poem about the uprising called “**The Solution**”. In it he asks whether it would not be simpler for the government “to dissolve the people and elect another”. In this way he made fun of the SED leadership, which distrusted the people. The poem was only published after Brecht’s death.

gewusst: The increased quotas were to be reached of all days by Ulbricht’s 60th birthday.
The Strasse des 17. Juni in Berlin got its name only five days after the uprising.

teile.einleitung: The Gang of Four was a group of four powerful politicians in China during the Cultural Revolution. It included Jiang Qing, the wife of Mao Zedong. Shortly after Mao’s death in 1976 the group was overthrown.
wichtigste: The Gang of Four were Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen.
Their power base was the city of Shanghai.
An article by Yao Wenyuan from 1965 is regarded as the opening shot of the Cultural Revolution.
In October 1976, about a month after Mao’s death, the group was arrested.
In 1980 and 1981 the four stood trial.

abschnitte.text: The **Gang of Four** consisted of **Jiang Qing**, **Zhang Chunqiao**, **Yao Wenyuan** and **Wang Hongwen**. Jiang Qing was a former actress and Mao’s fourth wife. During the **Cultural Revolution** she controlled mainly the arts and culture. The three men had begun their rise in **Shanghai**. The city was therefore regarded as the group’s power base.

abschnitte.titel: The start of the Cultural Revolution
abschnitte.text: In November 1965 the writer **Yao Wenyuan** attacked a play in a Shanghai newspaper. It was called “**Hai Rui Dismissed from Office**” and was by Wu Han. The debate about it set off the **Cultural Revolution**. It lasted from 1966 to 1976. During this time many people were persecuted and cultural treasures were destroyed.

**Mao Zedong** died in September 1976. About a month later, in **October 1976**, the new leadership had the four arrested. Mao’s successor **Hua Guofeng**, who did not himself belong to the Gang of Four, was involved. The arrest is regarded as the end of the Cultural Revolution. In 1980 and 1981 a **show trial** took place, which was broadcast on television. Jiang Qing defended herself by saying that she had only followed Mao’s instructions.

Jiang Qing was at first sentenced **to death with a reprieve**. This is a death sentence that can be changed after a waiting period. In 1983 her sentence was changed to **life imprisonment**. Jiang Qing died in 1991. The other members also received long prison sentences. The party blamed the Gang of Four for many of the mistakes of the Cultural Revolution.

gewusst: Jiang Qing was Mao’s fourth wife and a former actress.
The trial of the Gang of Four was shown on Chinese television.

teile.einleitung: The People’s Republic of China is a huge country in East Asia. It was founded in 1949 and is governed by the Communist Party. China is known for the Great Wall, the giant panda and eating with chopsticks.
wichtigste: The People’s Republic of China was founded on 1 October 1949.
The capital is Beijing.
There are five yellow stars on the flag.
The money in China is called the yuan.
The giant panda lives in the wild only in China.
According to the UN, since about 2023 India has had slightly more inhabitants than China.

abschnitte.text: The **People’s Republic of China** was proclaimed in Beijing by **Mao Zedong** on **1 October 1949**. Since then the **Communist Party** has governed. The capital is **Beijing**. In the middle of the city lies the huge **Tiananmen Square**, meaning “Square of the Gate of Heavenly Peace”. It is one of the largest squares in the world.

China’s flag is red and shows **five yellow stars**: one big one and four small ones. In China people pay with the **yuan**. The yen, on the other hand, is the money of Japan. For a long time China was the country with the most people. According to the UN, since about **2023** **India** has had slightly more inhabitants.

The **Great Wall of China** is a huge old defensive wall. It stretches for thousands of kilometres across **northern China**. Over many centuries various emperors had it built and extended. It was meant to protect the country from attacks from the north. Today it is one of the most famous structures in the world.

In the wild, the **giant panda** lives only in the **mountain forests** of China. It eats mainly **bamboo**. When eating, many people in China use **chopsticks** instead of a fork. They use them to pick up rice, vegetables and meat. This tradition has existed in China for a very long time.

gewusst: In 1950 Switzerland was one of the first Western countries to recognise the People’s Republic of China.
Tiananmen Square is one of the largest squares in the world.

teile.einleitung: The National People’s Congress is the parliament of the People’s Republic of China. According to the constitution it is the highest organ of state power. In reality, however, the Communist Party of China decides policy.
wichtigste: The National People’s Congress has just under 3,000 deputies.
It meets once a year in March in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing.
A term of office lasts five years.
Officially the People’s Congress elects the president of the state.
Between sessions the Standing Committee does the work.
The Congress almost always approves the party’s proposals.

abschnitte.text: The National People’s Congress has just under **3,000 deputies**. This makes it one of the largest parliaments in the world. The deputies are not elected directly by the people. They are chosen by the people’s congresses of the provinces and by the army. A **term of office** lasts five years.

The full assembly takes place **once a year** in March and lasts only about a week. It meets in the **Great Hall of the People** on Tiananmen Square in Beijing, which was completed in 1959. At the same time the **Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference** meets. It is an advisory body with no right to pass laws. Because both meet at the same time, people speak of the “Two Sessions”.

Between sessions the **Standing Committee**, with about 170 members, does the work. It meets regularly and passes a large share of the laws. Since March 2023 **Zhao Leji** has been its chairman. He was previously head of the party’s Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. He also belongs to the innermost leadership circle of the Communist Party.

According to the constitution, the People’s Congress elects the **president of the state** and passes the laws. However, the candidates and proposals are decided beforehand by the **Communist Party**. Votes usually end with very large majorities. There is no real opposition. That is why critics often call the People’s Congress a **“rubber-stamp parliament”**.

gewusst: The Great Hall of the People was built in less than a year and finished in 1959.
The Swiss Federal Assembly has 246 members; the Chinese People’s Congress has more than ten times as many.

teile.einleitung: Trotskyism is a strand of communism that goes back to the Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky. Trotsky was an opponent of Stalin and believed that a revolution must not be limited to a single country.
wichtigste: Trotsky’s real name was Lev Bronstein, and he was born in 1879.
His most important idea is the theory of permanent revolution.
Stalin, on the other hand, relied on “socialism in one country”.
In 1938 Trotsky founded the Fourth International.
In 1940 he was murdered by a Soviet agent while in exile in Mexico.
Trotsky regarded Stalin’s Soviet Union as a “degenerated workers’ state”.

abschnitte.text: Leon Trotsky was born **Lev Davidovich Bronstein** in 1879 in what is now Ukraine. He took the name Trotsky after escaping from exile. In the Russian Revolution of 1917 he was one of the most important leaders alongside Lenin. After Lenin’s death he lost the power struggle against **Stalin**. He was expelled from the party and had to leave the country.

Around 1905 Trotsky, together with the Marxist **Parvus**, developed the theory of **permanent revolution**. Permanent means lasting. Even in backward countries the workers were to take power. But socialism would only be possible if the revolution spread to other countries. From 1924 Stalin argued the opposite: **socialism in one country**.

In exile Trotsky wrote the book “**The Revolution Betrayed**”. In it he called the Soviet Union a **degenerated workers’ state**. He meant that property was still socialist, but that a **bureaucracy** had seized power. Other left-wingers, on the other hand, spoke of state capitalism. In 1938, near Paris, Trotsky founded the **Fourth International** as a counterpart to the Comintern.

In the end Trotsky lived in **Coyoacán** near Mexico City. In 1940 he was attacked there by the Spanish agent **Ramón Mercader** on Stalin’s orders. Trotsky died the next day. His followers founded small groups and parties in many countries. Some use the tactic of **entryism**: they join larger parties as a group in order to win members there.

gewusst: In 1934 Trotsky recommended entryism to his followers in France.
In 1915 Trotsky took part in the Zimmerwald Conference in the canton of Bern, a meeting of socialists against the First World War.

teile.einleitung: During the night of 25 to 26 April 1986, a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power station. It was the worst accident at a nuclear power station up to that time. Radioactive substances spread over large parts of Europe, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The disaster happened on 26 April 1986 in Unit 4 of the power station.
Chernobyl is in the north of Ukraine, which at that time belonged to the Soviet Union.
The nearby town of Pripyat was evacuated and is still abandoned today.
Sweden was the first country abroad to notice the increased radiation.
In Switzerland, Ticino was the worst affected.
The accident was given the highest level, 7, on the INES scale.

abschnitte.text: The Chernobyl nuclear power station is in the north of present-day **Ukraine**, near the border with Belarus. During the night of 25 to 26 April 1986 a safety test was being carried out in **Unit 4**. During the test the reactor got out of control and exploded. It was of the **RBMK** type, a Soviet design with dangerous construction faults. At low power this reactor was particularly unstable.

Very close by was **Pripyat**, a town for the power station’s workers with about 49,000 inhabitants. It was evacuated the day after the accident and is still abandoned today. A large **exclusion zone** was set up around the power station. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, firefighters and workers cleaned up and contained the radiation. They are known as **liquidators**, and many of them received high doses of radiation.

In the first few days the Soviet leadership kept quiet about how serious it was. Even the May Day celebrations in Kyiv went ahead. On 28 April the measuring instruments at the Swedish nuclear power station **Forsmark** raised the alarm. That is how the world found out about the accident. The disaster showed how much more openness was needed and strengthened the policy of **glasnost** under Mikhail Gorbachev.

The wind carried a radioactive cloud over large parts of Europe. When it passed over Switzerland, it rained particularly heavily in **Ticino**. That is why the most radioactivity reached the ground there. On the international rating scale **INES**, which goes from 0 to 7, Chernobyl was given the highest level, 7. Today a huge protective steel shell stands over the destroyed reactor.

gewusst: The new protective shell over the reactor was built next to the building and then slid over it on rails.
Today many wild animals such as wolves and wild horses live in the abandoned exclusion zone.

teile.einleitung: When the Soviet Union launched the first satellite into space in October 1957, the West was alarmed. This fright is called the Sputnik shock or Sputnik crisis. It changed politics, the military and schools in the USA.
wichtigste: Sputnik 1 was launched on the R-7, the world’s first intercontinental missile.
The chief designer was Sergei Korolev, and his name was kept secret for a long time.
Many people in the West feared a “missile gap”.
A failed American launch in December 1957 was mocked as “Flopnik”.
In 1958 the USA founded NASA.
With a law passed in 1958 the USA promoted maths and science.

abschnitte.titel: Why the fright was so great
abschnitte.text: Sputnik 1 was launched from the **Baikonur** cosmodrome in what is now Kazakhstan. The rocket was an **R-7**, the world’s first **intercontinental missile**. A missile like this can fly from one continent to another. So it could also have carried **nuclear warheads** as far as the USA. That is why many people in the West became afraid.

The Soviet rocket programme was led by **Sergei Korolev**. He was the chief designer, but his name was kept secret during his lifetime. The world knew him only as the “Chief Designer”. Korolev was also behind **Yuri Gagarin’s** flight in 1961. Gagarin was the first person in space and was also launched from Baikonur.

After Sputnik many people believed that the Soviet Union had many more nuclear missiles. This catchphrase was called the **missile gap**. Later it turned out that the USA actually had more missiles. In December 1957 an American **Vanguard rocket** exploded in front of the cameras shortly after lift-off. The press made fun of the “**Flopnik**”.

The president at that time was **Dwight D. Eisenhower**, from 1953 to 1961. Critics accused his government of having neglected space travel. In 1958 the USA founded the space agency **NASA**. It was meant to bring all efforts together and catch up with the Soviet Union. This is how the **space race** began, reaching a high point in 1969 with the first American Moon landing.

Many people thought that the Soviet Union was training more and better engineers. In 1958 Congress therefore passed the **National Defense Education Act**. More than a billion dollars flowed into schools, grants and universities. **Maths** and **science** received particular support. People speak of an **education drive**.

gewusst: Sergei Korolev’s name only became publicly known after his death.
Both Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin were launched from Baikonur.

teile.einleitung: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the communist states of Eastern Europe under the leadership of the Soviet Union. It was founded in 1955 and lasted until 1991. In the Cold War it was the counterpart to NATO, the alliance of the Western states.
wichtigste: The Warsaw Pact was founded in Warsaw on 14 May 1955.
Its members were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, the GDR and Albania.
It was the response to West Germany joining NATO.
The Soviet Union called the shots in the alliance.
In 1968 troops of the Pact invaded Czechoslovakia.
On 1 July 1991 the Warsaw Pact was dissolved.

abschnitte.text: The **Warsaw Pact** was a **military alliance**: its members promised to defend one another if one of them was attacked. Its official name was the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. It was signed in Warsaw, the capital of Poland, hence the name. Supreme command over the joint troops was always held by a Soviet general.

The founding members were the **Soviet Union**, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Albania. The **GDR** also belonged; its army was integrated in 1956. Albania withdrew after a dispute with the Soviet Union and officially left in 1968. Hungary wanted to leave in 1956, but the uprising was crushed.

**NATO** had been founded in 1949 by the USA, Canada and Western European countries. When the Federal Republic of Germany joined NATO in 1955, the Soviet Union founded the Warsaw Pact in response. Both alliances built up huge arsenals during the **Cold War**, including nuclear weapons. But there was never a direct war between them.

The Pact’s troops were never used against the West, but they were used against the Pact’s own members. In August 1968 they ended the **Prague Spring** in Czechoslovakia. The Soviet Union justified this with the Brezhnev Doctrine. It said that socialist countries were only allowed to decide their own path to a limited extent.

After the peaceful revolutions of 1989 the countries of Eastern Europe wanted to decide for themselves. On 1 July 1991 the Warsaw Pact was officially dissolved, and a few months later the Soviet Union also broke apart. Today almost all the former members in Eastern Europe are themselves members of **NATO** and the European Union. Switzerland remained **neutral** throughout the Cold War and belonged to neither alliance.

begriffe.erklaerung: An agreement between states to help one another militarily.
The Western defence alliance, which includes the USA and many European countries.
The communist states of Eastern Europe under the influence of the Soviet Union.
The rule that the Soviet Union was allowed to intervene in socialist countries.

gewusst: Romania was a member but refused to take part in the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.
The GDR’s army did not take part directly in the invasion in 1968, but it stood ready.
The Warsaw Pact lasted exactly 36 years.

teile.einleitung: Mao Zedong was the founder of the People's Republic of China and its most powerful ruler from 1949 until his death in 1976. He led the Communists to victory in the civil war. His policies brought China great changes, but also famines and much suffering.
wichtigste: Mao Zedong was born in 1893 in Shaoshan in Hunan province.
In 1921 he was one of the founders of the Communist Party of China.
He led the Communists on the Long March in 1934 and 1935.
On 1 October 1949 he proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing.
His “Great Leap Forward” led to a famine in which many millions died.
In 1966 he started the Cultural Revolution.
He died in Beijing on 9 September 1976.

abschnitte.text: Mao was born on 26 December 1893 into a farming family in **Shaoshan**. He went to a teacher training school and later worked in a library in Beijing. There he got to know the ideas of Karl Marx. In 1921 he was present at the founding of the Communist Party of China in Shanghai.

The Communists were fighting against the **Kuomintang** government under Chiang Kai-shek. In 1934 they had to flee and covered about 10,000 kilometres on the **Long March**. Only a small part of the soldiers arrived. During this march, Mao became the party's most important leader.

After victory in the civil war, on 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the **People's Republic of China** at the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with his followers. Mao had landowners' property taken away and companies nationalised. Opponents were harshly persecuted, and many died.

From 1958, with the **Great Leap Forward**, Mao wanted to turn China into an industrial country within a few years. The peasants had to work in people's communes and even produce steel in small furnaces. The result was a famine in which many millions died. In 1966 he started the **Cultural Revolution**, which brought ten years of violence and chaos.

Mao died on 9 September 1976, and his body lies in a mausoleum in Beijing. In China he is still officially revered today, and his picture is on all yuan banknotes. The party says his achievements outweigh his mistakes. Many historians, on the other hand, see him as a dictator under whose rule a great many people died.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official name of today's Chinese state since 1949.
The nationalist party that Mao fought against in the civil war.
A large tomb building for a famous person.
Mao's plan from 1958 to industrialise China very quickly.

gewusst: In Western books his name is often also written “Mao Tse-tung”.
Mao's portrait on the Gate of Heavenly Peace is about six metres high.

teile.einleitung: Red Square is the most famous square in Moscow, the capital of Russia. It lies right next to the Kremlin. Around the square stand well-known buildings such as the colourful St Basil’s Cathedral.
wichtigste: Red Square lies in the middle of Moscow next to the Kremlin.
In old Russian, “red” also meant “beautiful”.
St Basil’s Cathedral has colourful onion domes.
Lenin’s body lies in the mausoleum on the square.
The Victory Parade usually takes place on 9 May.
Since 1990 Red Square and the Kremlin have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Many people think the name comes from the red colour of the walls or from communism. But the name is older. The Russian word “**krasnaya**” used to mean “**beautiful**” as well. So Red Square was originally the “beautiful square”. It is very large and paved with cobblestones. On one side stands the red wall of the **Kremlin**, where the government has its seat.

At the end of the square stands **St Basil’s Cathedral**. It was built almost 500 years ago. Its towers are painted in bright colours and have domes that are round at the bottom and pointed at the top. They are called **onion domes** because they look like onions. The church is a landmark of Moscow and of the whole of Russia.

The **Lenin Mausoleum** stands by the Kremlin wall. Lenin founded the world’s first communist state. After his death in 1924 his body was embalmed and put on display. Opposite stands **GUM**, a long department store with glass roofs. It was built more than 100 years ago and has many small shops.

Big celebrations take place in Red Square. On **9 May** Russia commemorates the end of the Second World War in Europe. Then soldiers and tanks move across the square in the **Victory Parade**. In winter there is sometimes an ice rink. Since 1990 Red Square and the Kremlin have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. This is meant to give them special protection.

gewusst: Red Square is about 330 metres long, as long as three football pitches in a row.
In Russian the name Kremlin means something like “castle” or “fortress”.

teile.einleitung: During the First World War, the Russian revolutionary Lenin lived in exile in Switzerland. From February 1916 to April 1917 he lived in Zurich's old town. In 1917 he travelled back to Russia from Zurich, where he soon took power.
wichtigste: Lenin came to Switzerland after the outbreak of war in 1914 and lived first in Bern.
In 1915 he took part in the Zimmerwald Conference.
From February 1916 he lived at Spiegelgasse 14 in Zurich.
He lived there with his wife Nadezhda Krupskaya.
He read and wrote a great deal in Zurich's libraries.
In 1916 he completed his work on imperialism.
Fritz Platten helped him organise his journey back to Russia.

abschnitte.text: **Lenin** was an opponent of the Russian Tsar and therefore had to live in **exile**, that is outside his homeland. After the start of the **First World War in 1914**, he came to neutral Switzerland from Austria-Hungary. At first he lived in **Bern**. In September **1915** he took part in the **Zimmerwald Conference** near Bern. Socialist opponents of the war met there, and Lenin represented the most radical group.

In **February 1916**, Lenin moved to **Zurich**. He lived in the house at **Spiegelgasse 14** in the old town, together with his wife **Nadezhda Krupskaya**. She was also his close colleague. The flat was small and simple. Today a **plaque** on the house commemorates Lenin's time in Zurich.

In Zurich, Lenin spent many hours in **libraries**. He read a lot and wrote articles and books. In **1916** he completed the work **“Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism”**. In it he explained the First World War as the result of the great powers' struggle for **markets** and **colonies**.

Just a few doors away, in February 1916, **Hugo Ball** opened the **Cabaret Voltaire** at Spiegelgasse 1. That is where the art movement **Dada** began. The Dadaists made crazy poems and performances against the war and against old rules. Whether Lenin himself ever went there has not been reliably proved.

In spring **1917**, the Tsar was overthrown in Russia. Lenin wanted to go back immediately. The Zurich socialist **Fritz Platten** negotiated with the German legation in Bern about a journey through **Germany**. In **April 1917** Lenin and other revolutionaries left Zurich by train. Platten accompanied the travellers through Germany.

gewusst: The Cabaret Voltaire still exists today on the Spiegelgasse in Zurich.
Lenin's train through Germany is often called the “sealed train”, because the travellers were not supposed to have any contact with Germans on the way.

teile.einleitung: In 1948 a dispute broke out between the Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin. Yugoslavia remained communist, but went its own way outside the Eastern Bloc.
wichtigste: On 28 June 1948 Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform.
After that the Cominform’s headquarters moved from Belgrade to Bucharest.
Supposed supporters of Stalin were sent to the prison camp on Goli Otok.
From 1950 Yugoslavia introduced workers’ self-management.
From 1949 the West supported Yugoslavia with loans and weapons.
In 1955 Khrushchev made peace with Tito in Belgrade.

abschnitte.text: Tito and his **partisans** had largely freed Yugoslavia from the German occupation by themselves. That is why he did not want to be told what to do by Moscow in everything. On top of this there was his plan for a **Balkan federation** with Bulgaria, which he was pursuing with **Georgi Dimitrov**. Stalin saw this as a threat to his control. On **28 June 1948** the **Cominform**, the Communist Information Bureau, expelled the Yugoslav communists.

Until then the Cominform had had its headquarters in **Belgrade**. After the expulsion it moved to **Bucharest**. In Yugoslavia Tito had supposed supporters of Stalin persecuted. From 1949 thousands of so-called “**Cominformists**” were held in a prison camp on the bare Adriatic island of **Goli Otok**. Conditions there were very harsh.

Yugoslavia wanted to set itself apart from the Soviet system. From 1950 it introduced **workers’ self-management**. Under this system **workers’ councils** were to help run the businesses. This distinguished Yugoslavia from the central **planned economy** of the Soviet Union. To keep the country away from the Eastern Bloc, the **USA** and other Western states helped it from 1949 with loans and weapons.

After Stalin’s death **Nikita Khrushchev** travelled to Belgrade in 1955. In the **Belgrade Declaration** the Soviet Union recognised that there could be different paths to socialism. Even so, Yugoslavia did not join either bloc. In 1961 in Belgrade, Tito founded the **Non-Aligned Movement** together with **Nehru** of India, **Nasser** of Egypt and others. It wanted to join neither the West nor the East.

gewusst: Yugoslavia was the first communist country to break openly with Stalin and still remain communist.
Goli Otok means “naked island”, because hardly anything grows there.

teile.einleitung: In December 1979 Soviet troops marched into Afghanistan. They wanted to prop up the communist government in Kabul. This turned into a war lasting almost ten years, which only ended in 1989 when the troops withdrew.
wichtigste: The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan at the end of December 1979.
The decision was taken by the leadership under Leonid Brezhnev.
The mujahideen fought against the Soviet troops.
From 1986 the USA supplied Stinger missiles to the fighters.
The withdrawal agreements were signed in Geneva in 1988.
On 15 February 1989 the last Soviet soldiers left the country.

abschnitte.text: Since 1978 Afghanistan had been ruled by a **communist party**. Its reforms met with resistance from many people, and there were uprisings all over the country. The Soviet Union feared losing its ally. Under **Leonid Brezhnev**, who led the country from 1964 to 1982, the decision to intervene was taken. At the end of **December 1979** Soviet troops moved into Afghanistan.

The **mujahideen** fought against the Soviet troops. These were various groups of resistance fighters. They knew the mountains well and often attacked by surprise. They were supported by, among others, the **USA** and **Pakistan**. From 1986 the USA supplied **Stinger missiles**. These anti-aircraft missiles were fired from the shoulder and made flying very dangerous for the Soviet **helicopters**.

The war hit the civilian population above all. Many villages were destroyed. **Several million** Afghans fled their homes. Most found refuge in the neighbouring countries of **Pakistan** and **Iran**. There they often lived for years in large refugee camps.

abschnitte.titel: The Geneva Accords and the withdrawal
abschnitte.text: In 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** took over the leadership of the Soviet Union. He thought the war was hopeless. In **April 1988** agreements on the withdrawal of the Soviet troops were signed in **Geneva**. This made Switzerland the place of important negotiations. On **15 February 1989** the last Soviet soldiers left Afghanistan. The war had lasted almost ten years.

gewusst: The war is sometimes called the “Soviet Union’s Vietnam”, because a superpower could not win it.
The negotiations in Geneva took place with the United Nations acting as mediator.

teile.einleitung: The Truman Doctrine was a promise made by the USA in 1947. President Harry S. Truman announced that the USA would support countries resisting communist pressure. It is regarded as one of the starting points of the Cold War.
wichtigste: Truman announced the doctrine to the US Congress on 12 March 1947.
Greece and Turkey were to receive help first.
Congress approved 400 million dollars for this.
The doctrine put the idea of containment into practice.
The diplomat George F. Kennan is regarded as the mastermind of this policy.
What was promised was mainly economic and military aid.

abschnitte.text: On **12 March 1947** President **Harry S. Truman** spoke to both houses of the **US Congress**. Congress had to approve the money for the planned aid. Truman promised support for **free peoples** who were resisting subjugation by armed minorities or pressure from outside. What he mainly had in mind was **communist influence**. These principles are called the **Truman Doctrine**.

The first aid went to **Greece** and **Turkey**. In Greece a **civil war** was raging: from 1946 to 1949 the government fought against communist-led partisans. Turkey was being put under pressure by the Soviet Union. Until then Great Britain had helped, but it could no longer afford to. In May 1947 Congress approved **400 million dollars** for military and economic aid.

Behind the doctrine lay the idea of **containment**. The influence of the Soviet Union was not to grow any further. In 1946 the diplomat **George F. Kennan** wrote his famous “**Long Telegram**” about this from Moscow. His thoughts became the basis of this policy. The USA supplied money, weapons and advisers to governments it wanted to support.

Shortly after the Truman Doctrine, in June 1947, the USA announced the **Marshall Plan**. It was meant to help Europe rebuild after the war. To distribute the aid, the **OEEC** was set up in 1948, and **Switzerland** was a member from the start. The Soviet Union rejected the plan. Europe divided more and more clearly into a western and an eastern bloc.

gewusst: Kennan’s telegram from Moscow was so long that it was called the “Long Telegram”.
The Truman Doctrine did not apply only to Europe, but was later applied worldwide.

teile.einleitung: During the Cold War the USA and the Soviet Union competed to see who would be ahead in space. This contest is called the Space Race. It began in 1957 with the first satellite and reached its high point in 1969 with the first Moon landing.
wichtigste: In 1957 the Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite into space, Sputnik 1.
In 1961 the Soviet citizen Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space.
In the same year US President John F. Kennedy set the goal of putting people on the Moon.
In 1959 the Soviet probe Luna 2 became the first object to hit the Moon, and in 1966 Luna 9 made a soft landing.
In July 1969, with Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon.
By 1972 a total of 12 astronauts had walked on the Moon.
In 1972 Apollo 17 was the last crewed Moon landing so far (as of 2026).

abschnitte.titel: The Soviet Union takes the lead
abschnitte.text: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put the satellite **Sputnik 1** into orbit around the Earth. In the USA people were greatly alarmed. In 1959 the probe **Luna 2** became the first human-made object to hit the Moon. On 12 April 1961 **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to orbit the Earth. For a long time the Soviet Union was ahead in the race.

On 25 May 1961 US President **John F. Kennedy** announced a big goal to Congress: before the end of the decade, people were to land on the Moon and return safely. To achieve this, the space agency **NASA** started the **Apollo programme**. Thousands of experts worked on it. But the Soviet Union remained strong: in 1966 **Luna 9** made the first soft landing on the Moon and radioed back the first photos of the surface.

In 1967 a fire broke out in the capsule of **Apollo 1** during a test on the ground. Three astronauts lost their lives. After that the spacecraft was built more safely. In December 1968 **Apollo 8** circled the Moon with three astronauts on board, without landing. The crew were the first people to see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes.

In July 1969 the lunar module of **Apollo 11** touched down on the Moon. **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to step onto the Moon, followed shortly afterwards by **Buzz Aldrin**. Michael Collins waited in the spacecraft in orbit around the Moon. With that the USA had won the race to the Moon. By 1972 six Apollo missions had landed, each with two astronauts, so **12 people** in total. The series ended with **Apollo 17** in December 1972.

Switzerland has also left traces on the Moon. Researchers at the **University of Bern** developed a **solar wind sail**. This was a thin sheet of foil that caught particles from the Sun. The Apollo 11 astronauts set up the sail as one of their first experiments. Later it was brought back to Earth and examined in Bern.

gewusst: The University of Bern’s solar wind sail was set up on the Moon even before the American flag.
No one has walked on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972 (as of 2026).
In 1975 an American and a Soviet spacecraft met in space, and the crews shook hands.

teile.einleitung: The Moscow Trials were three large show trials in the Soviet Union between 1936 and 1938. In them, Stalin had former companions of Lenin convicted of invented crimes. The trials belong to the period of the “Great Terror”.
wichtigste: There were three big Moscow Trials: in 1936, 1937 and 1938.
The first trial was directed against Zinoviev and Kamenev.
The prosecutor was the Prosecutor General Andrey Vyshinsky.
The accusations of a conspiracy with Trotsky were invented.
The verdicts were based almost entirely on forced confessions.
Most of the accused were sentenced to death and shot.

abschnitte.text: On 1 December 1934 **Sergei Kirov**, the party leader of Leningrad, was shot dead. Stalin used this murder as a pretext to take action against real and supposed opponents. The crime was blamed on opposition members within the party. In the following years a great many people were arrested. This period is known as the **Great Terror**.

A **show trial** is a court case whose verdict has been decided in advance. In August 1936 **Grigory Zinoviev** and **Lev Kamenev** stood trial along with 14 other defendants. A second trial followed in 1937 and a third in 1938, among others against **Nikolai Bukharin**. In the dock there was also the former secret police chief **Genrikh Yagoda**, who had himself prepared the first trial. Each time the prosecutor was **Andrey Vyshinsky**.

The prosecution claimed that the defendants had plotted attacks and sabotage with **Leon Trotsky**, who had been exiled abroad, and with foreign secret services. There was hardly any evidence. The verdicts were based almost entirely on **confessions**. These were forced out of people under heavy pressure, for example through threats against their relatives. Many of the defendants were old revolutionaries who had once worked closely with Lenin.

In 1937, in Mexico, the **Dewey Commission** led by the American philosopher John Dewey examined the accusations against Trotsky. It declared him innocent and called the trials frauds. The writer **Arthur Koestler** wrote about the trials in 1940 in the novel **“Darkness at Noon”**. In it, an old revolutionary confesses to crimes he never committed. The book helped people in the West to understand how such confessions came about.

gewusst: Genrikh Yagoda prepared the first trial and was himself convicted two years later.
In the Soviet Union many of those convicted were only officially declared innocent decades later.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Điện Biên Phủ took place in Vietnam in 1954. There the Vietnamese independence movement Việt Minh defeated the French colonial army. Afterwards the future of Indochina was decided at a conference in Geneva.
wichtigste: The battle lasted from 13 March to 7 May 1954.
The Việt Minh were led by General Võ Nguyên Giáp.
The French garrison was commanded by Christian de Castries.
The Việt Minh brought guns up onto the hills around the valley.
At the Indochina Conference in Geneva, Vietnam was provisionally divided.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia belonged to the French colony of **Indochina**. After the Second World War the communist-led **Việt Minh** fought for Vietnam’s independence. This led to the **Indochina War**. The French built a large base in the valley of Điện Biên Phủ in north-western Vietnam. From there they wanted to lure their opponents into a decisive battle.

abschnitte.titel: The trap in the valley basin
abschnitte.text: The base lay in a **valley basin** with hills all around. The French did not believe that the Việt Minh could bring heavy weapons there. But General **Võ Nguyên Giáp** had **guns** laboriously hauled up onto the surrounding hills. This allowed him to shell the **airstrip** and the positions. Supplies could now only come by air and soon were no longer enough.

The battle began on **13 March 1954**. The commander of the surrounded garrison was **Christian de Castries**. His superior, the commander-in-chief in Indochina, was Henri Navarre. After almost two months of hard fighting, the French garrison had to surrender on **7 May 1954**. The victory made Giáp one of the best-known strategists of the 20th century.

Even during the battle, representatives of several states met in **Geneva**. At the **Indochina Conference** of 1954, Vietnam was provisionally divided at the **17th parallel**. The North became communist, and the South was supported by the West. In this way Switzerland hosted an important meeting of the **Cold War**. For France the outcome meant the end of its rule in Indochina.

gewusst: Many of the Việt Minh’s guns were taken apart and carried through the jungle by people and on bicycles.
The defeat was so serious for France that the government in Paris resigned shortly afterwards.

teile.einleitung: The Red Army was the army of Soviet Russia and later of the Soviet Union. It was founded by the Bolsheviks in 1918 and fought in the Russian Civil War and in the Second World War. In 1946 it was renamed the Soviet Army.
wichtigste: The Red Army was founded at the beginning of 1918 as the Workers’ and Peasants’ Red Army.
Leon Trotsky built it up as People’s Commissar for Military Affairs.
Its badge was the red five-pointed star.
Political commissars made sure that officers stayed loyal to the party.
In 1920 it was defeated by Poland outside Warsaw.
In 1946 it was renamed the Soviet Army.

abschnitte.text: After the **October Revolution** of 1917 the tsar’s old army fell apart. The **Bolsheviks** needed troops of their own to secure their power. At the beginning of 1918 they founded the **Workers’ and Peasants’ Red Army**. Its emblem became the **red five-pointed star** on the cap. It later became a symbol of the whole Soviet Union.

**Leon Trotsky** was People’s Commissar for Military Affairs, a kind of defence minister. He turned volunteer units into a large, tightly led army. In doing so he travelled from front to front in an armoured train. Because experienced people were lacking, thousands of **officers of the old tsarist army** were brought in as “military specialists”. To make sure they stayed loyal, every commander had a **political commissar** from the party at his side.

abschnitte.titel: Civil war and war with Poland
abschnitte.text: In the **Russian Civil War** the Red Army fought against the “Whites” and won. The **First Cavalry Army** under Semyon Budyonny was famous. The soldiers’ pointed cloth cap was named the “budyonovka” after him. In 1920 the Red Army fought in the **Polish-Soviet War**. Outside Warsaw it was driven back by the Polish army in the Battle of the Vistula.

abschnitte.titel: From world war to Soviet Army
abschnitte.text: In the **Second World War** the Red Army bore the main burden of the fight against Germany in the East. It suffered huge losses but in the end pushed forward as far as **Berlin**. In 1946 it was renamed the **Soviet Army**. Under this name it existed until the end of the Soviet Union in 1991.

gewusst: The name “budyonovka” for the pointed cap recalls the cavalry general Semyon Budyonny.
Among other things, Trotsky’s armoured train had its own printing press on board.

teile.einleitung: Absolutism is the name for a form of rule in which a king or queen governs with unlimited power. The ruler stands above the law and does not have to ask anyone’s permission. In Europe absolutism was widespread above all in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the best-known example is King Louis XIV of France.
wichtigste: Under absolutism the monarch has all the power in the state.
He makes the laws, governs and is the highest judge at the same time.
The power was often justified by the divine right of kings, the belief that God had appointed the king.
The best-known example is Louis XIV, the “Sun King” of France.
With the French Revolution of 1789 the end of absolutism began.
A few countries, such as Saudi Arabia, are still absolute monarchies today.

abschnitte.text: The term comes from the Latin word absolutus, which means “released” or “detached”. It refers to a ruler who is released from all laws and checks. In an **absolute monarchy** there is no parliament with a say, or it is not called together. There is also no **separation of powers** as we know it today.

**Louis XIV** ruled France from 1643 to 1715, so for 72 years. He had himself portrayed as the **Sun King**, around whom everything revolves like the planets around the Sun. The sentence “I am the state” is attributed to him, although it is uncertain whether he really said it. He had the magnificent **Palace of Versailles** built, where the nobility had to live under his watchful eye.

The king relied on a **standing army**, in other words an army that was always ready. Officials collected taxes and enforced his orders throughout the country. To have plenty of money for wars and buildings, the state promoted trade and manufactories; this is called **mercantilism**. The ordinary farmers had to pay high dues for it.

In the 18th century thinkers of the **Enlightenment** spread the idea that people are born free and equal. Some rulers, such as Frederick II of Prussia or Joseph II of Austria, adopted parts of these ideas. Frederick II called himself the “first servant of the state” and, for example, largely abolished torture. But even these rulers did not give up their power.

With the **French Revolution** of 1789 people demanded liberty, equality and a say in government. There was no king in Switzerland, but in towns such as Bern a few rich families, the patricians, ruled at that time. Today Switzerland is regarded as the opposite of absolutism, because the people can have a direct say through votes. Only a few absolute monarchies remain, such as Saudi Arabia, Brunei, Eswatini and Vatican City.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of state headed by a king, a queen or a prince.
The idea that the king received his power directly from God.
Dividing power between parliament, government and the courts.
An economic policy that was meant to bring as much money as possible into the country.

gewusst: Louis XIV became king at the age of only four, so at first his mother ruled for him with a minister.
At the Palace of Versailles the court even watched when the king got up and dressed in the morning.
Louis XIV reigned for 72 years, longer than any other king in European history.

teile.einleitung: The Ministry for State Security, known as the Stasi for short, was the secret police and intelligence service of the GDR (East Germany). It spied on its own citizens and persecuted anyone who criticised the state. The Stasi was feared because it had informers almost everywhere.
wichtigste: The Stasi was the feared secret police of the GDR.
It was founded on 8 February 1950.
It called itself the “shield and sword of the Party”.
In 1989 it had about 91,000 full-time staff.
On top of that there were almost 190,000 unofficial collaborators, in other words informers.
Erich Mielke was its minister from 1957 to 1989.
Today people who were affected can read their Stasi files.

abschnitte.text: The Stasi was a **secret police**, an intelligence service and an investigating authority all at once. Its job was to protect the rule of the SED party. To do this, it watched people who were seen as opponents, but also completely ordinary citizens. Its headquarters were in Berlin-Lichtenberg on Normannenstrasse.

The Stasi tapped telephones, opened letters and hid cameras and microphones in people’s homes. Particularly important were the **unofficial collaborators**, or IM for short.
