These were neighbours, friends, workmates and sometimes even family members who secretly reported on others. The Stasi kept **files** on millions of people.

Anyone who criticised the GDR, wanted to flee or was active in churches and environmental groups was often persecuted. The Stasi arrested people and interrogated them in its own prisons, for example in **Hohenschönhausen** in Berlin. It also secretly destroyed careers and friendships to make people feel insecure. It called this method “Zersetzung”, meaning “decomposition”.

In the autumn of 1989 people also protested against the Stasi. When Stasi officers began to destroy files, citizens occupied the offices from December 1989 onwards. On 15 January 1990 demonstrators stormed the headquarters in Berlin. In this way many files were saved, and the Stasi was dissolved.

Since 1992 people have been able to read what the Stasi had collected about them. Many found out in this way who had been spying on them. Since 2021 the files have belonged to the **Federal Archives**; their shelves would stretch more than 100 kilometres if placed end to end. The former headquarters is now the **Stasi Museum**, and the Hohenschönhausen prison is a memorial.

begriffe.erklaerung: A police force that works in secret and persecutes political opponents.
A person who secretly spied on others for the Stasi.
A collection of papers about a person or a matter.
The ruling party of the GDR, which governed on its own.

gewusst: The Stasi even collected people’s smell samples in sealed jars so that sniffer dogs could track them down.
To this day, experts are piecing together torn Stasi files from thousands of sacks.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Party of Labour, PdA for short, is a communist party. It was founded in Basel in 1944. In French-speaking Switzerland it sometimes appears under the name POP.
wichtigste: The PdA was founded in Basel on 21 May 1944.
It is the successor to the Communist Party of Switzerland, which was banned in 1940.
Its first president was Léon Nicole from Geneva.
In 1947 it won seven seats in the National Council, its best result.
Its German-language newspaper is called “Vorwärts”.
Its strongholds are Le Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds.

abschnitte.text: During the Second World War, in November 1940, the **Federal Council** banned the **Communist Party of Switzerland**, KPS for short. Other left-wing groups were banned too. On 21 May 1944 communists and left-wing socialists founded a new party in **Basel**, the **Party of Labour**. Its first president was **Léon Nicole** from Geneva. He had previously been a member of the Geneva cantonal government as a Social Democrat.

In the **1947 National Council elections** the PdA won 5.1 per cent of the vote and **seven seats**. That was its best result. With the start of the **Cold War** its share then fell sharply. Many people in Switzerland distrusted the communists because they were close to the Soviet Union. Since then the PdA has been a small party.

In the cantons of **Neuchâtel**, **Vaud** and **Jura** the party is called the **Parti ouvrier populaire**, POP for short. In French its national name is Parti suisse du Travail. It is particularly well rooted in the watchmaking towns of **Le Locle** and **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. There has long been a strong working class there. In some towns the party is also represented in municipal and cantonal parliaments.

The PdA’s German-language newspaper is called **“Vorwärts”** (Forward). It reports on politics and the world of work from the party’s point of view. Other left-wing newspapers such as the “Volksrecht” or the “Berner Tagwacht”, on the other hand, belonged to the Social Democrats. According to its own statements, the PdA campaigns for workers, lower rents and a strong welfare state. Today it plays a small role in Swiss politics.

gewusst: When it was founded, the PdA attracted so many supporters that only three years later it had seven members of the National Council.
Because of their watchmaking industry, Le Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Apartheid was the separation of people by skin colour ordered by the state in South Africa. From 1948 until the beginning of the 1990s a white minority ruled over the black majority.
wichtigste: “Apartheid” means something like “separateness” in Afrikaans.
From 1948 the National Party made apartheid state policy.
Black people were not allowed to vote in national elections.
Many black people were resettled in so-called homelands.
In 1990 President Frederik Willem de Klerk released Nelson Mandela.
In 1994 all adults were allowed to vote for the first time.

abschnitte.text: After the election victory of the **National Party** under Daniel François Malan in 1948, the **apartheid laws** were introduced step by step. Every person was officially assigned to a group, such as “white” or “black”. Schools, buses, hospitals, beaches and residential areas were separated. Black people had to carry a pass with them and were not allowed to live freely wherever they wanted.

The government created so-called **homelands**, also called **Bantustans**. They were supposedly separate states for the black population. In reality they were mostly poor, fragmented areas without real independence. Many people were resettled there against their will and as a result lost their rights as citizens of South Africa.

The main force fighting against apartheid was the **African National Congress** (ANC). The government banned it in 1960, and Nelson Mandela was sentenced to life imprisonment. On 16 June 1976, in **Soweto**, thousands of school pupils protested against Afrikaans as the language of teaching. The police fired on them, and many young people died. Criticism grew worldwide, and many states imposed sanctions.

From 1990 President **Frederik Willem de Klerk** set change in motion. He lifted the ban on the ANC and released **Nelson Mandela** after 27 years in prison. In April 1994 all adults were allowed to vote for the first time, regardless of their skin colour. Mandela became South Africa’s first black president.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: The **Truth and Reconciliation Commission** under Archbishop **Desmond Tutu** heard victims and perpetrators. Anyone who told the whole truth about their deeds could, under certain conditions, be granted immunity from punishment. In this way the country was to find peace without forgetting the crimes. In Switzerland, too, there was later debate about the business that Swiss companies and banks had done with the apartheid state.

gewusst: Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.
In the 1994 election people queued outside the polling stations in lines kilometres long.
Today 16 June is a public holiday in South Africa, Youth Day.

teile.einleitung: Unidad Popular, which means “Popular Unity”, was an alliance of left-wing parties in Chile. With its candidate Salvador Allende it won the presidential election in 1970. Its government ended in 1973 with a military coup.
wichtigste: Salvador Allende became president in 1970 as the candidate of Unidad Popular.
He received about 36 per cent of the vote, and Congress confirmed him.
The aim was a “Chilean road to socialism” through elections and laws.
In 1971 copper mining was nationalised.
Strikes and very high inflation led to a severe crisis.
On 11 September 1973 the army under Augusto Pinochet staged a coup.

abschnitte.text: In **Unidad Popular**, socialists, communists and other left-wing groups joined together. In the 1970 election its candidate **Salvador Allende** won about **36 per cent** of the vote. That was a little more than a third and was just enough for first place. Because nobody had an absolute majority, **Congress** decided. It confirmed Allende as president.

Allende was regarded as the first freely elected **Marxist** president in Latin America. He did not want to introduce socialism through an armed revolution. Instead it was to come through **elections and laws**. This was called the **Chilean road to socialism**. Supporters saw it as a fair path, while opponents feared for property and freedom.

**Copper** was Chile’s most important raw material. In 1971 Congress decided **unanimously** to **nationalise** the big copper mines. The US companies whose property was taken received hardly any compensation. Soon the economy fell into a crisis. In 1973 **inflation**, in other words rising prices, reached several hundred per cent. There were empty shops and black markets.

The country was deeply divided politically. In October 1972 the **lorry owners** brought transport to a standstill with a nationwide **strike**. This made the supply crisis worse. Other groups also protested against the government. At the same time many workers and poor people continued to stand by Allende.

On **11 September 1973** General **Augusto Pinochet** led a **military coup**. He had only recently become commander-in-chief of the army. Fighter planes bombed the presidential palace, **La Moneda**. Allende died there; investigations later confirmed that he had taken his own life. After that Pinochet ruled Chile as a **dictator** until 1990.

gewusst: In 1971 the nationalisation of copper was also supported by the opposition in Congress.
Unidad Popular means “Popular Unity”.

teile.einleitung: António de Oliveira Salazar ruled Portugal as a dictator from 1932 to 1968. His authoritarian state was called the “Estado Novo”, the New State. He was one of the longest-ruling dictators in Europe.
wichtigste: Salazar was prime minister of Portugal from 1932 to 1968.
Before that he was a professor of economics at the University of Coimbra.
From 1933 his state was called the “Estado Novo”, the New State.
The feared secret police was called the PIDE.
From 1961 Portugal fought colonial wars in Africa.
In the Second World War Portugal remained neutral.

abschnitte.text: **António de Oliveira Salazar** taught **economics** at the University of **Coimbra**. In 1928 he was brought into the government as **finance minister**. He put the state’s finances in order and in this way gained great influence. In 1932 he became **prime minister** of Portugal. He ruled until 1968, which made him one of the longest-ruling dictators in Europe.

In 1933 Portugal was given a new constitution. Salazar’s state was called the “**Estado Novo**”, which means “New State”. It was an **authoritarian state** without free parties and with **censorship**. Its motto was “Deus, Pátria, Família”, meaning “**God, Fatherland, Family**”. It emphasised the Church, the nation and the traditional family. The feared secret police, the **PIDE**, kept watch on the population and persecuted opponents of the regime.

abschnitte.titel: Neutrality in the Second World War
abschnitte.text: In the **Second World War** Portugal remained **neutral** and did not enter the war. The capital, **Lisbon**, became an important port for **refugees**. Many people fleeing the war and persecution travelled on from there to America.

Portugal had colonies in Africa, including **Angola**, **Mozambique** and **Guinea-Bissau**. From **1961** movements there fought for **independence**. Salazar did not want to give up the colonies, and Portugal fought long **colonial wars**. These wars cost the country many lives and a lot of money.

In 1968 Salazar fell off a chair and suffered a **brain haemorrhage**. After that he was no longer able to govern, and **Marcelo Caetano** took over the government. Salazar died in 1970. The Estado Novo lasted until the **Carnation Revolution** on 25 April 1974. At that time officers overthrew the regime almost without bloodshed, and Portugal became a democracy. The PIDE was dissolved.

gewusst: The Carnation Revolution got its name because people put red carnations into the barrels of the soldiers’ rifles.
After the Carnation Revolution, Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau became independent.

teile.einleitung: Alexander Lukashenko has been president of Belarus since 1994. He rules the country in an authoritarian way and without interruption. Critics often call him Europe’s last dictator.
wichtigste: Lukashenko has been president of Belarus since 1994.
The capital of Belarus is Minsk.
Before his political career he ran a sovkhoz, a state farm.
After the election in August 2020 there were mass protests against election fraud.
Belarus is the only country in Europe that still carries out the death penalty.
The secret service is still called the KGB today.

abschnitte.text: **Belarus**, sometimes called **White Russia** in German, lies in Eastern Europe between Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. The capital and largest city is **Minsk**, which lies roughly in the middle of the country. Belarus belonged to the **Soviet Union** and became independent in 1991. The country is closely linked with Russia.

In Soviet times **Alexander Lukashenko** ran a **sovkhoz**, a state farm, in the Shklou district. In 1994 he won the first **presidential election** in Belarus. Since then he has ruled without interruption. He has kept extending his power and still cultivates the image of a down-to-earth farmer. Independent observers have judged many elections in Belarus to be neither free nor fair.

In the election in August 2020 **Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya** stood against Lukashenko after her husband had been arrested. Lukashenko declared himself the winner with about 80 per cent. Hundreds of thousands of people protested against **election fraud**, and many were arrested. Tsikhanouskaya had to flee into **exile** in Lithuania. In 2021 Belarus forced a **Ryanair flight** from Athens to Vilnius to land in Minsk and arrested the journalist **Raman Pratasevich**, a critic of the regime.

In Belarus critics of the government are severely persecuted. As in the days of the Soviet Union, the secret service is called the **KGB**, and it keeps watch on opposition figures. The human rights campaigner **Ales Bialiatski** founded the organisation **Viasna**. He was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 2022 while he was in prison. Belarus is also the only country in Europe that still carries out the **death penalty**, which is one reason why it is not a member of the **Council of Europe**.

gewusst: Lukashenko is the longest-serving head of state in Europe.
Belarus has kept the Soviet name KGB for its secret service.

teile.einleitung: Vietnam is a long, narrow country in South-East Asia. It is governed by a Communist Party. Vietnam is known for its rice fields, its food and Ha Long Bay.
wichtigste: The capital of Vietnam is Hanoi.
The largest city is called Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon.
Vietnam is long and narrow, shaped like an S.
In the Vietnam War the USA fought against North Vietnam; the war ended in 1975.
Rice is the most important food.
Ha Long Bay is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.titel: A country shaped like an S
abschnitte.text: Vietnam stretches a long way along the coast of the South China Sea. On the map its shape is reminiscent of the letter **S**. In the north lies the capital, **Hanoi**. In the south lies the largest city, **Ho Chi Minh City**. It used to be called **Saigon** and was named after the leader **Ho Chi Minh** in 1976.

Vietnam used to be divided into a north and a south. The north was **communist**. The **USA** supported South Vietnam with many soldiers and fought against North Vietnam. In April 1975 the troops from the north captured Saigon. With that the war was over in **1975**, and the country was reunited. Since then Hanoi has been the capital of the whole country.

In Vietnam there are many **rice fields** standing in water. **Rice** is the most important food there. When working in the fields, many people wear a pointed **conical hat** made of woven palm leaves. It protects against sun and rain. Vietnam also grows a great deal of **coffee** and sells it all over the world.

The best-known dish is **pho**, a soup with rice noodles, herbs and often beef. Ramen, on the other hand, comes from Japan. In the north lies **Ha Long Bay**. There almost 2,000 limestone rocks rise out of the sea. The bay is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by many tourists.

gewusst: Vietnam is one of the largest coffee producers in the world.
In Ha Long Bay almost 2,000 rocky islands stand in the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Stalin cult was the excessive worship of the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin. Pictures, songs, place names and prizes celebrated him like a hero, and criticism was forbidden.
wichtigste: A personality cult presents a ruler as infallible.
Propaganda called Stalin the “Father of Nations”.
Opponents were later retouched out of photos.
Many places bore Stalin’s name, for example Stalinabad, today’s Dushanbe.
In art, socialist realism was compulsory.
In 1956 Khrushchev publicly criticised the personality cult in front of the party.

abschnitte.text: In a **personality cult** a leader is presented like a hero or almost like a god. He is regarded as wise, kind and infallible. Criticising him is forbidden and punished. Under Stalin this cult was particularly strong. **Propaganda** celebrated him as the “**Father of Nations**”, who cared for all the people of the Soviet Union.

Songs, poems, paintings and statues praised Stalin. Art had to follow **socialist realism**. It was supposed to show life under socialism in a positive and easily understood way. Common subjects were Stalin and happy workers. From 1941 the **Stalin Prize** was awarded to artists and scientists.

Many towns, streets and factories were named after Stalin. From 1929 to 1961 the capital of Tajikistan was called **Stalinabad**; today it is called **Dushanbe**. The city of Stalingrad is also well known. In East Berlin the **Stalinallee** was built, with grand buildings in the Soviet style. Today it is called Karl-Marx-Allee and Frankfurter Allee.

Anyone who fell out of favour with Stalin was often arrested. After that he also disappeared from history: he was **retouched** out of old photos. Retouching means changing a picture afterwards. A well-known example is the secret police chief **Nikolai Yezhov**. It was meant to look as if he had never been at Stalin’s side.

For Stalin’s **70th birthday** in December 1949 there were celebrations throughout the Eastern Bloc. After Stalin’s death in 1953, **Nikita Khrushchev** gave a speech in 1956 about the personality cult and its consequences. After that **de-Stalinisation** began. Statues were removed and many places were renamed. The Stalin Prize was also given a different name.

gewusst: For Stalin’s 70th birthday, presents arrived in Moscow from many countries.
The Stalinallee in East Berlin was renamed in 1961.

teile.einleitung: From 1949 to 1990 West Berlin was the western part of the divided city of Berlin. The city lay in the middle of the GDR and yet was closely linked with the West. That is why it was often called an “island”.
wichtigste: After the Second World War Berlin was divided into four sectors.
The three western sectors of the USA, Great Britain and France formed West Berlin.
West Berlin was surrounded on all sides by GDR territory.
During the blockade of 1948 and 1949 the “raisin bombers” supplied the city from the air.
From 1961 the Berlin Wall separated West Berlin from East Berlin and the surrounding area.
West Berlin was closely linked with the Federal Republic of Germany and paid with the Deutschmark.
With the fall of the Wall in 1989 and unity in 1990 the division ended.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the Second World War in 1945 the four victorious powers divided Berlin into **sectors**. The Soviet Union administered the East, and the three western sectors belonged to the **USA**, **Great Britain** and **France**. These three sectors became West Berlin. Because Berlin itself lay in the middle of the Soviet zone, West Berlin was surrounded on all sides by territory that belonged to the GDR from 1949. That is why people spoke of an **island** in the East.

In June 1948 the Soviet Union blocked all routes over land and water into West Berlin. This is called the **Berlin Blockade**. The Western powers responded with an **airlift**: for almost a year aircraft brought food, coal and other goods into the city. Some pilots dropped small parachutes with sweets for the children. That is why the Berliners called the planes **raisin bombers**. In May 1949 the blockade was lifted.

Many people fled from the GDR to the West via Berlin. To stop this, the GDR leadership had the **Berlin Wall** built on **13 August 1961**. Families and friends were suddenly separated. People from West Berlin could still travel to many countries, including Switzerland. People from East Berlin, on the other hand, were usually only allowed to travel to other Eastern Bloc countries. Only on **9 November 1989** did the Wall open.

Several US presidents showed through their visits that they stood by West Berlin. In June 1963 **John F. Kennedy** said in front of a huge crowd: “Ich bin ein Berliner” (I am a Berliner). In 1987 **Ronald Reagan** spoke in front of the **Brandenburg Gate**. He called on the Soviet party leader Mikhail Gorbachev to tear down the Wall. Both speeches are still famous today.

abschnitte.titel: Closely linked with the Federal Republic
abschnitte.text: West Berlin had a **special status**: the three Western powers kept supreme authority there until 1990. Even so, the city was closely linked with the **Federal Republic of Germany**. People paid with the **Deutschmark**, and many laws of the Federal Republic also applied here. After German unity on 3 October 1990, West and East Berlin became one city again. Today Berlin is the capital of Germany.

gewusst: At times during the airlift, a plane landed in West Berlin every few minutes.
Because of the special status, young men from West Berlin did not have to do military service in the Bundeswehr.

teile.einleitung: For Karl Marx, the proletariat is the class of workers who do not own any factories or machines of their own. They live by selling their labour for wages. Marx believed that one day the proletariat would change society.
wichtigste: According to Marx, proletarians own nothing but their labour.
The word comes from the Latin “proles”, meaning offspring.
Marx spoke of surplus value and alienation.
Class consciousness means recognising your own situation.
The “dictatorship of the proletariat” was meant as a transition.
The goal was a classless society.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from ancient Rome. **“Proles”** means offspring in Latin. **Proletarians** were citizens whose only wealth was their children. In the 19th century, the time of **industrialisation**, the word took on a new meaning. Now it referred to the workers in the factories.

According to **Karl Marx**, a proletarian owns no factories or machines. He has to sell his **labour** to an employer for wages. According to Marx, workers produce more value than they receive in wages. He called this surplus **surplus value**, and according to his theory the factory owner keeps it. Marx called the class of owners the **bourgeoisie**.

In a factory a worker often makes only a small part of a product that does not belong to him. Marx thought that in this way he became a stranger to his own work. He called this **alienation**. For anything to change, the workers would have to realise that they are all in a similar situation. Marx called this realisation **class consciousness**.

Marx expected that after a revolution the workers would take over the state for a time. He called this transition period the **dictatorship of the proletariat**. After that a **classless society** was to come about, in which the state would no longer be needed. Marx and Engels called the lowest layer of society without regular work the **lumpenproletariat**, and they did not think it would play any revolutionary role. In Switzerland, among other things, the **Factory Act** of 1877 improved the situation of workers.

gewusst: The Communist Manifesto of 1848 ends with the call “Workers of all countries, unite!”.
The Swiss Factory Act of 1877 limited working hours in factories to eleven hours a day.

teile.einleitung: In the Cuban Revolution, Fidel Castro and his fighters overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. On 1 January 1959 Batista fled the country. After that, Cuba became a socialist state and a close ally of the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: Fulgencio Batista had seized power in a coup in 1952.
On 26 July 1953 Castro attacked the Moncada Barracks; the attack failed.
In 1956 Castro and 82 fighters sailed to Cuba on the yacht “Granma”.
The rebels fought a guerrilla war in the Sierra Maestra.
At the end of 1958, under Che Guevara, they captured the city of Santa Clara.
On 1 January 1959 Batista fled Cuba.
From 1960 the USA imposed a trade embargo.

abschnitte.text: **Fulgencio Batista** seized power in Cuba in **1952** through a **coup**. A coup is a violent seizure of power. His regime was corrupt and dealt harshly with opponents. On **26 July 1953**, the young lawyer **Fidel Castro** and a group attacked the **Moncada Barracks** in Santiago de Cuba. The attack failed, but it gave his movement its name, the **26th of July Movement**.

In 1956 Castro and **82 fighters** sailed from **Mexico** to Cuba on the yacht **“Granma”**. The landing cost many lives. The survivors withdrew into the **Sierra Maestra**, a mountain range in eastern Cuba. From there they waged a **guerrilla war**, that is a war fought by small, mobile groups. Little by little their rebel army grew.

One important leader was **Ernesto “Che” Guevara**, a doctor from **Argentina** who had studied medicine in Buenos Aires. He became a **comandante**. At the end of December **1958**, his troops captured the city of **Santa Clara**. This was the turning point. On New Year's Eve Batista fled, and on **1 January 1959** the revolutionaries had won. Che Guevara then headed the national bank and the ministry of industry, among other things.

The new government **nationalised** many companies, including American ones. In response, from 1960 the **USA** imposed a **trade embargo**, most of which still applies today. Cuba turned to the **Soviet Union**. It bought oil from it and sold it sugar. When the Soviet Union collapsed in **1991**, Cuba fell into a severe **economic crisis**.

gewusst: The newspaper of the Communist Party of Cuba is also called “Granma”, after the yacht.
Fidel Castro ruled Cuba for almost 50 years, and then his brother Raúl took over.

teile.einleitung: Nikita Khrushchev was head of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964. After Stalin’s death he criticised Stalin’s crimes and began “de-Stalinisation”. At the same time, in the Cuban Missile Crisis, he brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
wichtigste: Nikita Khrushchev was born in 1894 and died in 1971.
After Stalin’s death in 1953 he became party leader of the Soviet Union.
In 1956 he condemned Stalin’s crimes in a secret speech.
This marked the start of de-Stalinisation, and many prisoners were released.
Under him the first satellite, Sputnik, was launched in 1957.
In 1962 he triggered the Cuban Missile Crisis with missiles on Cuba.
In 1964 he was removed from power by his own party.

abschnitte.text: Khrushchev was born in 1894 in the village of Kalinovka in Russia, near the border with Ukraine. As a boy he herded cows, and later he worked as a metalworker in mines. He joined the Bolsheviks in 1918 and rose through the party under **Stalin**. For a long time he led the party in Moscow and in Ukraine.

After Stalin’s death in March 1953, Khrushchev won through as **First Secretary**. On 25 February 1956, at the 20th Party Congress, he gave a **secret speech**. In it he accused Stalin of persecuting innocent people and creating a personality cult. The audience was shocked, and the speech soon became known abroad too.

The period that followed is called the **Thaw**, because life became somewhat freer. Hundreds of thousands of prisoners were released from the labour camps, and Stalin’s pictures and monuments disappeared. Khrushchev had simple blocks of flats built for families. But he had uprisings, such as the one in Hungary in 1956, crushed by tanks.

In 1957 the Soviet Union sent the first satellite into space, **Sputnik 1**, and in 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space. In 1961 the Berlin Wall was built with Khrushchev’s approval. In 1962 he had nuclear missiles set up on Cuba, which led to the **Cuban Missile Crisis**. After thirteen days he agreed with US President John F. Kennedy to withdraw the missiles.

Many party leaders were unhappy with Khrushchev’s erratic decisions and his failures in agriculture. In October 1964 they removed him, and **Leonid Brezhnev** became his successor. Unlike under Stalin, Khrushchev was not killed but lived as a pensioner near Moscow. He died in 1971, having first written his memoirs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning away from Stalin’s rule of violence and his personality cult.
Khrushchev’s speech of 1956 in which he denounced Stalin’s crimes.
The period after Stalin when life in the Soviet Union became somewhat freer.
An object that circles the Earth in space.

gewusst: In 1954 Khrushchev gave the Crimean peninsula to what was then the Ukrainian Soviet Republic.
On his visit to the USA in 1959 he wanted to visit Disneyland, but was not allowed to for security reasons.

teile.einleitung: The Assad regime is the name for the rule of the Assad family in Syria from 1970 to 2024. First Hafez al-Assad ruled, and then his son Bashar. The regime was known for oppression and serious crimes.
wichtigste: Hafez al-Assad came to power in a coup in 1970.
The Assad family belongs to the Alawite minority.
In 1982 Hafez al-Assad had an uprising in Hama crushed with great bloodshed.
Bashar al-Assad was a trained eye doctor.
From 2011 the violence against protests led to a civil war.
In December 2024 Assad was overthrown and fled to Russia.

abschnitte.text: The defence minister **Hafez al-Assad** took power in a coup in November 1970. He called it the “Corrective Movement” and became president in 1971. He ruled with the **Baath Party**, the army and powerful intelligence services. Many key posts went to **Alawites**, a religious minority to which the Assad family also belongs. In 1982 he had an uprising by the Muslim Brotherhood in **Hama** crushed, and many thousands of people died.

**Bashar al-Assad** studied medicine and trained further as an **eye doctor** in London. After his brother Basil died in an accident in 1994, he was groomed as successor. When his father died in 2000, Bashar became president. At first many people hoped for reforms, but the system remained strictly authoritarian.

In 2011 many people in Syria also protested, as part of the Arab Spring. The regime responded with violence, and this led to a long **civil war**. In August 2013 hundreds of people died in an attack with the poison gas **sarin** on the **Ghouta** region near Damascus. After that Syria had to disclose its chemical weapons. The regime’s most important allies were **Russia** and **Iran**.

At the end of November 2024 the rebel group **Hayat Tahrir al-Sham** launched an offensive from Idlib province. Within about two weeks Aleppo, Hama, Homs and finally Damascus fell. Bashar al-Assad fled to **Russia**, where he was granted asylum. The prisoners in **Saydnaya** prison were freed. It is regarded as a symbol of torture and executions under Assad.

gewusst: Several rounds of peace talks on Syria took place in Geneva under the leadership of the UN.
During the war millions of Syrians fled abroad, many to Turkey, Lebanon and Europe.

teile.einleitung: The theory of surplus value is a central part of Karl Marx's teachings. It is meant to explain where profit comes from under capitalism. According to Marx, it arises because workers create more value than they receive as wages.
wichtigste: Marx described the circuit of capital with the formula M-C-M'.
The worker sells their labour power to the capitalist.
According to Marx, only variable capital creates new value.
The rate of surplus value is surplus labour divided by necessary labour.
Absolute surplus value arises from a longer working day.
Relative surplus value arises from higher productivity.
The rate of profit is surplus value divided by the total capital.

abschnitte.text: In **1867** Marx published the first volume of his work **“Das Kapital”**. In it he distinguishes two circuits. In simple exchange, **C-M-C**, you sell a commodity in order to buy another. The capitalist, on the other hand, uses money (**M**) to buy commodities (**C**) and sells them for more money (**M'**). In German the letters are G for Geld (money) and W for Ware (commodity). The formula **M-C-M'** shows: money is meant to turn into more money. Marx calls the increase **surplus value**.

Marx distinguishes between **labour power** and **labour**. The worker sells their **labour power** to the capitalist. What is paid is its value, roughly what the worker needs to live. But the labour itself creates more value. This difference is the **surplus value**. Marx calls the money spent on wages **variable capital**, because only it creates new value. Machines and raw materials are called **constant capital**; they only pass on their own value.

abschnitte.titel: Calculating the rate of surplus value
abschnitte.text: The part of the working day in which the worker creates the value of their wages is called **necessary labour time**. The rest is **surplus labour**. The **rate of surplus value** is surplus labour divided by necessary labour. An example: the working day lasts 10 hours, and the necessary labour time is 4 hours. Then the surplus labour is 6 hours, and 6 divided by 4 makes **150 per cent**.

If the working day becomes **longer** while the necessary labour time stays the same, surplus labour grows. Marx calls this **absolute surplus value**. If food and other goods become cheaper through higher **productivity**, the value of labour power falls. With a working day of the same length, more time is then left for surplus labour. This is called **relative surplus value**.

The **rate of profit** is the surplus value divided by the **total** capital. For example, a business has 600 francs of constant capital and 200 francs of variable capital and produces 200 francs of surplus value. Then the rate of profit is 200 divided by 800, which is **25 per cent**. In the third volume of “Das Kapital”, Marx describes the **law of the tendency of the rate of profit to fall**: if more and more is invested in machines, the rate of profit falls in the long run. Many economists today regard the theory of surplus value as controversial.

gewusst: Volumes two and three of “Das Kapital” were only published by Friedrich Engels after Marx's death.
The idea that labour creates value originally comes from earlier economists such as Adam Smith and David Ricardo.

teile.einleitung: The Long March was the retreat of the Chinese Communists in 1934 and 1935. They fled from the Kuomintang army from the south to the north of China. Only a small part of them arrived, but Mao Zedong rose to become their leader along the way.
wichtigste: The Long March began in October 1934 and ended in October 1935.
The Communists were fleeing from the Kuomintang army under Chiang Kai-shek.
They set out from Jiangxi province, where their Soviet Republic was.
At the Zunyi Conference in 1935, Mao's rise to military leadership began.
Traditionally, a distance of around 12,500 kilometres is given.
Of more than 85,000 people, only about 7,000 reached the destination.
The march ended in Shaanxi province.

abschnitte.text: At that time in China, the **Communists** were fighting the nationalist **Kuomintang** under **Chiang Kai-shek**. In **1931** the Communists had proclaimed the **Chinese Soviet Republic** in **Ruijin**. Its chairman was **Mao Zedong**. The area lay in **Jiangxi** province. Kuomintang troops surrounded it. To avoid being wiped out, the Red Army broke out in **October 1934**.

The Communists moved north over high mountains, through swamps and across raging rivers. Many died in fighting or from **hunger**, **cold** or disease. Of more than **85,000** people who set out, only about **7,000** reached the destination. The capture of the **Luding Bridge**, a chain bridge over the **Dadu** river, in 1935 became famous.

In **January 1935**, an important conference took place in **Zunyi** in Guizhou province. There the previous military leadership around the German adviser **Otto Braun** was removed. After that, military leadership gradually passed to **Mao Zedong**. In **October 1935** the march ended in **Shaanxi** province. **Yan'an** then became the centre of the Communists for many years.

The party traditionally gives a distance of around **12,500 kilometres** for the main group. This figure comes from the official history. Some researchers think the distance actually covered was **much shorter**. For the **Communist Party of China**, the Long March is a **heroic epic** and an important founding myth of the People's Republic. It is meant to show courage and perseverance.

gewusst: The main group was on the move for just over a year.
The People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, fourteen years after the end of the Long March.

teile.einleitung: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean and a country with around 10 million inhabitants. It has been governed by communists since the revolution of 1959. Cuba is known for colourful vintage cars, music, cigars and its long dispute with the USA.
wichtigste: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, and its capital is Havana.
A communist party has governed there since the revolution of 1959.
The leaders of the revolution were Fidel Castro and Che Guevara.
In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
From 1960 the USA imposed a trade embargo on Cuba.
From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba.
People in Cuba speak Spanish.

abschnitte.text: Cuba lies in the Caribbean Sea, only about 150 kilometres south of Florida in the USA. The main island is about 1,250 kilometres long and narrow. There are sandy beaches, coral reefs, tobacco fields and mountains such as the **Sierra Maestra**. The climate is tropically warm, and from June to November there is a risk of hurricanes.

Before 1959 the dictator **Fulgencio Batista** ruled, supported by the USA. Rebels led by **Fidel Castro** and the Argentinian Che Guevara fought against him from the mountains of the Sierra Maestra. On 1 January 1959 Batista fled, and the rebels took power. Castro soon nationalised companies and land and allied himself with the Soviet Union.

In 1961 an attack by Cuban exiles supported by the USA failed at the **Bay of Pigs**. In 1962 the Soviet Union secretly set up nuclear missiles in Cuba, which led to the **Cuban Missile Crisis**. After thirteen dangerous days the missiles were withdrawn again. The US trade embargo still exists today.

Fidel Castro ruled for almost 50 years, then his brother Raúl took over, and since 2019 Miguel Díaz-Canel has been president. Schools and healthcare are free, and Cuba has many doctors. At the same time there is poverty, power cuts and a shortage of food, and there are no free elections. In recent years a great many people have emigrated.

Cuba is famous for music such as **salsa** and son, and for cigars, rum and sugar cane. In Havana many American cars from the 1950s are still driving around. The old town of Havana is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland was the **protecting power** for the USA in Cuba, because the two countries had no embassies in each other's country.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rapid, often violent overthrow of the government.
A ban on trading with a country.
A dangerous dispute in 1962 over Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba.
A country that represents the interests of another country in a third country.

gewusst: Because hardly any new cars could be imported, Cubans have been repairing their old vintage cars with great ingenuity for decades.
The smallest bird in the world, the bee hummingbird, lives in Cuba.

teile.einleitung: The MPLA is a political movement in Angola in south-western Africa. It fought against Portuguese colonial rule and has governed the country since independence in 1975. For a long time it followed the ideas of Marxism-Leninism.
wichtigste: Agostinho Neto was the leader of the MPLA and the first president of Angola.
The Carnation Revolution in Portugal in 1974 paved the way to independence.
On 11 November 1975 the MPLA declared independence in Luanda.
In the civil war, UNITA under Jonas Savimbi was the most important opponent.
From 1975 Cuba sent tens of thousands of soldiers to support the MPLA.
The civil war ended in 2002 after Savimbi’s death.
José Eduardo dos Santos ruled from 1979 to 2017.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Angola was a **colony of Portugal**. The **MPLA** fought together with other movements for **independence**. Its leader was **Agostinho Neto**, a doctor and poet. On **25 April 1974** the **Carnation Revolution** overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal. The new government ended the colonial wars in Africa.

On **11 November 1975** the MPLA declared independence in the capital, **Luanda**. Neto became the **first president**. At the same time, fighting with the rivals **FNLA** and **UNITA** was already raging. UNITA had been founded in 1966 by **Jonas Savimbi**. It received help from **South Africa** and at times from the **USA**. In this way the civil war also became part of the **Cold War**.

From 1975 **Cuba** intervened with **Operation Carlota** and sent tens of thousands of soldiers. The Soviet Union supported the MPLA with weapons. In **1987 and 1988** the two sides fought at **Cuito Cuanavale**. There the South African advance came to a halt. Agreements followed that also led to the independence of **Namibia**. The Cuban troops stayed until **1991**.

Neto died in **1979**. He was succeeded by **José Eduardo dos Santos**, who ruled for **38 years**. In **February 2002** the UNITA leader Savimbi was killed in battle. A few weeks later the government and UNITA agreed a **ceasefire**, and the long civil war ended. In 2017 **João Lourenço** took over as president.

gewusst: MPLA is the Portuguese abbreviation for “People’s Movement for the Liberation of Angola”.
In Angola, Portuguese is still the official language today.

teile.einleitung: Lech Wałęsa is a Polish electrician who became the leader of the trade union Solidarność (Solidarity). Through non-violent resistance he helped to end communist rule in Poland. In 1983 he received the Nobel Peace Prize, and later he became president of Poland.
wichtigste: Lech Wałęsa worked as an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk.
In August 1980 he led a big strike there.
In September 1980 the independent trade union Solidarność was founded.
After martial law was declared in December 1981, he was interned.
In 1983 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1989 the government and the opposition negotiated at the Round Table.
From 1990 to 1995 Wałęsa was president of Poland.

abschnitte.text: Lech Wałęsa worked as an **electrician** at the **Lenin Shipyard** in **Danzig**, in Polish **Gdańsk**. He campaigned for workers' rights. Because of this he was dismissed in **1976**. In August **1980**, the crane operator **Anna Walentynowicz** was dismissed shortly before her retirement. After that, a **strike** began at the shipyard, which Wałęsa led.

After the strikes in August 1980, the government had to allow **free trade unions**. That is how **Solidarność**, meaning **“Solidarity”**, came into being in **September 1980**. It was the first trade union in the **Eastern Bloc** that was independent of the state. Soon it had around **ten million** members. Wałęsa was its leader.

abschnitte.titel: Martial law and the Nobel Prize
abschnitte.text: On **13 December 1981**, General **Jaruzelski** declared **martial law**. Solidarność was banned, and Wałęsa was arrested and **interned**. In **1983** he received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for his non-violent work for workers' rights. His wife accepted the prize in **Oslo**. He feared he would otherwise not be allowed back into Poland.

From February to April **1989**, the government and Solidarność negotiated at the **Round Table**. Partly free elections were agreed. On **4 June 1989** Solidarność won almost all of the freely contested seats. Shortly afterwards **Tadeusz Mazowiecki** became the first non-communist head of government in the Eastern Bloc. In December **1990** the Polish people elected Wałęsa **president**. He stayed in office until **1995**.

gewusst: Gdańsk airport is now named after Lech Wałęsa.
The events in Poland also encouraged people in other Eastern Bloc countries, for example in the GDR.

teile.einleitung: The Marshall Plan was a large US aid programme for rebuilding Europe after the Second World War. It is named after US Secretary of State George C. Marshall. From 1948 to 1952, around 13 billion dollars went to Europe.
wichtigste: George C. Marshall was US Secretary of State in 1947.
On 5 June 1947 he presented the plan in a speech at Harvard University.
From 1948 to 1952 the USA provided around 13 billion dollars.
The OEEC distributed the aid in Europe, and Switzerland was a founding member.
The Soviet Union refused and also kept its allies away.
As a counterpart, the Eastern Bloc founded the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance in 1949.
Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, many cities, factories and roads in Europe had been destroyed. There was a shortage of food, coal and money. On **5 June 1947**, US Secretary of State **George C. Marshall** gave a famous speech at **Harvard University**. In it he proposed an aid programme for **rebuilding Europe**. During the war, Marshall had been **Chief of Staff** of the US Army.

From **1948 to 1952** the USA provided around **13 billion dollars**. At the time, that was an enormous sum. In the USA, the **Economic Cooperation Administration**, **ECA** for short, managed the money. European importers paid for the goods delivered in their own currency. This money went into funds, known as **counterpart funds**. They were used to give loans for investment in the country itself.

In **1948** the **OEEC**, the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, was founded. It coordinated the aid among the European countries. **Switzerland** was a **founding member**. The cooperation encouraged trade between the European states. In **1961** the OEEC became the **OECD**, which still exists today.

In July 1947 the Soviet foreign minister **Vyacheslav Molotov** left the Paris conference on the Marshall Plan. The **Soviet Union** feared the influence of the USA. Under pressure from Moscow, **Poland** and **Czechoslovakia** also had to decline. In **1949** the Eastern Bloc states founded the **Council for Mutual Economic Assistance**, **CMEA** or **Comecon** for short, as a counterpart. So the Marshall Plan also deepened the division of Europe.

For his plan, George C. Marshall received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1953**. He is still the only US Army general to have received this prize. Officially, the programme was called the **European Recovery Program**, **ERP** for short. Many see the Marshall Plan as an important reason for Western Europe's rapid economic recovery after the war.

gewusst: In Germany there is still an ERP special fund today, which comes from the Marshall Plan and supports companies with loans.
George C. Marshall later also became US Secretary of Defense.

teile.einleitung: The Communist Party of China has governed the People's Republic of China as the only party since 1949. With about 100 million members it is one of the largest parties in the world. It controls politics, the economy and the media in this populous country.
wichtigste: China is the largest country in which a communist party still governs alone today.
The party was founded in Shanghai in 1921.
Its best-known leader was Mao Zedong, who proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949.
From 1978 Deng Xiaoping opened the economy to markets and trade.
Since 2012 Xi Jinping has been general secretary of the party.
In 2024 the party had about 100 million members.
Other parties may not challenge its power, and criticism is strictly controlled.

abschnitte.text: The party was founded in **Shanghai** in July 1921 by a small group that included Mao Zedong. For a long time it fought against the nationalist Kuomintang. During the **Long March** in 1934 and 1935, the Red Army fled thousands of kilometres across China. After winning the civil war, Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.

Under Mao the party tried to transform China quickly. During the “Great Leap Forward” from 1958 there was a famine in which many millions died. From 1966 to 1976 came the **Cultural Revolution**, with a great deal of violence and chaos. The party itself later described this period as a great mistake.

After Mao's death in 1976, **Deng Xiaoping** came out on top. From 1978 he allowed private companies, trade with other countries and markets. As a result China became one of the world's largest economic powers. Politically, however, everything stayed with the party; in 1989 it had the protests on Tiananmen Square in Beijing ended by force.

A **party congress** takes place every five years, most recently the 20th Party Congress in 2022. The greatest power lies with the Standing Committee of the Politburo, which has seven members. At the top is the **general secretary**, since 2012 Xi Jinping, who is also president of the state. The party has groups in companies, schools, universities and the military.

The party controls newspapers, television and the internet, and many Western websites are blocked in China. Human rights organisations criticise its treatment of minorities such as the Uyghurs and Tibetans. At the same time China is an important trading partner for many countries. In 2013 Switzerland was one of the first European countries to sign a **free trade agreement** with China.

begriffe.erklaerung: The top leader of the party.
The small group of the most powerful party leaders.
A large meeting at which the party decides on its leadership and goals.
The retreat of the communist army across China in 1934 and 1935.

gewusst: With around 100 million members, the party has more members than Germany has inhabitants.
A huge picture of Mao Zedong still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing today.

teile.einleitung: The “Ernst Thälmann” Pioneer Organisation was the children’s organisation of the GDR. Almost all schoolchildren belonged to it. You could recognise the Pioneers by their blue or red neckerchief.
wichtigste: The organisation was founded on 13 December 1948.
It was named after the communist Ernst Thälmann.
Young Pioneers wore a blue neckerchief, Thälmann Pioneers a red one.
The greeting was “Be prepared!”, and the reply “Always prepared!”.
In 1989 about 98 per cent of schoolchildren were Pioneers.
The children’s magazine “FRÖSI” was popular with the Pioneers.

abschnitte.text: The Pioneer Organisation was founded on **13 December 1948**. This day was celebrated every year as the **Pioneers’ birthday**. It was named after **Ernst Thälmann**, the former leader of the Communist Party of Germany. He was murdered in Buchenwald concentration camp in 1944. The GDR honoured him as a role model for children.

Children from Year 1 to Year 3 were **Young Pioneers** and wore a **blue** triangular neckerchief. Older children became **Thälmann Pioneers**. From December 1973 they wore a **red** neckerchief, like the Pioneers in the Soviet Union. When greeting, the children raised their right hand flat above their head. To “Be prepared!” they replied **“Always prepared!”**.

The Pioneers offered many leisure activities: clubs, sport, crafts and holiday camps. The large camp called **Pioneer Republic Wilhelm Pieck** on **Lake Werbellin** north of Berlin opened in 1952. In 1979 the **Pioneer Palace** opened in the Wuhlheide in Berlin. Among other things it had a swimming pool and a training centre for cosmonauts. Today the complex is called **FEZ**.

The popular magazine **“FRÖSI”** was published from 1953 to 1991, with stories, puzzles, cut-out craft sheets and comics. In 1989 almost two million children, about **98 per cent** of schoolchildren, belonged to the organisation. Anyone who did not take part stood out in class. The Pioneers were meant to bring children up in the spirit of the ruling party. With the end of the GDR the Pioneer Organisation was also dissolved.

gewusst: The name “FRÖSI” stood for “Fröhlich sein und singen” (being cheerful and singing).
After the Pioneers, young people usually went on to the Free German Youth, FDJ for short.

teile.einleitung: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin was a Russian revolutionary and politician. In 1917 he led the Bolsheviks to power in the October Revolution and founded the world’s first communist state. His ideas strongly shaped the 20th century.
wichtigste: Lenin’s real name was Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov; “Lenin” was an alias.
He was born on 22 April 1870 in Simbirsk on the Volga.
He led the Bolsheviks, a group within the Russian Social Democrats.
With the slogan “peace, land and bread” he won many supporters in 1917.
After the October Revolution he became chairman of the Council of People’s Commissars.
Before the revolution he lived in exile for many years, including in Switzerland.
After his death in 1924 Petrograd was renamed Leningrad.

abschnitte.text: Lenin was born on **22 April 1870** in **Simbirsk** on the Volga. His real name was **Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov**. In 1887 his elder brother **Alexander** was executed because he had been involved in a plot against Tsar Alexander III. This event had a strong effect on the young Vladimir. He studied law and became interested in the ideas of **Karl Marx**. Later, like many revolutionaries, he used an **alias**: Lenin.

Because he fought against the tsar, Lenin was exiled and lived **abroad** for many years. In 1900 he helped to found the newspaper **Iskra**. The word means “spark”. It was printed abroad and secretly smuggled into Russia. In 1903 the Russian Social Democratic Party split. Lenin led the **Bolsheviks**; the others were called **Mensheviks**. During the First World War Lenin lived in **Switzerland**, first in Bern and then in Zurich.

In the spring of 1917 the tsar was overthrown in Russia. Lenin travelled back to Russia by train from Zurich through Germany. The Bolsheviks promised “**peace, land and bread**”: peace for the war-weary people, land for the farmers and bread for the hungry. In the **October Revolution** they took power. Lenin became **chairman of the Council of People’s Commissars**, roughly the head of government.

In March 1918 Lenin’s government made the **Treaty of Brest-Litovsk** with **Germany**. Russia left the First World War, but had to give up large territories. A harsh **civil war** followed. The Bolsheviks banned other parties and persecuted their opponents with great harshness. In 1922 the **Soviet Union** was founded. By then Lenin was already seriously ill.

Lenin died in January **1924**. A few days after his death the city of **Petrograd** was renamed **Leningrad** in his honour. Since 1991 it has been called St Petersburg again. His birthplace, Simbirsk, was also renamed and has been called **Ulyanovsk** since 1924. Lenin’s body was embalmed and still lies in a **mausoleum** on Red Square in Moscow today. Opinions about Lenin still differ greatly today.

gewusst: In Zurich a plaque on Spiegelgasse marks the house where Lenin lived in 1916 and 1917.
The motto of the newspaper Iskra was “From the spark will come the flame”.

teile.einleitung: The New Ostpolitik (Eastern Policy) was the policy of Federal Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1969. West Germany moved closer to the GDR, the Soviet Union and the other states of the Eastern Bloc. Instead of keeping them at a distance, talks and treaties were meant to secure peace in Europe.
wichtigste: The New Ostpolitik was a policy of rapprochement between West Germany and the GDR and the Eastern Bloc.
It was put into practice by Federal Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1969.
Its guiding principle was “change through rapprochement”.
Important treaties were concluded with the Soviet Union and Poland in 1970.
In 1972 the Basic Treaty set out relations with the GDR.
Brandt was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971.
The Ostpolitik was highly controversial in West Germany.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided into two states. For a long time the Federal Republic did not recognise the GDR as a state and broke off contacts with countries that did. From 1969 the government of **Willy Brandt** chose a new path. It wanted to make life easier for people in East and West through talks.

Brandt’s adviser **Egon Bahr** had already described the plan in 1963 in a speech in Tutzing. The basic idea was called **change through rapprochement**. The hope was that if you talk and work together with the East, conditions there will slowly change. To do this, the existing borders in Europe also had to be recognised for the time being.

In 1970 the Federal Republic concluded the **Treaty of Moscow** with the Soviet Union and the Treaty of Warsaw with Poland. In them the countries renounced violence and recognised the borders, including the Oder-Neisse border with Poland. In 1971 there followed an agreement between the four victorious powers on Berlin. In 1972 the **Basic Treaty** set out relations with the GDR, and in 1973 a treaty with Czechoslovakia was added.

On 7 December 1970 Brandt visited the memorial to the uprising in the Jewish ghetto in Warsaw. There he suddenly knelt down in silence. With this gesture he asked forgiveness for the crimes committed by Germans in the Second World War. The **Warsaw Genuflection** made headlines around the world.

Many opposition politicians accused Brandt of giving up German territories in the East. In 1972 he narrowly survived a **vote of no confidence** in the Bundestag. Thanks to the treaties, visits and travel between East and West became easier, and in 1973 both German states became members of the UN. Many historians see the Ostpolitik as a step towards the peaceful end of the Cold War.

begriffe.erklaerung: The states in Eastern Europe that were under the influence of the Soviet Union.
The head of government of Germany.
A vote in parliament intended to remove a head of government.
Treaty of 1972 between the Federal Republic and the GDR about their relationship.

gewusst: The Federal Republic and the GDR did not set up embassies, but so-called Permanent Missions.
Brandt resigned in 1974 because a close aide, Günter Guillaume, had been exposed as a GDR spy.

teile.einleitung: From 1922 to 1991 the Soviet Union was the largest state on Earth, and it was ruled by communists throughout this time. It was made up of 15 republics, the largest of which was Russia. In the Cold War it was the world’s second superpower alongside the USA.
wichtigste: The Soviet Union was founded on 30 December 1922 and dissolved at the end of December 1991.
Its official name was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, or USSR for short.
The capital was Moscow.
The Communist Party was the only party allowed.
Well-known leaders were Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev.
In 1961 the Soviet Union sent the first person into space, Yuri Gagarin.
After its collapse, 15 independent states came into being, including Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

abschnitte.text: The **Soviet Union** stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific and from the Arctic to Central Asia. With about 22 million square kilometres it was more than 500 times the size of Switzerland. In 1991 about 290 million people lived there, speaking more than a hundred different languages. The country stretched across eleven time zones.

In 1917 the **Bolsheviks** under **Lenin** took power in Russia in the October Revolution. After a bloody civil war they founded the Soviet Union in 1922. The word soviet means council and originally referred to councils of workers and soldiers. In reality, however, power lay with the Communist Party and its leaders.

abschnitte.titel: Stalin and the Second World War
abschnitte.text: Under **Joseph Stalin** the country was rapidly industrialised, while at the same time millions of people died from hunger, in camps and through persecution. In 1941 Nazi Germany attacked the Soviet Union. In the Second World War the Soviet Union lost about 27 million people, more than any other country. At the end the Red Army stood in Berlin, and Eastern Europe came under Soviet influence.

After 1945 the Soviet Union and the USA faced each other in the **Cold War**. Both built huge numbers of nuclear weapons. In 1957 the Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite into space, **Sputnik**, and in 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person to orbit the Earth. In everyday life, however, people often suffered from shortages and a lack of freedom.

From 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** tried to save the country with reforms such as perestroika and glasnost. But the economy collapsed, and more and more republics wanted to become independent. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet Union ceased to exist. For Switzerland the Soviet Union was a difficult partner; the two countries only established diplomatic relations in 1946.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
Russian word for council.
A member state of the Soviet Union, rather like a large canton.
The long conflict between East and West without a direct war between the superpowers.
A state with enormous influence all over the world.

gewusst: In 1957 the dog Laika, on board Sputnik 2, became the first living creature to go into orbit around the Earth.
As early as March 1918 the capital was moved from Petrograd, today’s St Petersburg, to Moscow.
Because a Soviet diplomat was murdered in Lausanne in 1923, there were no diplomatic relations between Switzerland and the Soviet Union for a long time.

t1rr8vm4.t: Special Period in Time of Peace

teile.einleitung: The “Special Period in Time of Peace” was a severe economic crisis in Cuba in the 1990s. It began when the Soviet Union collapsed and Cuba lost its most important trading partners. People had to live with great shortages and find many new solutions.
wichtigste: The Special Period was triggered by the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc.
Cuba’s economic output fell by about a third.
Because of the fuel shortage, Cuba bought about 1.2 million bicycles from China.
Organic vegetable gardens, the organopónicos, were set up in the cities.
Tourism became the most important new source of foreign currency.
From 2000 Venezuela helped with cheap oil.

abschnitte.text: Cuba has been a socialist state since 1959. For a long time the country received cheap oil and a lot of money from the **Soviet Union**. With the end of the Eastern Bloc and the Soviet Union, this help disappeared. **Fidel Castro’s** government then declared the **Special Period in Time of Peace**. The **gross domestic product**, the value of all goods and services, fell by about 35 per cent by the mid-1990s.

Above all there was a shortage of **oil**, spare parts and food. Buses ran rarely, and there were frequent power cuts. Cuba therefore bought about **1.2 million bicycles** from China. In many places they replaced cars and buses. Because fertiliser and pesticides were lacking, people in the cities created organic vegetable gardens, the **organopónicos**. They helped to secure the supply of vegetables.

The **USA** had had an **embargo** against Cuba, in other words a trade ban, since the 1960s. During the Special Period it was tightened. In 1992 this was done with the **Torricelli Act**. In 1996 the **Helms-Burton Act** followed. It also threatened foreign companies that invested in Cuba. Cuba’s government blamed the embargo for many problems, whereas critics tended to blame the planned economy.

In August 1994 thousands protested in Havana, especially on the seafront promenade, the **Malecón**. These protests are called the **Maleconazo**. Afterwards the government let many people leave the country. They set off towards the USA on home-made rafts and were called **balseros**. The crossing was dangerous.

Cuba opened up to foreign **tourists** and investment in hotels. Tourism brought in urgently needed **foreign currency**, in other words money from abroad. Small private businesses were also partly allowed. From 2000 **Venezuela** under President Hugo Chávez supplied oil on favourable terms. In return Cuba sent doctors, among other things, to Venezuela.

gewusst: The name “Special Period in Time of Peace” comes from emergency plans that were actually intended for a war.
The word “balsero” comes from the Spanish “balsa”, which means raft.

teile.einleitung: Rosa Luxemburg was a well-known politician and thinker of the labour movement. She campaigned for a socialist revolution but also criticised the oppression of people who thought differently. Part of her life took place in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Rosa Luxemburg was born in 1871 in Zamość in what is now Poland.
In 1897 she gained her doctorate at the University of Zurich.
In 1899 she answered Eduard Bernstein with the pamphlet “Reform or Revolution?”.
Her famous sentence is: “Freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently.”
At the turn of the year 1918/1919 she helped to found the KPD.
In January 1919 she was murdered in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: Rosa Luxemburg was born in **Zamość** in 1871. At that time the town belonged to the Russian-ruled part of Poland. Because she was politically active, she went to Switzerland. At the **University of Zurich** women were already able to study at that time. In 1897 she gained her **doctorate** there, which means she received the title of doctor. Her doctoral thesis dealt with the industrial development of Poland.

Later Luxemburg lived in Germany and became a member of the SPD. When Eduard Bernstein demanded that socialism be achieved through reforms, she strongly disagreed. In 1899 her pamphlet “**Reform or Revolution?**” was published. In it she wrote that reforms alone could not overcome capitalism. In 1913 she published her main economic work, “**The Accumulation of Capital**”. With it she wanted to explain imperialism.

In the **First World War** the SPD voted for the war loans. Luxemburg firmly rejected this and was sent to prison for it. There, in 1915, under the pseudonym **Junius**, she wrote “The Crisis of Social Democracy”. The Junius Pamphlet was published in 1916. It contains the slogan “Socialism or barbarism”.

abschnitte.titel: Freedom for those who think differently
abschnitte.text: In 1918 Luxemburg wrote “The Russian Revolution”. She welcomed the revolution but criticised the fact that the **Bolsheviks** were suppressing the opposition. In a note in the margin stands her famous sentence: “**Freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently.**” It is still often quoted today, even by people with completely different political views.

Together with **Karl Liebknecht** she led the **Spartacus League**. At the turn of the year 1918/1919 this became the **Communist Party of Germany** (KPD) in Berlin. In January 1919 there was fighting in Berlin. On 15 January 1919 Rosa Luxemburg was murdered by soldiers of a Freikorps (volunteer militia). Her body was thrown into the **Landwehr Canal** and was only found at the end of May.

gewusst: The University of Zurich was one of the first universities in Europe where women could study.
Today a memorial by the Landwehr Canal in Berlin commemorates Rosa Luxemburg.

teile.einleitung: Leon Trotsky was one of the most important leaders of the Russian October Revolution of 1917. He founded the Red Army and, after Lenin, was one of the most powerful men in the Soviet Union. He lost the power struggle with Stalin, was exiled and was murdered in Mexico in 1940.
wichtigste: Leon Trotsky's real name was Lev Bronstein, and he was born in 1879 in what is now Ukraine.
In 1917 he helped organise the uprising of the October Revolution in Petrograd.
He built up the Red Army and led it in the civil war.
After Lenin's death he lost the power struggle with Stalin.
In 1929 he was banished from the Soviet Union.
In 1940 he was murdered in Mexico by one of Stalin's agents.

abschnitte.text: Trotsky was born in 1879 as Lev Davidovich **Bronstein** in a village in what is now Ukraine. Even as a young man he fought against the rule of the Tsar. He was arrested several times and exiled to Siberia, but escaped. He took the name Trotsky as a pseudonym.

During the first Russian revolution in 1905 he led the workers' council, the **Soviet**, in St Petersburg. After that he lived abroad for a long time, in places including Vienna and New York. In 1917 he returned and joined Lenin's Bolsheviks. As head of the Petrograd Soviet he helped plan the seizure of power in the **October Revolution**.

After the revolution, Trotsky first led the peace negotiations with Germany at Brest-Litovsk. Then he became People's Commissar for War. He built up the **Red Army**, which soon had millions of soldiers. In the civil war he travelled from front to front in an armoured train and did a great deal for the Bolsheviks' victory.

After Lenin's death in 1924, Trotsky and **Joseph Stalin** fought for the leadership. Trotsky wanted to spread the revolution throughout the world, the so-called **permanent revolution**. Stalin won and had Trotsky expelled from the party in 1927. In 1929 he was banished from the Soviet Union.

Trotsky then lived in Turkey, France, Norway and, from 1937, Mexico. From there he sharply criticised Stalin and in 1938 founded the so-called Fourth International. In August 1940 he was attacked in his house in **Coyoacán** near Mexico City by one of Stalin's agents and died. His house is now a museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: Russian word for “council”, an assembly of workers and soldiers.
The army of the Bolsheviks and later of the Soviet Union.
Living abroad because you are persecuted in your own country.
Followers of Trotsky's ideas.

gewusst: Stalin had Trotsky removed from many official photos, as if he had never existed.
Trotsky wrote a great many books, including a history of the Russian Revolution and an autobiography.

teile.einleitung: The Treuhandanstalt (Trust Agency) was an authority that took over the state-owned businesses after the end of the GDR. Its job was to sell them, restructure them or close them down. For many people in eastern Germany the Treuhand is still a sore point today.
wichtigste: The Treuhandanstalt was founded on 1 March 1990.
In the summer of 1990 about 8,500 businesses were under its control.
At first about four million people worked in these businesses.
Its president, Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, was murdered in April 1991.
After that Birgit Breuel led the Treuhand until the end of 1994.
From 1995 the BvS took over the remaining tasks.

abschnitte.text: In the GDR almost all businesses officially belonged to the people; this was called **people’s property**. On **1 March 1990** the GDR Council of Ministers under **Hans Modrow** decided to found the **Treuhandanstalt**. It was to manage the people’s property as a trustee. Being a trustee means looking after something on behalf of others. After reunification in October 1990 it continued to work as a federal authority.

On 1 July 1990 about **8,500 businesses** with some 45,000 sites were under the control of the Treuhand. It was one of the largest networks of companies in the world. At first about **four million people** worked there. Many businesses were out of date and could not survive competition. The Treuhand sold them, restructured them or closed them. A great many people lost their jobs in the process.

Its president, **Detlev Karsten Rohwedder**, was shot dead in Düsseldorf on **1 April 1991**. The terrorist group RAF claimed responsibility, but the culprits were never clearly identified. His successor was **Birgit Breuel**, previously finance minister of Lower Saxony. She led the Treuhand until the end of 1994. After that the **Federal Agency for Special Tasks Arising from Unification** (BvS) took over the remaining contracts.

There was a lot of resistance to the Treuhand’s policy. In 1993 the miners of **Bischofferode** in Thuringia went on **hunger strike**. They wanted to prevent the closure of their potash mine. The protest became a symbol against the Treuhand. People still argue today about whether it acted correctly or whether much could have been saved.

gewusst: The former headquarters of the Treuhand in Berlin is now called the Detlev-Rohwedder-Haus.
Since 1999 the Federal Ministry of Finance has used this building, which used to be the Reich Air Ministry.

teile.einleitung: Samizdat is Russian and means “self-publishing”. In the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc this was the name for banned texts that people secretly copied themselves and passed on. Samizdat was an important way of reading and thinking freely despite censorship.
wichtigste: Samizdat translates as self-publishing.
The texts were often copied with a typewriter and carbon paper.
Tamizdat were texts that were printed in the West and smuggled back in.
Magnitizdat was the name for banned songs on private tape recordings.
“The Gulag Archipelago” by Alexander Solzhenitsyn was also spread in this way.
Anyone who spread samizdat risked a labour camp, exile or loss of citizenship.

abschnitte.text: In the **Soviet Union** the state controlled all publishers, newspapers and printing works. Anything the government did not like was not allowed to appear. This is called **censorship**. Some people wanted to read critical poems, novels or political texts all the same. So they produced the texts themselves. This is how **samizdat**, “self-publishing”, came about.

Photocopiers were rare and strictly monitored. That is why people typed the texts out on a **typewriter**. With **carbon paper** between the sheets, several copies were made at once. Readers often copied the texts out again and passed them on to friends. This is how “**The Gulag Archipelago**” by Alexander Solzhenitsyn spread, for example. The book described the system of Soviet prison camps and was banned.

Besides samizdat there were other ways. “Tam” means “there” in Russian. **Tamizdat** were works printed by exile publishers in the West and then smuggled into the country. **Magnitizdat** was about music: concerts by singer-songwriters were secretly recorded and copied onto **tapes**. From the 1970s cassettes were also used for this.

There was underground literature in other Eastern Bloc states too. In **Poland** it was called “drugi obieg”, meaning the **second circulation**. In the 1980s there was a great deal of it there. In the **GDR** the Initiative for Peace and Human Rights published the magazine “**Grenzfall**”. In 1987 the Stasi seized a printing machine at the Environmental Library in Berlin.

Anyone who produced or spread samizdat took a great risk. The authorities often treated it as **anti-Soviet agitation**. The penalties were a **labour camp**, exile or loss of citizenship. Even so, many people read these texts. They helped to make sure that criticism of the government was never completely silenced.

gewusst: With carbon paper a typewriter could usually make only a few readable copies at a time, which is why every copy was valuable.
The term samizdat is a playful twist on the names of state publishing houses, which often ended in “-izdat”.

teile.einleitung: The Cheka was the first secret police of Soviet Russia. The Bolsheviks founded it shortly after the October Revolution of 1917 in order to persecute their opponents. It became the model for later secret services such as the NKVD and the KGB.
wichtigste: Cheka means “Extraordinary Commission”.
Its first head was Felix Dzerzhinsky.
In September 1918 the government declared the Red Terror.
The Cheka could convict people and carry out sentences without a court.
Its headquarters in Moscow was the Lubyanka.
In February 1922 it was replaced by the GPU.

abschnitte.text: The name **Cheka** is made from the Russian initials of **Chrezvychaynaya Komissiya**. This means **Extraordinary Commission**. The Bolsheviks founded it in December 1917, a few weeks after they had taken power. Its job was to fight opponents of the revolution. Its first head was **Felix Dzerzhinsky**, who came from a Polish noble family.

The Cheka had unusually great power. It could **arrest** suspects, **sentence** them and have them **shot** without any court being involved. So it was police, prosecutor and judge all at once. In 1918 the Latvian Chekist **Martin Latsis** wrote that the main thing to ask about an accused person was their **background**. Often social class counted for more than any deed.

At the end of August 1918 an assassination attempt was made on **Lenin**. On **5 September 1918** a decree officially declared the **Red Terror**. Thousands of hostages and supposed opponents were shot. In 1918 the Cheka moved into the former building of an insurance company on **Lubyanka** Square in Moscow. The building became the symbol of the Soviet secret police.

In **February 1922** the Cheka was turned into the **GPU**, the State Political Directorate. Later came the NKVD and the **KGB**, which also used the Lubyanka. From 1923 a camp was set up in an old monastery on the **Solovetsky Islands** in the White Sea. **Forced labour** was tried out there. The camp is regarded as the forerunner of the later **Gulag** system.

gewusst: Dzerzhinsky led the Cheka and its successors until his death in 1926.
For a long time afterwards, staff of the Soviet secret services still called themselves “Chekists”.

teile.einleitung: An arms race means that two sides build more and more, and ever more powerful, weapons in order to be stronger than their opponent. In the Cold War it was mainly the USA and the Soviet Union that armed themselves against each other. Nuclear weapons were particularly feared.
wichtigste: In the arms race the USA and the Soviet Union built more and more weapons.
The most dangerous weapons were atomic bombs, which can destroy whole cities.
In 1945 the USA was the first country to test an atomic bomb, and the Soviet Union followed in 1949.
Around 1986 there were about 70,000 nuclear weapons in the world.
Neither side attacked, because both would have been destroyed: the “balance of terror”.
The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 is meant to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
In disarmament, weapons are reduced.

abschnitte.text: In 1945 the USA tested the first **atomic bomb**. In the same year it used atomic bombs against the Japanese cities of **Hiroshima** and **Nagasaki**. In August 1949 the **Soviet Union** also detonated its first atomic bomb. Now both **superpowers** had this weapon. From then on each side tried to have more and better weapons than the other. This is called an **arms race**.

abschnitte.titel: Bigger and bigger, more and more
abschnitte.text: Soon even more powerful **hydrogen bombs** were added, together with missiles that could carry bombs thousands of kilometres.
