In 1961 the Soviet Union tested the **Tsar Bomba**, the most powerful bomb ever detonated. Its explosive force was more than 3,000 times greater than that of the Hiroshima bomb. In the 1980s there were **tens of thousands** of nuclear weapons worldwide, about 70,000 around 1986. Almost all of them belonged to the USA and the Soviet Union.

Why did neither superpower use its atomic bombs against the other? Each side could have struck back immediately, and **both would have been destroyed**. This was called the “**balance of terror**”. Even so, many people were afraid. In the USA schoolchildren practised “**duck and cover**”, ducking under their desks and protecting their heads when the alarm sounded. In 1962 the **Cuban Missile Crisis** brought the world very close to nuclear war.

States tried to slow down the arms race. The **Non-Proliferation Treaty** was signed in 1968 and came into force in 1970. In it, states without nuclear weapons promise not to acquire any. Later the USA and the Soviet Union concluded treaties on **disarmament**. In disarmament, weapons are destroyed or no longer built. It is the opposite of **rearmament**. In 1987, for example, they agreed to get rid of a whole group of intermediate-range missiles.

Neutral Switzerland also felt the fear of nuclear war. It built **shelters** in houses and municipalities. Today there is a place in a shelter for almost every inhabitant of Switzerland. This is unique in the world. Switzerland has joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty and has no nuclear weapons.

gewusst: The Tsar Bomba of 1961 had an explosive force of about 50 megatonnes of TNT.
Many Swiss houses have a shelter in the cellar with thick concrete walls and a heavy door.

teile.einleitung: Nicolae Ceaușescu was the communist dictator of Romania from 1965 to 1989. He had himself worshipped like a hero while many people went hungry and cold. In December 1989 he was overthrown in a revolution and executed.
wichtigste: Nicolae Ceaușescu was born in Scornicești in 1918.
In 1965 he became head of the Romanian Communist Party.
From 1974 he was also president of the state.
He and his wife Elena had themselves celebrated with a huge personality cult.
The Securitate secret police kept watch on the population.
In the 1980s Romania was short of food, electricity and heating.
In December 1989 he was overthrown and executed on 25 December.

abschnitte.text: Ceaușescu came from a poor farming family and became a communist while still a teenager. Before 1944 he was imprisoned several times for this. In 1965 he became **party leader**, and in 1974 also **president of the state**. At first he was popular with many Romanians and in the West.

In 1968 Ceaușescu publicly criticised the invasion of Czechoslovakia by Warsaw Pact troops. Romania did not take part. That is why Western politicians saw him as a brave opponent of Moscow. He was even received by US presidents and by the British Queen.

Ceaușescu called himself “Conducător”, which means leader, and had himself celebrated everywhere. His wife **Elena** also became very powerful. The **Securitate** secret police spied on people; even typewriters had to be registered. Anyone who criticised the regime was arrested or persecuted.

To pay back debts abroad, Ceaușescu had a lot of food exported in the 1980s. For the population, food, electricity and heating were strictly rationed. At the same time he had the enormous **Palace of the People** built in Bucharest, for which an entire district of the old town was demolished. Today it is the seat of parliament and one of the largest buildings in the world.

In December 1989 protests began in the city of **Timișoara** and spread quickly. During a speech in Bucharest on 21 December, Ceaușescu was booed by the crowd. On 22 December he fled with Elena by helicopter, but both were captured. After a brief, hasty trial they were shot in Târgoviște on 25 December 1989, and afterwards Romania became a democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who decides everything alone and without any checks.
The secret police in communist Romania.
When a leader is worshipped excessively.
When everyone only gets a small, fixed amount of a product.

gewusst: Ceaușescu’s fall was the only violent overthrow among the revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe.
His last speech on 21 December 1989 was shown live on television until the broadcast suddenly broke off.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Stalin died on 5 March 1953 after a stroke. His death was a turning point: the Soviet Union looked for a new leadership, and much of Stalin’s violent rule was reversed.
wichtigste: Stalin died on 5 March 1953 at the age of 74.
He suffered a stroke at his dacha near Moscow.
At the funeral, many people died in the crush.
Georgy Malenkov became head of government, and Khrushchev became party leader in September 1953.
The invented Doctors’ Plot was declared false in April 1953.
An amnesty freed more than a million prisoners.

abschnitte.text: Stalin spent his last years mostly at his country house, the **dacha**, in **Kuntsevo** on the outskirts of Moscow. At the beginning of March 1953 he suffered a **stroke** there, a bleed in the brain. Out of fear, his guards did not check on him for a long time. That is why he received help only late. On **5 March 1953** he died at the age of 74.

Stalin had ruled the Soviet Union for about 30 years. Hundreds of thousands wanted to see the dead Stalin in Moscow. In the huge **crush** many people were crushed to death. The exact number of victims is still unknown today. Stalin’s body was laid out next to Lenin’s in the **mausoleum** on Red Square.

At first several politicians governed together; this is called a **collective leadership**. **Georgy Malenkov** became chairman of the Council of Ministers, in other words head of government. But he had to give up the post in 1955. In September 1953 **Nikita Khrushchev** became First Secretary of the Communist Party. Over the following years he won out against his rivals.

At the beginning of 1953 mainly Jewish doctors had been accused of wanting to poison party leaders. This **Doctors’ Plot** was invented. In April 1953 the doctors were released. As early as March the new leadership decided on an **amnesty** for more than a million prisoners with shorter sentences. At first, however, political prisoners hardly benefited from it.

gewusst: Out of fear, Stalin’s guards did not dare to check on him for a long time.
The exact number of people who died in the crush at the funeral is still not known today.

teile.einleitung: Ostalgie is a German word made from “Ost” (East) and “Nostalgie” (nostalgia). It describes a wistful, often rose-tinted memory of everyday life in the GDR. Since the 1990s there have been films, shows and products that remind people of that time.
wichtigste: Ostalgie combines the German words “Ost” (East) and “Nostalgie” (nostalgia).
It means a rose-tinted memory of everyday life in the GDR.
Films such as “Sonnenallee” and “Good Bye, Lenin!” contributed to the wave of Ostalgie.
The Trabant is regarded as a cult car and was mockingly called the “racing cardboard”.
The Jugendweihe (youth coming-of-age ceremony) is still celebrated in eastern Germany today.
Critics accuse Ostalgie of playing down the dictatorship.

abschnitte.text: **Nostalgia** is a longing for the past. After the end of the GDR in 1990, the lives of many East Germans changed very quickly. Many products, habits and jobs disappeared. That is why some people liked to remember the familiar things from their childhood and youth. This memory of everyday life, community and products is called **Ostalgie**.

In 1999 **Leander Haussmann** made the comedy **“Sonnenallee”** about teenagers in East Berlin in the 1970s. In 2003 there followed **“Good Bye, Lenin!”** by Wolfgang Becker. In it, young Alex recreates a GDR that no longer exists in the flat for his sick mother. In the same year several GDR shows were broadcast on television. One of them was presented by the former figure skater **Katarina Witt**.

One symbol of Ostalgie is the **Trabant**, or Trabi for short. Its body was made of **Duroplast**, a plastic reinforced with cotton fibres. That is why it was mockingly but affectionately called the “Rennpappe” (racing cardboard). Customs live on too. The **Jugendweihe** is a non-religious celebration at which young people of about 14 mark the step into adult life.

Many historians take a critical view of Ostalgie. It mainly recalls the pleasant sides of everyday life. In doing so, the **Stasi**, the **Wall** and political persecution are often left out. Critics say that this plays down the **dictatorship**. Others think that people simply do not want to dismiss their own life story completely.

gewusst: The Trabant was built in Zwickau, and many families had to wait years for a new car.
In the GDR the Jugendweihe was almost compulsory; today it is voluntary but still popular.

teile.einleitung: East Berlin was the eastern part of the city of Berlin. From 1949 to 1990 it belonged to the GDR and was its capital. From 1961 the Berlin Wall separated East Berlin from West Berlin.
wichtigste: After the Second World War the Soviet Union administered the eastern part of Berlin.
East Berlin was the capital of the GDR.
From 1961 the Wall separated East and West Berlin.
After that, most people were no longer allowed to travel to the West.
The TV Tower on Alexanderplatz dates from the time of East Berlin.
Since 1990 Berlin has been one city again.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Berlin was divided into **four sectors**. The USA, Great Britain and France administered the West, and the **Soviet Union** the East. When the GDR was founded in 1949, East Berlin became its **capital**. The western sectors became West Berlin. A border between two worlds now ran right through the middle of the city.

Many people fled from the GDR to the West via Berlin. That is why the GDR leadership had the **Berlin Wall** built in August 1961. After that, most people from East Berlin were no longer allowed to go to the West. Only a few, for example pensioners, later got permission. In this way families and friends were separated for years.

The best-known structure is the **TV Tower** with its silver sphere. It was completed in 1969 and is more than 360 metres tall. It stands near **Alexanderplatz**, an important square in East Berlin. On **4 November 1989** a huge demonstration for more freedom took place there. Five days later, on 9 November, the Wall opened.

Some things from East Berlin are popular throughout Germany today. The **Ampelmännchen**, the little traffic-light man with his hat, now lights up on many traffic lights all over Berlin. The **Sandmännchen** (Little Sandman), which was first shown in 1959, comes from GDR television. Every evening it sent children off to bed with a short story. Since reunification on 3 October 1990, Berlin has been one city again and the capital of the whole of Germany.

gewusst: The Sandmännchen is still shown on German television today.
The Berlin TV Tower is the tallest structure in Germany.

teile.einleitung: The Soviet Union was once the largest state on Earth. In 1991 it broke apart, and its 15 republics became 15 separate countries. With its end, the Cold War between East and West also came to an end.
wichtigste: The full name of the Soviet Union was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, or USSR for short.
It was made up of 15 republics.
From 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev wanted to renew the Soviet Union with reforms.
In 1991 more and more republics declared their independence.
In December 1991 former Soviet republics founded the CIS.
On 25 December 1991 the flag of the Soviet Union was lowered at the Kremlin for the last time.
With the end of the Soviet Union the Cold War was over.

abschnitte.text: The **USSR**, the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics**, came into being in 1922. It stretched from Europe to the Pacific. It was made up of **15 republics**, for example Russia, **Ukraine**, **Kazakhstan** and the three countries on the Baltic Sea. It was ruled by the Communist Party. After the Second World War the Soviet Union and the USA faced each other as enemies in the **Cold War**, without fighting a war directly against each other.

In the 1980s the Soviet Union was in a severe economic crisis. In 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** came to power. With **perestroika**, the restructuring, he wanted to improve the economy. With **glasnost**, openness, people were allowed to speak and write more freely. But this also brought old problems to light. In many republics the wish for **independence** grew.

In August 1991 opponents of the reforms tried to remove Gorbachev from power in a **coup**. The coup failed after a few days, partly because the Russian president **Boris Yeltsin** stood up against it. After that many republics declared their independence. **Ukraine** did so in August 1991. **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania**, the **Baltic states**, regained their independence. In December 1991 Kazakhstan also became a state of its own.

In December 1991 several former Soviet republics founded the **CIS**, the **Commonwealth of Independent States**. Through it they wanted to continue working together. On **25 December 1991** Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union. That evening the red flag was lowered at the **Kremlin** in Moscow and the flag of Russia was raised. A few days later the Soviet Union no longer existed.

The Soviet Union became **15 countries**. Russia took over the Soviet Union’s seat on the **UN Security Council**. For many people a difficult time began, with unemployment and rising prices. The Baltic states later joined the EU and NATO. Switzerland recognised the new states and established diplomatic relations with them.

gewusst: By area the Soviet Union was about 540 times the size of Switzerland.
Gorbachev was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

teile.einleitung: In an autocracy a single person decides about a whole country. Everyone else has to obey and has no say. The opposite is democracy, in which many people take part in decisions.
wichtigste: In an autocracy only one person has power.
An autocrat does not have to ask anyone’s permission.
He even decides alone about war and peace.
One disadvantage is that other opinions do not count.
A ruler who governs cruelly is called a tyrant.
It is very difficult for the people to remove an autocrat.

abschnitte.text: In an **autocracy** only **one person** has power. They decide about laws, taxes and even about **war and peace**. They do not have to ask anyone’s permission. The people are not asked. Autocrats can be, for example, kings with unlimited power or **dictators**.

Imagine that in a class one child alone decides which game everyone plays. The others have no say. An autocracy is rather like that. In a **vote**, on the other hand, everyone would be allowed to take part in the decision, and the majority would win. That is how a **democracy** works.

When one person decides alone, **other opinions do not count**. People’s wishes are often ignored. If the ruler makes a mistake, it is often not put right, because nobody is allowed to disagree. A ruler who uses his power cruelly is called a **tyrant**. The word comes from **Greek**.

The people **cannot simply vote out** an autocrat. He often has the **army** and the **police** on his side. Anyone who criticises him can be punished. In **Switzerland** things are completely different: the government, the **Federal Council**, consists of seven people who decide together. Parliament is elected by the people, and the people can vote on many questions.

gewusst: Switzerland has no single person at the top: the President of the Confederation changes every year.
The Greek word “monarchy” literally means “rule by one person”.

teile.einleitung: Russia is the largest country in the world. It stretches from Europe far into Asia as far as the Pacific. The country has huge forests, long rivers and the deepest lake on Earth.
wichtigste: Russia is almost twice as big as Canada, the second-largest country.
The capital is Moscow, and the second-largest city is St Petersburg.
Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is more than 9,000 kilometres long.
Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world.
Well-known wooden dolls from Russia are called matryoshkas.

abschnitte.text: Russia lies in **Europe** and in **Asia**. It is so big that it has eleven different time zones. When people in Moscow are having their evening meal, the next morning is already beginning in the east. The largest part, in the east, is called **Siberia**. It is very cold there in winter, and there are vast forests called the **taiga**. Switzerland would fit into Russia about 400 times.

The capital is **Moscow**, with the Kremlin and Red Square. The second-largest city is **St Petersburg** on the Baltic Sea. It used to be the capital of the Russian **tsars**, in other words the emperors. From 1922 to 1991 Russia belonged to the **Soviet Union**, a communist state. After the Soviet Union ended, Russia became a state of its own. In 1991 **Boris Yeltsin** became its first president.

In Russia people speak **Russian**. It is written in the **Cyrillic alphabet**. Some letters look like ours but sound different. The Russian “Р”, for example, is pronounced like an R, and the “Н” like an N. Other countries such as Bulgaria or Serbia also use the Cyrillic alphabet.

The **Trans-Siberian Railway** runs from Moscow to Vladivostok on the Pacific. The line is more than 9,000 kilometres long, and the whole journey takes about a week. **Lake Baikal** lies in Siberia. It is more than 1,600 metres deep, which makes it the deepest lake in the world. The **Volga**, the longest river in Europe, also flows through Russia.

A well-known toy from Russia is the **matryoshka**. This is a painted wooden doll that you can open. Inside it is a smaller doll, inside that an even smaller one, and so on. Russia is also known for ballet, chess and famous writers such as **Leo Tolstoy**. Dishes include, for example, borscht, a soup made from beetroot.

gewusst: Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of the liquid fresh water on the Earth’s surface.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is regarded as the longest railway line in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Thaw is the name for the period after Stalin’s death, when the Soviet Union under Nikita Khrushchev became somewhat more open. Artists and writers had more freedom, but not without limits.
wichtigste: The Thaw began after Stalin’s death in 1953 and lasted until about 1964.
The name goes back to a novel by Ilya Ehrenburg.
In 1962 Solzhenitsyn’s story about one day in a camp was allowed to be published.
Pasternak’s “Doctor Zhivago” remained banned and was published in Italy in 1957.
In 1957 tens of thousands of young guests came to Moscow for the World Festival.
With Khrushchev’s fall in 1964 the Thaw came to an end.

abschnitte.text: After Stalin’s death in 1953, life in the Soviet Union became somewhat freer. Like ice in spring, the strict control thawed a little. The name **Thaw** comes from a novel by the writer **Ilya Ehrenburg** from 1954. In 1956 **Khrushchev** publicly criticised the personality cult around Stalin. Many prisoners were released from the camps.

The literary magazine **Novy Mir** became the most important mouthpiece of the Thaw. In 1962 it printed **Alexander Solzhenitsyn’s** story about one day in the life of a camp prisoner. The editor-in-chief, **Alexander Tvardovsky**, personally obtained Khrushchev’s approval for it. In 1961 the poet **Yevgeny Yevtushenko** denounced in his poem “**Babi Yar**” the fact that no memorial commemorated the murdered Jews of Kyiv.

Cinema also became more human. The film “**The Cranes Are Flying**” by Mikhail Kalatozov won the **Palme d’Or** in Cannes in 1958. It shows people with doubts instead of only heroes. In 1957 the **World Festival of Youth and Students** took place in Moscow. For young Soviet citizens it was a rare contact with Western fashion and music.

The Thaw had clear limits. **Boris Pasternak’s** novel “**Doctor Zhivago**” remained banned and was first published in Italy in 1957. Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958, but under pressure he had to turn it down. In 1962, at the **Manege** exhibition hall in Moscow, Khrushchev insulted young artists who were showing **abstract art**. Criticism of the system itself remained forbidden.

In 1964 Khrushchev was overthrown, and **Leonid Brezhnev** came to power. After that, culture was controlled more strictly again. In 1966 the writers **Sinyavsky** and **Daniel** were convicted in a show trial. This showed clearly that the time of relaxation was over.

gewusst: “Doctor Zhivago” was first published by the Milan publisher Feltrinelli.
The poem “Babi Yar” broke a taboo, because the Jewish victims were hardly ever spoken about.

teile.einleitung: Pol Pot was the leader of the Khmer Rouge, a communist movement in Cambodia. From 1975 to 1979 he set up one of the cruellest dictatorships of the 20th century there. Almost a quarter of the population died during this time.
wichtigste: Pol Pot’s real name was Saloth Sar, and he was born in Cambodia around 1925.
He led the Khmer Rouge, who captured the capital, Phnom Penh, in April 1975.
The Khmer Rouge drove the city dwellers into the countryside and forced them to work in the fields.
Money, schools, religion and markets were banned.
About 1.7 to 2 million people died from hunger, forced labour, disease and murder.
At the beginning of 1979 Vietnamese troops drove the Khmer Rouge from power.
Pol Pot died in 1998 without ever having stood trial.

abschnitte.text: **Pol Pot** was born Saloth Sar into a well-off farming family. Around 1950 he studied in **Paris**, where he came into contact with communist ideas. Back in Cambodia he first worked as a teacher. Later he went underground and became head of the Communist Party of Cambodia.

Cambodia lies in South-East Asia, between Thailand, Laos and Vietnam. During the **Vietnam War** the country was drawn into the fighting and bombed by the USA. The **Khmer Rouge** took advantage of the chaos and won many supporters in the countryside. On 17 April 1975 they marched into the capital, Phnom Penh.

The Khmer Rouge wanted to create a society made up only of farmers and declared **Year Zero**. Within a few days the cities were emptied and the people were sent to labour camps in the countryside. Families were separated, and children often had to testify against their parents. Anyone who was educated, wore glasses or spoke a foreign language was quickly regarded as an enemy.

In the **Tuol Sleng** prison, also known as S-21, thousands of people were tortured and then murdered. In fields outside the towns, the so-called Killing Fields, there are mass graves. In total about 1.7 to 2 million people died out of a population of about eight million. Many experts speak of a **genocide**.

abschnitte.titel: End and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: After fighting along the border, Vietnam invaded Cambodia at the end of 1978 and overthrew the Khmer Rouge in January 1979. Pol Pot fled into the jungle on the border with Thailand and carried on fighting there. He died in 1998 while under house arrest imposed by his own people. A **tribunal** supported by the UN later sentenced several of his most important helpers to life imprisonment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The communist movement that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979.
A crime in which a whole group of people is meant to be destroyed.
A special court for serious crimes.
A form of rule in which one person or group decides everything alone.

gewusst: The former Tuol Sleng prison in Phnom Penh is now a museum that commemorates the victims.
Under the Khmer Rouge there was no money in Cambodia, and the national bank was blown up.
The name Pol Pot was an alias, under which the leader remained almost unknown for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Shenzhen is a city of millions in southern China, right on the border with Hong Kong. In 1980 it became one of the country’s first special economic zones. In just a few decades a small town with fishing villages became one of the largest cities in China.
wichtigste: Shenzhen was declared a special economic zone in 1980.
The city lies in Guangdong province and borders directly on Hong Kong.
Deng Xiaoping is regarded as the father of the special economic zones.
In the zone, foreign companies were allowed to invest and were given tax advantages.
In the 2020 census Shenzhen had about 17.6 million inhabitants.
Today Shenzhen is known for electronics and technology companies.

abschnitte.titel: From fishing village to big city
abschnitte.text: Shenzhen lies in southern China in **Guangdong** province on the **Pearl River Delta**. Before 1980 it was a small town with fishing villages. Until 1979 the main town of **Bao’an** county had only about 30,000 inhabitants. In the 2020 census Shenzhen had about **17.6 million** inhabitants. That is about twice as many people as live in the whole of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What is a special economic zone?
abschnitte.text: From 1978 **Deng Xiaoping** pushed through the policy of **reform and opening-up** in China. The country was to modernise its economy. For this, **special economic zones** were created. There, freer rules applied to companies, and there were **tax advantages**. Foreign companies were allowed to invest. In this way foreign money and modern technology were to come into the country. In 1988 the whole island of **Hainan** even became a province and a special economic zone.

Shenzhen lies just north of **Hong Kong**. At that time Hong Kong was still a British colony with a strong economy. This location was important for attracting money and companies from Hong Kong. Many factories moved across the border to Shenzhen because land and labour were cheaper there. Millions of people from other parts of China came to the city to find work.

After 1989 there was disagreement in the party about how far the reforms should go. In 1992 Deng Xiaoping, then almost 88 years old, made his **Southern Tour**. He visited Shenzhen and other cities and called for the economic reforms to continue. After that the economy grew even faster. Today a large **billboard** in Shenzhen commemorates Deng.

Today Shenzhen is known worldwide for **electronics** and **technology companies**. A great many mobile phones, computer parts and drones are developed and built here. That is why the city is often called “**China’s Silicon Valley**”, after the famous technology area in California. Many electronic parts found in devices all over the world come from the area around Shenzhen.

gewusst: The provincial capital of Guangdong is Canton, in Chinese Guangzhou.
Shenzhen is one of the fastest-growing cities in human history.

t1yclwcn.t: Communist Party of the Soviet Union

teile.einleitung: The Communist Party of the Soviet Union, CPSU for short, was the only party allowed in the Soviet Union. From 1917 to 1991 it decided almost everything in the huge country. Its leaders, the general secretaries, were the most powerful people in the state.
wichtigste: The CPSU was the only party allowed in the Soviet Union.
It grew out of the Bolsheviks under Lenin.
The name CPSU was used from 1952; before that it had other names.
The general secretary was the real ruler of the country.
Well-known party leaders were Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev.
In the 1980s it had almost 19 million members.
After the attempted coup in 1991 the party was banned, and shortly afterwards the Soviet Union broke up.

abschnitte.text: The party grew out of the **Bolsheviks**, a group of Russian socialists under Lenin. They split from more moderate socialists in 1903. With the October Revolution of 1917 they took power in Russia. After that the party changed its name several times; from 1952 it was called the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

No other party was allowed to exist in the Soviet Union. At the top were the **Politburo** and the **general secretary**. The party decided about the government, the army, the economy, schools and newspapers. Party membership was almost always necessary for a good career.

After Lenin, **Joseph Stalin** ruled with great harshness from the 1920s until his death in 1953. He was followed by Nikita Khrushchev and, from 1964, by Leonid Brezhnev. After short periods under Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko, Mikhail Gorbachev became general secretary in 1985. He tried to renew the country with reforms.

Under Stalin the party had millions of people persecuted, and many were sent to the labour camps of the **Gulag**. Even many party members were killed in the purges of the 1930s. Later too, critics were locked up or put in psychiatric hospitals. The secret police, the KGB, served the party as its tool.

In August 1991 old party leaders tried to stop Gorbachev's reforms with a coup. The coup failed after three days, partly because of the resistance led by Boris Yeltsin. After that the activities of the CPSU were banned. In December 1991 the **Soviet Union** dissolved, and 15 new states came into being.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group around Lenin from which the party emerged; the word means “members of the majority”.
The small, most powerful leadership body of the party.
The system of labour camps in the Soviet Union.
An attempt to overthrow the government by force.

gewusst: The Kremlin in Moscow was the seat of the party leadership and is today the seat of the Russian president.
Gorbachev was the only general secretary who was also elected President of the Soviet Union by parliament.

teile.einleitung: The Monday demonstrations were peaceful protests against the government of the GDR in the autumn of 1989. They began in Leipzig after the prayers for peace in St Nicholas Church. With candles and the chant “We are the people!” they helped to bring down the Wall.
wichtigste: The demonstrations started at St Nicholas Church in Leipzig.
Prayers for peace had been held there every Monday since 1982.
The first Monday demonstration took place on 4 September 1989.
The best-known chant was “We are the people!”.
With “No violence!” and candles, people showed that they were peaceful.
On 23 October 1989 more than 300,000 people demonstrated.
Since then Leipzig has often been called the “City of Heroes”.

abschnitte.text: In the **GDR** the SED party decided almost everything, and speaking your mind freely was dangerous. In **St Nicholas Church** in **Leipzig**, **prayers for peace** were held every Monday from **1982**. The pastor **Christian Führer** opened the church under the motto **“open to all”**. After the prayers, people gathered in the square in front of the church. In this way the church became a place where people could talk openly.

On **4 September 1989**, after the prayer for peace, young people held up banners such as **“For an open country with free people”**. The **Stasi**, the GDR’s secret police, tore the placards out of their hands. This is regarded as the first **Monday demonstration**. The demonstrators marched from the church along the **inner ring road** around Leipzig’s old town. More people came from week to week.

The demonstrators chanted **“No violence!”** and often carried **burning candles**. Anyone carrying a candle needs both hands and cannot throw stones. The candle became the symbol of the **Peaceful Revolution**. On **9 October 1989** people were very afraid that the police and army would step in. The conductor **Kurt Masur** read out the **“Appeal of the Leipzig Six”** over the city’s loudspeakers, calling for calm. The situation stayed peaceful.

The best-known chant was **“We are the people!”**. With it, people showed that the people should decide, not the party. On **23 October 1989** **more than 300,000** people marched through Leipzig, more than ever before. On **9 November 1989** the **Berlin Wall** fell. Later many chanted **“We are one people!”**, as they wished for reunification.

gewusst: Kurt Masur was the conductor of the famous Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig.
Because of the Monday demonstrations, Leipzig is often called the “City of Heroes”.

teile.einleitung: Alfredo Stroessner was a general who ruled Paraguay as a dictator from 1954 to 1989. His rule was one of the longest in South America. It ended with a military coup.
wichtigste: Stroessner ruled Paraguay for about 35 years, from 1954 to 1989.
His father was an immigrant from Hof in Bavaria.
His rule relied on the Colorado Party.
In February 1989 General Andrés Rodríguez overthrew him.
He fled to Brazil and died in Brasília in 2006.
Under his rule the Itaipú hydroelectric power station was built together with Brazil.

abschnitte.text: **Alfredo Stroessner** was a general from **Paraguay**. His father was an immigrant from **Hof in Bavaria**, which is why Stroessner had a German surname. In May 1954 he staged a coup, and in August 1954 he became **president**. He ruled for about **35 years**, until 1989. It was one of the longest dictatorships in South America.

Stroessner governed with the **Colorado Party**. For state employees, membership was almost compulsory. Formally there were elections, but Stroessner always won them, and the opposition hardly stood a chance. Critics were persecuted, and many had to go into exile. The Colorado Party is still the strongest political force in Paraguay today.

Under Stroessner, in 1973, Paraguay and **Brazil** signed the treaty for a huge hydroelectric power station on the **Paraná** river. **Itaipú** is still one of the largest hydroelectric power stations in the world today. A border town was named **Puerto Presidente Stroessner** in his honour. After his fall it was given the name **Ciudad del Este**, “City of the East”.

Under Stroessner, wanted people also found refuge in Paraguay. The best known was **Josef Mengele**, who as a concentration camp doctor in **Auschwitz** had taken part in terrible crimes. He was granted Paraguayan citizenship in 1959. Mengele died in Brazil in 1979 without ever standing trial.

In **February 1989** General **Andrés Rodríguez**, a close confidant, overthrew him in a **military coup**. Stroessner fled to **Brazil** and lived in exile in **Brasília**. He died there in 2006 without ever having been put on trial. After his fall Paraguay set out on the road to democracy.

gewusst: In 1992 the so-called “Archives of Terror” were found in Paraguay, with many files on the persecution of opponents of the regime.
Paraguay is a landlocked country, but thanks to rivers such as the Paraná it has access to the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Red Guards were groups of school pupils and students in China. They came into being in 1966 at the start of the Cultural Revolution and followed Mao Zedong enthusiastically. Within a few years they caused great damage.
wichtigste: The Red Guards were made up mainly of school pupils and students.
They came into being in Beijing in the spring of 1966.
They appeared during the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, which lasted from 1966 to 1976.
They were meant to take action against the “Four Olds”: old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits.
Mao received millions of Red Guards in Tiananmen Square.
From 1968 most of them were sent to the countryside.

abschnitte.text: In the spring of 1966 the first Red Guards were formed at **Beijing secondary schools** and universities. The young people worshipped **Mao Zedong** and carried his “Little Red Book” of quotations with them. Mao used their enthusiasm against opponents within his own party. The movement was part of the **Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution**, which lasted from 1966 to 1976.

In August 1966 Mao wrote his own **big-character poster** entitled “Bombard the Headquarters”. Big-character posters were large posters with political texts. With it Mao targeted leading politicians such as **Liu Shaoqi** and **Deng Xiaoping**. The Red Guards understood it as a call to attack “those in power” within the party. From August 1966 Mao received millions of young people at eight rallies in **Tiananmen Square**.

The Red Guards were meant to fight the “**Four Olds**”: old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits. In doing so they destroyed **temples**, works of art and books. Teachers, intellectuals and party officials were publicly humiliated and persecuted. The president at the time, **Liu Shaoqi**, was also attacked. He was expelled from the party in 1968 and died in custody in 1969. In 1980 he was rehabilitated, in other words officially cleared of the accusations.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Red Guards
abschnitte.text: Soon different groups of Red Guards were fighting one another, often with bloodshed. The leadership wanted to restore order. From 1968 it sent millions of young people to the countryside, “**up to the mountains and down to the villages**”. There they were supposed to learn from the farmers. With that the Red Guards were largely disbanded. Many of these young people lost years of their education.

gewusst: A total of about 11 to 13 million young people are said to have taken part in the rallies in Tiananmen Square.
The young people who were sent to the countryside at that time are called “zhiqing” in Chinese, which means “educated youth”.

teile.einleitung: The Trabant, affectionately called the “Trabi”, was the best-known car of the GDR. The small car with its rattling two-stroke engine and plastic body was built in Zwickau. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 it became a symbol of the peaceful change.
wichtigste: The Trabant was built from 1957 to 1991 at VEB Sachsenring in Zwickau.
In total about three million Trabis were made.
The body was made of Duroplast, a plastic containing cotton fibres.
The engine was a small two-stroke that rattled loudly and gave off clouds of blue exhaust.
In the GDR people often had to wait more than ten years for a new Trabant.
The best-known model was the Trabant 601.

abschnitte.text: The **Trabant** was a small car from the **GDR**, the communist part of Germany. The name means “companion” and recalls the Soviet satellite Sputnik, which flew into space in 1957. For many families in the GDR the Trabi was the only car they could buy at all. There was a saloon, an estate and even an open-topped version for the army.

The Trabi was made at **VEB Sachsenring** in Zwickau in Saxony. VEB means “people’s own enterprise”, so the factory belonged to the state. From 1964 the **Trabant 601** model was built, and it was then produced almost unchanged for more than 25 years. By the end of production in April 1991 about three million Trabis had come off the assembly line.

The body was made of **Duroplast**, a hard plastic made from cotton waste and synthetic resin. Because sheet steel was in short supply in the GDR, this was a practical solution. The two-stroke engine in the Trabant 601 had only 26 horsepower, and the car could go at most about 100 kilometres per hour. There was no fuel gauge; you checked the tank with a dipstick.

In the GDR’s **planned economy** there were far fewer cars than people who wanted one. Anyone who ordered a Trabi often waited twelve to fifteen years for it to be delivered. That is why some parents put their children’s names down for a car early on. Second-hand Trabis were therefore often more expensive than new ones.

After the **Berlin Wall** opened on 9 November 1989, thousands of Trabis drove across the border into the West. The pictures of rattling Trabis among cheering people went round the world. After reunification most people quickly bought cars from the West. Today the Trabi is a popular collector’s car, and there are even Trabi tours of Berlin.

begriffe.erklaerung: German Democratic Republic, the communist state in eastern Germany from 1949 to 1990.
A hard plastic that never becomes soft again once it has set.
A simple engine in which oil is mixed into the petrol.
People’s own enterprise, a company in the GDR that belonged to the state.

gewusst: Because of its plastic body, the Trabi was mockingly called the “Rennpappe” (racing cardboard).
The body of a Trabant hardly rusted at all, because Duroplast cannot rust.
Today there is a museum in Zwickau that shows the history of the Trabant and other cars from the town.

teile.einleitung: The Prague Spring was an attempt by Czechoslovakia in 1968 to make communism more humane and free. Suddenly people were allowed to speak openly, and newspapers wrote without censorship. During the night of 20 to 21 August 1968, troops from the Soviet Union and its allies ended the experiment with tanks.
wichtigste: The Prague Spring began in January 1968, when Alexander Dubček became party leader.
His aim was “socialism with a human face”.
Censorship was lifted, and people were allowed to travel and speak more freely.
On 21 August 1968 Warsaw Pact troops invaded.
Afterwards the reforms were reversed in the so-called normalisation.
Many Czechs and Slovaks fled abroad, including to Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War **Czechoslovakia** was a communist state under the influence of the Soviet Union. At the beginning of 1968 the Communist Party chose **Alexander Dubček** as its leader. He wanted to keep socialism but combine it with more freedom. Because the reforms blossomed in the spring of 1968, they were called the Prague Spring, after the capital, Prague.

**Censorship** of newspapers, radio and television was largely abolished. People discussed politics openly, and new associations and clubs were formed. The government also planned economic reforms and more freedom to travel. Many citizens supported Dubček enthusiastically.

The leadership of the Soviet Union under **Leonid Brezhnev** feared that freedom could spread to other countries. During the night of 20 to 21 August 1968, hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria moved in. The population mainly put up non-violent resistance, for example turning street signs round and arguing with the soldiers. Even so, more than a hundred people lost their lives during the invasion.

Dubček was taken to Moscow and had to reverse the reforms. In January 1969 the student **Jan Palach** set himself on fire in Prague in protest. In 1969 Gustáv Husák took power and carried out the so-called **normalisation**. Critics lost their jobs, and censorship returned.

After the invasion tens of thousands of people fled to the West. Switzerland took in more than 10,000 refugees from Czechoslovakia and welcomed them very warmly. The Prague Spring showed that the Soviet Union would not tolerate real reforms within its sphere of power. Only with the **Velvet Revolution** of 1989 did Czechoslovakia become free.

begriffe.erklaerung: A change that is meant to improve something.
When the state controls and bans what appears in newspapers or books.
The military alliance of the Soviet Union with communist states in Eastern Europe.
The period after 1969 when the reforms were reversed.

gewusst: Romania did not take part in the invasion and even criticised it publicly.
After the changes of 1989, Alexander Dubček became president of the parliament of Czechoslovakia.
Many of the Czechs and Slovaks who fled to Switzerland in 1968 stayed for good and became Swiss citizens.

teile.einleitung: Forced collectivisation is the name for the policy with which Stalin, from 1929, forced the farmers in the Soviet Union to put their farms into large collective farms. The farmers lost their own land and livestock. The consequences were severe: many people were persecuted, and millions starved to death.
wichtigste: At the end of 1929 Stalin began mass forced collectivisation.
A kolkhoz was a collective farm, while a sovkhoz belonged directly to the state.
Better-off farmers were persecuted as “kulaks”.
Many farmers slaughtered their livestock in protest.
The Law of Spikelets of 1932 harshly punished even gathering a few ears of grain.
In 1932 and 1933 millions of people starved to death in Ukraine; this is called the Holodomor.

abschnitte.text: Stalin wanted to bring agriculture under the control of the state. The farmers had to pool their land, their livestock and their tools in a **kolkhoz**. Formally this was a cooperative, in other words a jointly run farm. Work was done according to the state’s instructions. A **sovkhoz**, on the other hand, belonged directly to the state, and people worked there for wages. Big machines were lent out by the state-run **machine and tractor stations**, which in this way also kept control over the farmers.

At the end of **1929** Stalin called for agriculture to be collectivised quickly. In December 1929 he announced the “**liquidation of the kulaks as a class**”. Farmers with a little more land or livestock were regarded as **kulaks**. Hundreds of thousands of families had their property **taken away**, were arrested or were **deported** to distant regions. Many died as a result. Within a few years most farms had been forced into kolkhozes.

Many farmers did not want to hand over their animals. They preferred to **slaughter their livestock** themselves. As a result the Soviet Union’s livestock numbers fell sharply. In March 1930 Stalin published the article “**Dizzy with Success**”. In it he blamed abuses on over-eager local officials. Many farmers then left the kolkhozes again. But soon the pressure increased once more.

The state demanded very high **grain deliveries**, even when the harvest was poor. In 1932 the so-called **Law of Spikelets** came in. It protected the “social property” of the kolkhozes. Even starving people who picked up a few ears of grain in the fields could be sentenced to a labour camp or to death. In 1932 and 1933 there was a severe **famine**. Ukraine and Kazakhstan were particularly badly affected.

In **Ukraine** **millions of people** starved to death in 1932 and 1933. This famine is called the **Holodomor**. The Ukrainian word means something like “killing by hunger”. In the Soviet Union it was not allowed to be spoken about for a long time. Today Ukraine remembers the victims every year in November. Many states and experts regard the Holodomor as genocide; others see it differently.

gewusst: Because the farmers slaughtered so many animals, it took decades for the Soviet Union to have as much livestock again.
The kolkhozes were usually allowed to leave their members only a small plot of land for their own use, and these small gardens were often particularly productive.

teile.einleitung: North Korea is the northern part of the Korean peninsula in East Asia. Korea has been divided since the Korean War, and to this day the North is ruled as a dictatorship by the Kim family. North Korea is regarded as one of the most closed-off countries in the world.
wichtigste: Korea has been divided since the Korean War, and the North is still ruled as a dictatorship today.
North Korea’s official name is the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
The capital is Pyongyang.
The country has been ruled by the Kim family since 1948.
Kim Jong-un has been in power since 2011.
North Korea has nuclear weapons and is strongly isolated internationally.
As a teenager, Kim Jong-un went to school in Bern for a while.

abschnitte.text: North Korea borders China, Russia along a short stretch, and South Korea to the south. The country is very mountainous; the highest mountain is **Paektu** on the border with China. The winters are long and cold. About 26 million people live in North Korea (as of 2023).

After the Second World War the Soviet Union occupied the north of Korea. In 1948 the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was founded there under **Kim Il-sung**. In 1950 he attacked the South, and the **Korean War** began. Since the ceasefire of 1953 a heavily guarded zone has separated the two Koreas.

Kim Il-sung was followed in 1994 by his son **Kim Jong-il** and in 2011 by his son **Kim Jong-un**. The three are worshipped with a huge personality cult, and their pictures hang in every home. The state ideology is called **Juche**, which means something like self-reliance. There are no free elections, no freedom of speech and no free internet.

Many people in North Korea are poor, and food is often scarce. In the 1990s a great many people died in a severe famine. Anyone who criticises the regime can be sent to a prison camp together with their whole family. Travel abroad is almost never allowed, yet tens of thousands have fled via China.

Since 2006 North Korea has carried out several **nuclear tests** and keeps testing missiles. The UN has therefore imposed strict sanctions. In the 1990s Kim Jong-un attended a school near **Bern** under a false name. In addition, members of the Swiss Armed Forces have been monitoring the ceasefire at Panmunjom since 1953.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of rule in which one person or group decides everything alone.
North Korea’s state ideology; it means something like self-reliance.
Penalties, for example bans on trade with a country.
A piece of land surrounded by water on three sides.

gewusst: At night North Korea is almost completely dark on satellite images because there is so little electricity.
In North Korea years are partly counted according to a calendar of its own, which begins with Kim Il-sung’s year of birth, 1912.

teile.einleitung: The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953 and was one of the first big wars of the Cold War. Communist North Korea attacked the south in order to unite the country. To this day there is no peace treaty, and Swiss officers still monitor the ceasefire.
wichtigste: On 25 June 1950 North Korea attacked South Korea.
The aim was to unite all of Korea under communist rule.
United Nations troops led by the USA helped South Korea.
From the autumn of 1950 China sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers to support the north.
On 27 July 1953 a ceasefire was signed in Panmunjom.
Millions of people died, including a great many civilians.
Switzerland is still part of the commission that monitors the ceasefire today.

abschnitte.text: From 1910 to 1945 Korea was a Japanese colony. After the Second World War the country was divided at the **38th parallel**. The Soviet Union occupied the north and the USA the south. In 1948 two states were formed, in the north under Kim Il-sung and in the south under Syngman Rhee.

On 25 June 1950 North Korean troops crossed the border. Within a few days they captured the capital, **Seoul**. The South Koreans were pushed back into a small corner around the city of Busan. The **United Nations** decided to help South Korea with troops from many countries.

abschnitte.titel: Back and forth at the front
abschnitte.text: In September 1950 UN troops under General Douglas MacArthur landed at **Incheon**, behind the North Koreans. They pushed the north back almost to the Chinese border. Then China intervened with hundreds of thousands of soldiers. After that the front stayed roughly at the 38th parallel for a long time.

After two years of negotiations a ceasefire was signed in **Panmunjom** on 27 July 1953. A peace treaty never followed, so legally the war has not ended. Since then a **demilitarised zone** about 4 kilometres wide has separated the two states. It is one of the most heavily guarded borders in the world.

An estimated several million people died in the war, many cities were destroyed, and families were separated for decades. Korea is still divided today; the south became a democracy and the north remained a dictatorship. Since 1953 Switzerland and Sweden have formed the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission**. To this day, members of the Swiss army serve there in Panmunjom.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fighting stops, but there is not yet a proper peace.
An imaginary line on the globe along which Korea was divided in 1945.
A border strip in which no army may be stationed.
The UN, a community of almost all the states in the world.

gewusst: The Korean War is sometimes called the “forgotten war”, because it is less well known in the West than other wars.
The Swiss delegation in Korea is the Swiss army's oldest mission abroad.

teile.einleitung: A communist party is a party that campaigns for the ideas of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. In some countries such a party governs on its own. In Switzerland there are small left-wing parties that are close to these ideas.
wichtigste: Communist parties refer to Marx and Engels.
In the Soviet Union only the Communist Party was allowed to govern.
China has been governed by the Communist Party since 1949 (as of 2026).
Cuba is also governed by a Communist Party (as of 2026).
The Communist Party of Switzerland was founded in 1921.
The Party of Labour (PdA) was founded in 1944.
The best-known song of the communists is called “The Internationale”.

abschnitte.text: In 1848 **Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** wrote the **“Manifesto of the Communist Party”**. In it they called for a society in which factories and land belong to everyone together. Parties that want to achieve this call themselves a **communist party**. Their best-known song is **“The Internationale”**. From 1922 to 1944 it was even the anthem of the Soviet Union.

In the **Soviet Union** only the Communist Party had power. Other parties were banned. This is called a **one-party state**. So in elections people could hardly **choose between parties**. There was no real choice, and criticising the party was dangerous.

In **China** the **Communist Party of China** has governed alone since **1949** (as of 2026). Other parties may not compete for power. In **Cuba** in the Caribbean too, a communist party has governed since the revolution of **1959**. For a long time **Fidel Castro** was the leader there; he ruled for almost 50 years. Other examples are Vietnam and Laos.

The **Communist Party of Switzerland** was founded in **1921**. It always remained a small party and was banned in 1940. In **1944** the **Party of Labour**, **PdA** for short, was founded. It is close to the ideas of communism and is also small. In Switzerland people can choose between **many parties** in elections.

gewusst: The “Manifesto of the Communist Party” was published in London in 1848.
The words of “The Internationale” were written by the Frenchman Eugène Pottier in 1871.

teile.einleitung: Private property means that a thing belongs to an individual person or a company. Whether there should be private ownership of factories, land and machines was one of the biggest points of dispute between communism and the market economy. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution protects property.
wichtigste: Private property means that something belongs to a person or a company.
Marx and Engels wanted to abolish private ownership of the means of production.
They did not, however, want to abolish personal possessions.
In 1840 Pierre-Joseph Proudhon wrote “Property is theft”.
In 1776 Adam Smith defended the free market.
In Switzerland Article 26 of the Federal Constitution guarantees property.

abschnitte.text: The person a thing belongs to is its **owner**. They may decide what happens to it, use it, sell it or give it away. This applies to a bicycle just as much as to a house or a factory. Economists distinguish between **personal possessions**, such as clothes or furniture, and the **means of production**. The means of production are things used to make goods, for example factories, machines and land.

In 1840 the French anarchist **Pierre-Joseph Proudhon** wrote the sentence **“Property is theft”** in his work “What is Property?”. **Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** wanted to abolish private ownership of the **means of production**. According to their teaching, factories should belong to everyone together. They did not want to abolish personal possessions. Marx did, however, later criticise Proudhon in several texts.

In 1776 the Scottish economist **Adam Smith** published the book **“The Wealth of Nations”**. He described how self-interest and competition can promote prosperity. He is regarded as the founder of classical economics. Supporters of the **market economy** say that private property encourages people to work well and to take care of things. In communist states, by contrast, businesses were nationalised and farms were merged into collectives.

In Switzerland **Article 26** of the Federal Constitution protects property. This is called the **guarantee of ownership**. The state may only take property away in exceptional cases, for example to build a road or a railway line. Such an **expropriation** must be fully compensated. Who owns a piece of land is recorded in the **land register**.

gewusst: The term “means of production” covers everything used to make something, including a field or a fishing boat.
In Switzerland the guarantee of ownership is one of the fundamental rights, like freedom of opinion.

teile.einleitung: In a planned economy the state plans what is produced, how much of it and what it costs. So it is not supply and demand that determine the economy, but authorities with their plans. This is how the economy worked in the Soviet Union, in the GDR and in other communist countries.
wichtigste: In a planned economy the state decides what is made and what it costs.
Factories and land usually belong to the state, not to private owners.
The plans often covered five years and were therefore called five-year plans.
The opposite is the market economy, such as the one in Switzerland.
In planned economies goods were often missing, and people had to queue for a long time.
Today a strict planned economy exists almost only in North Korea.

abschnitte.text: In a **planned economy** a central authority lays down which goods are produced and in what quantities. It also sets prices and wages. Experts therefore also speak of a **centrally administered economy**. The idea behind it was that everyone should be provided for fairly and nobody should become rich at the expense of others.

In the Soviet Union the planning authority **Gosplan** did this work. From 1928 it drew up big **five-year plans** for the whole country. Every factory was told how many shoes, tractors or tonnes of steel it had to deliver. In the GDR this task was carried out by the State Planning Commission.

In a **market economy** companies and customers decide for themselves what is bought and sold. If demand for a product rises, the price usually rises too, and companies make more of it. Switzerland has a market economy, but the state sets rules, for example to protect employees. Today almost all countries in the world mix the market with state rules.

The planners could not know exactly what millions of people needed. That is why there was often too little of important things and too much of unpopular goods. In the GDR people waited more than ten years for a car such as the **Trabant**. Because the factories only had to meet the planned figures, they often paid little attention to quality.

After 1989 the countries of Eastern Europe switched to a market economy. From 1978 China introduced a market economy step by step, even though the Communist Party continues to rule. Cuba now also allows more small private businesses. **North Korea** is regarded as one of the last countries with an almost complete planned economy.

begriffe.erklaerung: An economy in which the state plans and prescribes everything.
An economy in which supply and demand determine prices and production.
A plan that sets out what is to be produced over the next five years.
When important goods are constantly missing and you have to wait a long time for them.

gewusst: In the Soviet Union huge quantities of shoes were sometimes produced in only a few sizes, because the plan only counted the number of items.
Anyone in the GDR who managed to get hold of bananas was lucky, because tropical fruit was very rare there.
In Switzerland, too, the state planned food production during the Second World War with the Wahlen Plan, so that people had enough to eat.

teile.einleitung: In the GDR, “Republikflucht” (flight from the republic) was the name for leaving the country without permission from the state. Anyone who did so, or tried to, was committing a crime. Even so, millions of people dared to do it, often at great risk.
wichtigste: Republikflucht meant leaving the GDR without permission.
Officially the offence was called “illegal border crossing” and was set out in Section 213 of the criminal code.
Between 1949 and the building of the Wall in 1961, about 2.7 million people left the GDR.
Many refugees first went to the Marienfelde emergency reception centre in West Berlin.
With an exit application you could ask to leave legally, but you had to expect disadvantages.
The Federal Republic paid to free political prisoners from the GDR.

abschnitte.titel: A country with a closed border
abschnitte.text: The GDR was a communist state in which the **SED** decided everything. Travel to the West was forbidden for most people. Anyone who left without permission was, in the eyes of the state, committing **Republikflucht**. **Section 213** threatened prison for it, in serious cases up to eight years. Even attempting or preparing an escape was punished.

Until 1961 the border in Berlin was still fairly open. About **2.7 million people** left the GDR during this time. Many of them were young and well trained, for example doctors, engineers or craftspeople. This exodus greatly weakened the economy. At the **Marienfelde emergency reception centre** in West Berlin the refugees were registered and looked after. Today there is a memorial there. In August 1961 the GDR built the **Berlin Wall**.

After the Wall was built, escaping became a matter of life and death. Border guards had orders to prevent escapes, if necessary with their weapons. Anyone who stopped an escape received **bonuses**, extra leave or medals. In August 1962 the young **Peter Fechter** was shot at the Wall and died in the death strip. Even so, people found inventive ways: in 1979 the **Strelzyk and Wetzel** families fled from Thuringia to Bavaria in a home-sewn **hot-air balloon**.

There was also a legal route: the **exit application**. However, anyone who submitted one often had to expect disadvantages at work or at school. Until the beginning of 1989 a refusal did not even have to be explained. Political prisoners could sometimes reach the West through the **buying of prisoners’ freedom**. In this the Federal Republic paid the GDR money or goods. Between 1964 and 1989 about 34,000 people were freed in this way.

gewusst: In total the GDR received about 3.4 billion Deutschmarks for releasing prisoners.
The balloon escape of 1979 lasted only about half an hour and was later made into a film several times.

teile.einleitung: For more than 150 years the red flag has been the symbol of the labour movement, of socialism and of communism. Red stands for the blood shed in the struggle for justice, and for revolution. Many communist states, such as the Soviet Union or China, made red the main colour of their flag.
wichtigste: Red is the colour most often associated with communism.
Red flags were already flown during the French Revolution and in the Paris Commune of 1871.
The flag of the Soviet Union was red with a hammer, sickle and a star.
The flag of the People’s Republic of China is also red, with five yellow stars.
At May Day marches, trade unions and left-wing parties often carry red flags.
Because of the red colour, communists used to be called simply “the Reds”.

abschnitte.titel: What does the red flag mean?
abschnitte.text: The **red flag** is a political symbol of revolution and of workers’ rights. The red colour is meant to recall the blood of people who fought for their rights. It also stands for courage, passion and the wish for change. Originally, however, a red flag was simply a warning sign, for example of danger or battle.

During the **French Revolution** red flags appeared as a sign of resistance. In 1871 the **Paris Commune**, a short workers’ uprising in Paris, chose the red flag as its banner. After that the labour movement all over Europe adopted the colour red. Socialist and communist parties made it their emblem.

The flag of the **Soviet Union** showed a golden **hammer and sickle** with a star above it on a red background. The hammer and sickle stood for the workers in the factories and the farmers in the fields. China, Vietnam and North Korea also have a lot of red in their flags. In the GDR, on the other hand, the state flag was black, red and gold with a hammer, a pair of compasses and a wreath of ears of grain.

At the beginning of May 1945, at the end of the Second World War, Soviet soldiers raised a red flag on the **Reichstag** in Berlin. The photographer Yevgeny Khaldei took a picture of it that became world-famous. It became a symbol of the Soviet Union’s victory over Nazi Germany. The photo was partly staged and was later even slightly retouched.

In Switzerland the **Social Democratic Party** and the trade unions use the colour red, even though they are democratic parties. At demonstrations for Labour Day on 1 May you can see many red flags in Zurich or Bern. The red Swiss flag with the white cross, however, has nothing to do with communism. It goes back to the old coat of arms of the canton of Schwyz.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign that stands for an idea or a group.
Tools that stand for workers and farmers in communism.
The joining together of workers who fought for better wages and rights.
An uprising in Paris in 1871 that lasted only about two months.

gewusst: On 25 December 1991 the red flag of the Soviet Union was lowered over the Kremlin in Moscow for the last time.
In English, “red flag” today often simply means a warning sign.
Not only communists use red: many very different countries also have red flags, for example Switzerland or Japan.

teile.einleitung: “Wall woodpeckers” (Mauerspechte) was the name for the people who knocked pieces out of the Berlin Wall after it fell in November 1989. With hammers and chisels they pecked at the concrete like a woodpecker. Many kept the pieces as souvenirs.
wichtigste: After the fall of the wall, wall woodpeckers knocked pieces out of the Berlin Wall.
They mostly worked with hammers and chisels.
The name comes from the woodpecker, which pecks at wood.
All along the wall you could hear knocking and hammering.
Many pieces of wall were colourfully painted on the western side.
Today pieces of the wall can be found in many countries of the world.

abschnitte.text: From **1961** to **1989**, the **Berlin Wall** separated the east and west of the city. The government of the **GDR** had it built so that people could not flee to the West. Border guards watched it closely. On **9 November 1989** the border was unexpectedly opened. Thousands of people celebrated at and on the wall.

In the days and weeks after the **fall of the wall**, many people came to the wall with **hammers and chisels**. They knocked small pieces out of the concrete. Like a **woodpecker** pecking at wood, they kept knocking tirelessly. That is why they were called **wall woodpeckers**. In many places you could hear constant **knocking and hammering**. They no longer had to be afraid of border guards.

On the **West Berlin** side, the wall had been painted with **graffiti** over many years. On the eastern side it was mostly grey, because nobody was allowed to get close to it. That is why many of the pieces knocked off were **colourful** on one side. These coloured pieces were especially sought after.

Many wall woodpeckers kept the pieces as **souvenirs**. Some also **sold** them to tourists. In this way pieces of the wall were taken **all over the world** and given as presents. From 1990 the wall was then officially dismantled. Today **pieces of the wall** can be found in museums, parks and homes in many countries.

gewusst: Because of all the holes made by the wall woodpeckers, in places you could already see right through the wall.
On the night of 9 November 1989, the border opened first at Bornholmer Strasse in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: The Politburo Standing Committee is a small circle at the top of the Communist Party of China. Because the party leads the state, it is in practice the most important centre of power in the country.
wichtigste: Since 2012 the Standing Committee has had seven members.
From 2002 to 2012 it had nine members.
Formally it is elected by the party’s Central Committee.
The Party Congress takes place every five years, most recently in October 2022.
The order of the members shows their rank.

abschnitte.text: In China there is only one leading party, the **Communist Party of China** (CPC). It has several levels: the Party Congress, the **Central Committee**, the **Politburo** and, at the very top, the **Standing Committee**. The most important decisions are taken in this small circle. Because the party steers the state, the committee is in practice China’s centre of power. It does not meet in public.

The **Party Congress** of the CPC takes place **every five years**. The 19th Party Congress was in 2017, and the 20th in October 2022. Afterwards the new Central Committee, at its first session, the **plenum**, elects the Politburo and the Standing Committee. But this election is mainly a formality. The choice is agreed beforehand among the party leadership.

From 2002 to 2012 the body had nine members, and since the 18th Party Congress in 2012 it has had **seven**. In 2022, 24 people were elected to the Politburo, and the seven members of the Standing Committee are among them. The **order** of the members is important: in first place is the **General Secretary**, who since 2012 has been Xi Jinping. The **premier** is usually in second place. Since March 2023 this has been **Li Qiang**.

gewusst: At public appearances the members walk onto the stage in order of rank.
Before becoming premier, Li Qiang was party leader of Shanghai.

teile.einleitung: The National People’s Army, NVA for short, was the army of the GDR. It existed from 1956 to 1990 and was part of the Warsaw Pact. After the reunification of Germany it was disbanded.
wichtigste: The NVA was founded in 1956; 1 March was regarded as its founding day.
From 1962 there was general conscription in the GDR.
From 1964 anyone who did not want to carry a weapon could become a construction soldier.
The NVA was part of the armed forces of the Warsaw Pact.
The Ministry of Defence was in Strausberg near Berlin.
In 1990 the NVA was disbanded, and parts of it went to the Bundeswehr.

abschnitte.text: Even before the NVA there were armed units in the GDR, the **Barracked People’s Police**. In January 1956 the National People’s Army was created by law. From then on **1 March** was regarded as its founding day. The NVA was integrated into the armed forces of the **Warsaw Pact**. That was the name of the military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies.

At first, service in the NVA was voluntary. Only in January 1962, after the Berlin Wall had been built, did the GDR introduce **general conscription**. Before that, it would probably have driven even more young men to flee to the West. There was no civilian alternative service. From 1964 anyone who refused to serve with a weapon could become a **construction soldier**, but often had to expect disadvantages in their education and career.

The **Ministry of National Defence** and the NVA command were based in **Strausberg**, east of Berlin. Strausberg lies in what is today the federal state of Brandenburg. From 1960 to 1985 **Heinz Hoffmann** was defence minister. He led the ministry for 25 years until his death. His successor was **Heinz Kessler**.

With **reunification** on 3 October 1990 the GDR ceased to exist. As a result, the NVA was also disbanded. Some of the soldiers and a lot of equipment were taken over by the **Bundeswehr**, the army of the Federal Republic. Many weapons and vehicles were later scrapped or sold. So the history of the second German army ended after only 34 years.

gewusst: The construction soldiers in the GDR wore a small spade as a badge on their shoulder.
The GDR was one of the few Warsaw Pact countries that for a long time had no conscription at all.

teile.einleitung: The revisionism dispute was a major quarrel within German Social Democracy around 1900. It was about whether socialism should be achieved through revolution or through gradual reforms. At its centre was the politician Eduard Bernstein.
wichtigste: Eduard Bernstein wanted to adapt Karl Marx’s teaching to how things had actually developed.
His main work of 1899 is called “The Preconditions of Socialism and the Tasks of Social Democracy”.
Bernstein did not believe that capitalism would collapse soon.
His opponent Karl Kautsky defended orthodox Marxism.
In the long run the reformist line won through in the SPD, especially with the Godesberg Programme of 1959.

abschnitte.text: Karl Marx had predicted that **capitalism** would break down because of its crises. After that the workers were to take power through a **revolution**. Eduard Bernstein saw things differently. He observed that the middle class was not disappearing and that economic crises were becoming milder. That is why he wanted to **revise** the teaching, in other words to rework it. This is where the word **revisionism** comes from.

While Germany’s **Anti-Socialist Laws** were in force, socialist newspapers were banned in Germany. Bernstein therefore ran the newspaper “Der Sozialdemokrat” in **Zurich**. It was printed in Switzerland and smuggled into Germany. In 1888 Bernstein was expelled and went to **London**. There he got to know the **Fabian Society**, a British movement that relied on gradual reforms. He lived in London until 1901.

In 1899 Bernstein’s book “The Preconditions of Socialism and the Tasks of Social Democracy” was published. In it he demanded that the SPD should openly see itself as a **democratic reform party**. His sentence became famous: “The final goal, whatever it may be, is nothing to me; the movement is everything.” What mattered to him were concrete improvements for the workers, such as better wages and more rights.

Many in the SPD rejected Bernstein’s ideas. The most important opponent was **Karl Kautsky**, who was called the “Pope of Marxism”. He published the journal “Die Neue Zeit” and had helped to shape the SPD’s **Erfurt Programme**. **Rosa Luxemburg** also wrote against Bernstein. Officially the party rejected revisionism at that time. In practice, however, it often already worked like a reform party.

In the long run Bernstein’s line won through. With the **Godesberg Programme** of 1959 the SPD finally abandoned Marxism as its foundation. It now saw itself as a **broad-based people’s party** and accepted the market economy. That is why the revisionism dispute is regarded as an important moment in the history of Social Democracy.

gewusst: The newspaper “Der Sozialdemokrat” was printed in Switzerland and secretly taken across the border into Germany.
The term revisionism comes from the Latin word “revidere”, which means “to look at again”.

teile.einleitung: In April 1917 Lenin travelled from his exile in Zurich back to Russia in the “sealed train”. In the middle of the First World War he travelled right across Germany with the permission of the German government. A few months later Lenin’s Bolsheviks took power in Russia.
wichtigste: Lenin left Zurich on Easter Monday, 9 April 1917.
The train crossed into Germany at Thayngen and Gottmadingen.
Germany hoped that Lenin would weaken Russia.
The travellers were not allowed to leave the carriage in Germany.
Just over 30 people travelled with Lenin.
On 16 April 1917 he arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd.

abschnitte.text: During the First World War Lenin lived in exile in **Switzerland**, most recently in **Zurich**. From here he tried to win over the socialists who opposed the war to the idea of a revolution. In 1915 they met in **Zimmerwald** and in April 1916 in the village of **Kiental** in the Bernese Oberland. In February 1917 a revolution broke out in Russia, and the tsar abdicated. Lenin now wanted to return as quickly as possible.

Russia and Germany were **enemies in the war**. Even so, the German government allowed Lenin to travel through. It hoped that he would weaken Russia through unrest and lead it out of the war. Germany could then have used its troops in the West. The revolutionary and businessman **Alexander Parvus** is regarded as the go-between, although Lenin himself did not want to meet him directly.

On Easter Monday, **9 April 1917**, Lenin and just over 30 companions left Zurich, among them Grigory Zinoviev and Karl Radek. At **Thayngen** and Gottmadingen the train crossed the border into Germany. The carriage was **“sealed”**: most of the doors were locked, and nobody was allowed to get out in Germany. From **Sassnitz** on the island of Rügen a ferry took the group to **Trelleborg** in Sweden. They continued to Russia via Stockholm and Finland.

On **16 April 1917**, shortly before midnight, Lenin reached the **Finland Station** in Petrograd. A large crowd welcomed him there. Straight away, in his **April Theses**, he demanded that power be handed over to the councils (soviets). In November 1917 the Bolsheviks took power in the October Revolution. **Winston Churchill** later compared the journey to smuggling dangerous germs into a city.

gewusst: In Zurich Lenin lived on Spiegelgasse in the old town.
The journey was organised with the help of the Swiss socialist Fritz Platten, who accompanied Lenin.

teile.einleitung: In the autumn of 1956 hundreds of thousands of people in Hungary rose up against the communist government and the rule of the Soviet Union. For a few days it looked as though Hungary might become free. Then Soviet tanks crushed the uprising with bloodshed.
wichtigste: The uprising began on 23 October 1956 with a student demonstration in Budapest.
People toppled a huge statue of Stalin in Budapest.
The reformist politician Imre Nagy became head of government and announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact.
On 4 November 1956 Soviet troops attacked and ended the uprising.
About 2,500 Hungarians were killed.
About 200,000 people fled abroad, more than 10,000 of them to Switzerland.
Today 23 October is a national holiday in Hungary.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War **Hungary** came under the influence of the Soviet Union. The Communist Party ruled with an iron fist, and a secret police kept watch on people. Many farmers had to give up their land, and food was scarce. After Stalin’s death in 1953 many people hoped for more freedom.

On 23 October 1956 students in **Budapest** demonstrated for freedom of speech, free elections and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Thousands joined in, and the people pulled the eight-metre-high **Stalin statue** off its pedestal. When the secret police fired on the crowd, the demonstration turned into an armed uprising. Workers, students and even teenagers fought against the police and Soviet soldiers.

The popular communist **Imre Nagy** became head of government and promised reforms. At the end of October the Soviet troops at first withdrew from Budapest. On 1 November Nagy declared that Hungary was leaving the **Warsaw Pact** and wanted to become neutral. The Soviet Union was determined not to allow this.

On 4 November 1956 thousands of Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. After fierce fighting the uprising was crushed within a few days. The Soviet Union installed **János Kádár** as the new head of government. Imre Nagy was arrested and executed in 1958 after a secret trial.
