About 200,000 people fled across the border into Austria and from there on to many countries. Switzerland took in more than 10,000 Hungarian **refugees**, and the population was very willing to help. Many of these people found a new home here. In 1989 Imre Nagy was solemnly reburied in Budapest, and 23 October became a **national holiday**.

begriffe.erklaerung: When many people in a country rise up against their government.
A police force that secretly watches people and persecutes opponents of the government.
When a country does not belong to any military alliance, like Switzerland.
A person who has had to flee their home because they were in danger there.

gewusst: All that was left of the toppled Stalin statue in Budapest were the boots, a copy of which now stands in Memento Park.
In December 1956, at the Olympic Games in Melbourne, Hungary and the Soviet Union played such a rough water polo match that it became known as the “Blood in the Water” match.
At the time the world was also distracted by the Suez Crisis, which was happening at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 was one of the most dangerous moments of the Cold War. The Soviet Union had secretly set up nuclear missiles in Cuba. For thirteen days the world feared a nuclear war between the USA and the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The Soviet Union secretly stationed nuclear missiles in Cuba.
On 14 October 1962 a U-2 spy plane photographed the missile sites.
President Kennedy responded with a naval blockade around Cuba.
Kennedy's opponent was Nikita Khrushchev.
By the usual count, the crisis lasted 13 days.
The USA secretly promised to withdraw its missiles from Turkey.
Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba.

abschnitte.text: **Fidel Castro** had taken power in **Cuba** in 1959. In April 1961 the **Bay of Pigs invasion** failed: Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed in Cuba but were quickly defeated. After that, Castro looked even more to the **Soviet Union** for protection. He agreed that it could set up **missiles with nuclear warheads** in Cuba. These could reach many cities in the USA.

On **14 October 1962**, a US **U-2 reconnaissance plane** photographed the launch sites. On **16 October**, President **John F. Kennedy** saw the aerial photographs. The **thirteen days** of the crisis are counted from this day. Kennedy discussed with his closest advisers how he should respond.

Kennedy had the US Navy seal Cuba off so that no more missiles could arrive. He called the **naval blockade** a **“quarantine”**. Soviet ships sailed towards the blockade, and the tension was enormous. Kennedy and the Soviet leader **Nikita Khrushchev** exchanged letters and looked for a solution.

On **28 October 1962**, Moscow agreed to **withdraw the missiles**. Publicly, the USA promised not to attack Cuba. Secretly, it also promised to withdraw its **Jupiter missiles** from **Turkey**. After the crisis, both sides set up a direct line between Washington and Moscow, the **“hotline”**.

The USA and Cuba had had no diplomatic relations since 1961. That is why **Switzerland** took on a **protecting power mandate**: it represented the interests of the USA in **Havana**. In this way it helped communication during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Switzerland held this mandate until **2015**.

gewusst: On 27 October 1962, a US U-2 plane was shot down over Cuba, and the pilot was killed.
In Cuba the crisis is called the “October Crisis” and in Russia the “Caribbean Crisis”.

teile.einleitung: In an absolute monarchy a king or queen has all the power. No constitution and no parliament limit the ruler. This form of state was widespread in Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries, and some countries still have it today.
wichtigste: In an absolute monarchy the monarch has all the power, without being limited by a constitution.
He combines law-making, government and the courts.
Louis XIV of France is regarded as the very model of absolutism.
Absolute rulers claimed the divine right of kings.
Today, for example, Saudi Arabia, Eswatini and Vatican City are absolute monarchies (as of 2025).
Frederick II of Prussia called himself the “first servant of the state”.

abschnitte.text: In an **absolute monarchy** all power lies with one person, the **monarch**. He makes the laws, governs and judges. It is said that he combines the three **powers of the state**. No constitution limits him, and nobody can check him. This power was often justified by the **divine right of kings**: the king was said to have his power directly from God and so did not have to answer to anyone.

**Louis XIV**, the “Sun King”, is regarded as the very model of **absolutism**. He ruled France from 1643 to 1715. The sentence “I am the state” is attributed to him. From 1661 he had the palace of **Versailles** magnificently extended and made it the seat of the court. The nobility had to live there and so were under his control.

In the 18th century the ideas of the **Enlightenment** spread. Some rulers continued to rule absolutely, but wanted to serve the good of the state. **Frederick II** of Prussia called himself the “**first servant of the state**”. This is known as **enlightened absolutism**. With the French Revolution of 1789 and the later constitutions, the age of absolute monarchies in Europe slowly came to an end.

Today there are only a few absolute monarchies left (as of 2025). In **Saudi Arabia** the king has supreme power, and there is no elected parliament. According to the Basic Law of 1992, the **Quran** and the **Sunna** are regarded as the constitution. In **Eswatini**, called Swaziland until 2018, King **Mswati III** has ruled with very far-reaching powers since 1986. **Vatican City** is an absolute **elective monarchy**: the Pope holds all the powers of the state and is elected by the cardinals.

Not every monarchy is absolute. In **Sweden**, **Spain** or **Great Britain** there is a king, but parliament makes the laws. They are called **parliamentary monarchies**. **Lesotho** in southern Africa is also a constitutional monarchy, in which a constitution limits the king’s power. Switzerland never had a king and is a federal state with rights for the people.

gewusst: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years, longer than almost any other monarch in Europe.
Vatican City is the smallest state in the world and at the same time an absolute monarchy.

teile.einleitung: The Arab Spring was a wave of protests that began in Tunisia at the end of 2010. Many people in Arab countries demanded freedom, jobs and an end to corruption.
wichtigste: The protests began in Tunisia in December 2010.
They were triggered when the vegetable seller Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire.
In Egypt Hosni Mubarak resigned in February 2011.
In Syria the protests turned into a long civil war.
Tunisia is regarded as the only country in which a democracy initially emerged.
The name recalls the Prague Spring of 1968.

abschnitte.text: On 17 December 2010 the vegetable seller **Mohamed Bouazizi** set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid. He was protesting against harassment by the authorities and died at the beginning of January 2011. His fate sparked protests throughout the country. In January 2011 President **Ben Ali** fled abroad after 23 years in power.

At the end of January 2011 hundreds of thousands gathered in **Tahrir Square** in Cairo. On 11 February 2011 **Hosni Mubarak**, who had ruled Egypt since 1981, resigned. In 2012 **Mohamed Morsi** became the first freely elected president. But in July 2013, after mass protests, the **army** under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi removed him from office again.

Many of the demonstrators were young. They used **social media** such as Facebook and Twitter as well as mobile phone videos to organise protests. Calls to action and pictures spread very quickly, even across national borders. That is why some governments shut down the internet for a time.

In **Bahrain** the protests on **Pearl Roundabout** in Manama were crushed, and the monument there was demolished. In Libya and Yemen there were wars. In **Syria** the government of Bashar al-Assad violently suppressed the protests, which led to a civil war with millions of refugees. Only **Tunisia** gave itself a democratic constitution in 2014, even though democracy there was later weakened again.

In 2011 the Federal Council had assets of the overthrown rulers of Tunisia and Egypt in Swiss banks frozen. The name “Arab Spring” recalls the **Prague Spring** of 1968 in Czechoslovakia. Spring stands for a new start and renewal.

gewusst: In 2015 four Tunisian organisations were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their mediation in the transition to democracy.
Pearl Roundabout in Bahrain was named after a monument with a large pearl.

teile.einleitung: In the Soviet Union, “nomenklatura” was the name for the list of important posts that the Communist Party decided how to fill. Later the people in these posts were called that too. They formed a privileged ruling class.
wichtigste: The nomenklatura was originally a list of leading posts that the party filled.
Later the word also referred to the people in these posts.
The Politburo decided on the highest posts.
The nomenklatura enjoyed privileges such as special shops and dachas.
Milovan Djilas and Michael Voslensky described it as a new ruling class.
After 1991 many former officials took over state-owned companies.

abschnitte.text: The word **nomenklatura** comes from the Latin word for a list of names. In the Soviet Union it was a list of important posts in the state, the economy and culture. For each of these posts a party committee decided who got it. The **Politburo** decided on the highest posts, while the Secretariat of the Central Committee or regional party committees decided on less important ones. State bodies merely confirmed these decisions as a formality.

Anyone who belonged to the nomenklatura lived better than most people. The elite could buy goods in closed **special shops** that were otherwise hard to get. On top of that there were **dachas**, meaning country houses, as well as official cars and their own hospitals. For ordinary citizens much of this remained out of reach. This contradicted the goal of a classless society.

As early as 1957 the Yugoslav communist **Milovan Djilas** wrote the book **“The New Class”**. He accused the party officials of forming a new ruling class. For this he spent several years in prison. In 1980 **Michael Voslensky** published his book “Nomenklatura”. He had himself been a Soviet official and had stayed in the West in 1972.

abschnitte.titel: After the end of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, many state-owned companies were privatised. Former officials often used their position and their knowledge to take over companies cheaply. This process is called **nomenklatura privatisation**. In this way political power turned into economic ownership. There were similar developments in other former Eastern Bloc countries too.

gewusst: Voslensky estimated that about 750,000 people belonged to the Soviet nomenklatura.
Other communist states, such as the GDR and Poland, also adopted the term nomenklatura.

teile.einleitung: In December 1989 the people of Romania overthrew the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu. Unlike in most other countries of Eastern Europe, this upheaval was very bloody. It began in the city of Timișoara and soon reached the capital, Bucharest.
wichtigste: The revolution began on 16 December 1989 in Timișoara, in German Temeswar.
It was triggered by the threatened eviction of the pastor László Tőkés.
At Ceaușescu’s last speech on 21 December, the crowd booed him.
On 22 December Ceaușescu fled Bucharest in a helicopter.
About 1,100 people died in the fighting.
Ion Iliescu became the new head of state.

abschnitte.text: **Nicolae Ceaușescu** had ruled Romania as a communist dictator since 1965. People suffered from shortages of food, electricity and heating. The feared secret police, the **Securitate**, kept watch on the population. Anyone who voiced criticism had to expect harsh punishments. In 1989 the communist governments fell in many neighbouring countries, but Ceaușescu clung to power.

In **Timișoara**, in German Temeswar, the Hungarian Reformed pastor **László Tőkés** openly criticised the regime. He was therefore to be forcibly transferred. Members of his congregation and other citizens stood in front of his flat to protect him. On **16 December 1989** this turned into a protest against the government. The security forces fired on the people, but the uprising spread across the whole country.

On **21 December** Ceaușescu gave a big speech in Bucharest. Instead of cheering, **the crowd whistled and booed**. The television broadcast was cut off, but many people had seen him losing his grip on power. On **22 December** Ceaușescu and his wife Elena fled from the roof of the party building in a **helicopter**. Rebels occupied the **television building** and broadcast live. That is why people spoke of a revolution on television.

The Ceaușescus were soon captured. In a barracks in **Târgoviște** both were condemned in a hasty trial and executed. During the days of the revolution, parts of the Securitate fought against the rebels. In total about **1,100 people** died. Power was taken over by the **National Salvation Front** under **Ion Iliescu**. In May 1990 he was elected president.

gewusst: The Romanian Revolution was the only upheaval in the Eastern Bloc in 1989 in which the head of state was executed.
At that time a sizeable German-speaking minority, the Banat Swabians, also lived in Timișoara.

teile.einleitung: The Sandinista National Liberation Front, FSLN for short, is a left-wing party in Nicaragua in Central America. In 1979 it overthrew the dictatorship of the Somoza family. To this day it shapes the country’s politics.
wichtigste: The FSLN is named after Augusto César Sandino.
It was founded in 1961 by Carlos Fonseca and Tomás Borge, among others.
In 1979 it overthrew the Somoza family dictatorship.
In the 1980s the Contras, supported by the USA, fought against it.
In 1990 it lost the election to Violeta Chamorro.
Since 2007 Daniel Ortega has been president again (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: From 1927 to 1933 **Augusto César Sandino** fought against the occupation of Nicaragua by the USA. In 1934 he was murdered. In Nicaragua he is regarded as a **national hero**. In 1961 **Carlos Fonseca**, **Tomás Borge** and others founded the FSLN and named it after him. Their model was the **Cuban Revolution**. They wanted to overthrow the dictatorship that had been in power since the 1930s.

The **Somoza** family ruled Nicaragua with an iron fist for decades. In the 1970s resistance grew throughout the country. After long fighting the dictator **Anastasio Somoza Debayle** fled. On **19 July 1979** the Sandinistas entered the capital, **Managua**. In 1980 they carried out a big **literacy campaign**: young volunteers taught people all over the country to read and write.

The USA saw the Sandinistas as a danger. It supported rebels known as the **Contras**. They fought mainly from **Honduras**. A secret way of funding them through arms sales to Iran became known as the **Iran-Contra affair**. In 1986 the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague ruled that the USA had broken international law by supporting the Contras and mining harbours. The USA did not recognise the ruling.

In the 1980s many volunteers from Europe travelled to Nicaragua to help. One of them was **Maurice Demierre** from **Bulle** in the canton of Fribourg. He worked in agriculture. On 16 February 1986 he was killed in a Contra ambush. He was the first Swiss development worker to die in the Contra War. His death moved many people in Switzerland.

In 1990 the Sandinistas lost the presidential election to **Violeta Barrios de Chamorro**. **Daniel Ortega**, president from 1985 to 1990, handed over power peacefully. In 2007 he returned to office. Since 2025 he has shared it with his wife **Rosario Murillo** as co-president (as of 2026). Critics accuse the government of ruling in an increasingly authoritarian way and suppressing opponents.

gewusst: The FSLN flag is red and black.
Thanks to the literacy campaign, the proportion of people who could not read and write fell considerably.

teile.einleitung: The October Revolution was the seizure of power in Russia by the Bolsheviks under Lenin in 1917. It marked the beginning of the world’s first communist regime. The Soviet Union later grew out of it.
wichtigste: The October Revolution took place in 1917 in Petrograd, today’s St Petersburg.
It was led by Lenin and the Bolsheviks.
According to the old Russian calendar it was 25 October; according to ours it was 7 November.
The revolutionaries occupied the Winter Palace, the seat of the government.
Lenin promised “peace, land and bread”.
A bloody civil war followed, lasting until about 1922.
In 1922 the Soviet Union was founded.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Russia was ruled by the **tsar**, an emperor with almost unlimited power. In the First World War Russia lost many soldiers, and there was hunger in the cities. In February 1917, after mass protests, Tsar Nicholas II abdicated; this was the **February Revolution**. After that a provisional government ruled, but it continued the war.

At that time **Lenin** was living in exile in Zurich. In April 1917, with the help of the German government, he travelled back to Russia on a train through Germany. Germany hoped that he would lead Russia out of the war. In Petrograd he won support for the Bolsheviks with the slogan “peace, land and bread”.

During the night of 25 October 1917 by the old calendar, armed workers, soldiers and sailors occupied important buildings in **Petrograd**. Leon Trotsky had helped to organise the uprising. A shot from the cruiser **Aurora** is regarded as the signal for the storming of the **Winter Palace**. There the government ministers were arrested, and the Bolsheviks took power.

In March 1918 the new government made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk. It took land and factories away from large landowners and factory owners. Many opponents, the so-called **Whites**, fought against the **Red Army**, and millions of people died in the war, from hunger and from epidemics. In 1918 the tsar’s family was also murdered.

At the end of 1922 the Bolsheviks founded the **Soviet Union**. The October Revolution became a model for communist movements all over the world. Instead of freedom, however, it brought a one-party dictatorship with a secret police and labour camps. In Switzerland a general strike took place in November 1918, which some politicians at the time wrongly saw as an attempted revolution on the Russian model.

begriffe.erklaerung: Lenin’s radical party, which took power in 1917.
The title of the Russian emperor.
A temporary government that is only meant to last for a certain time.
The former palace of the tsars in St Petersburg, today part of the Hermitage Museum.

gewusst: Because Russia still used the old Julian calendar at the time, the Soviet Union celebrated the October Revolution every year in November.
The cruiser Aurora is still moored in St Petersburg today as a museum ship.

teile.einleitung: P-26 was a secret organisation in Switzerland at the time of the Cold War. Its job was to prepare resistance in case the country was occupied. In 1990 a parliamentary commission of inquiry uncovered it, and afterwards it was dissolved.
wichtigste: P-26 was intended as a resistance organisation in case of an occupation.
The PUK EMD commission of inquiry under Councillor of States Carlo Schmid made it public in 1990.
It was led by Efrem Cattelan under the code name “Rico”.
When it was dissolved in 1990 it had about 320 members.
Alongside it there was a secret intelligence service called P-27.

abschnitte.text: During the Cold War people in Switzerland feared an attack from the East. In the event of an **occupation**, **P-26** was meant to keep up the population’s will to resist. It did not have an actual combat mission. The name refers to **paragraph 426** of the Federal Council’s 1973 report on security policy, which deals with resistance in occupied territory. The members were organised in small **cells**; 800 people were planned, and when it was dissolved there were about 320.

From 1979 to 1990 General Staff Colonel **Efrem Cattelan** led the organisation under the code name “Rico”. The magazine “Weltwoche” revealed his identity in November 1990. From 1983 P-26 used a secret fortress in **Gstaad** with the cover name “Schweizerhof”. It was used for training and command. Besides P-26 there was the secret intelligence service **P-27**, outside the normal structures.

In 1990 a **Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry**, or PUK for short, investigated what was then the Military Department, the EMD. Under Councillor of States **Carlo Schmid** it presented its report in November 1990 and made P-26 public. The main criticism was that parliament and the public had known nothing about it. The organisation was then dissolved. In 1991 the examining magistrate **Pierre Cornu** found no cooperation with NATO or the CIA, but close links with British agencies.

gewusst: Many members of P-26 knew only a few other members, so that if someone was captured, the whole organisation could not be betrayed.

teile.einleitung: The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia in 1989. It is called that because it happened almost without violence. Within a few weeks the writer Václav Havel became president.
wichtigste: The Velvet Revolution took place in Czechoslovakia in November and December 1989.
It began on 17 November 1989 with a student demonstration in Prague.
On 19 November the citizens’ movement Civic Forum was founded.
The demonstrators jingled their keys.
On 29 December 1989 Václav Havel was elected president.
In 1993 the country split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

abschnitte.text: On **17 November 1989** students marched through **Prague**. What was officially allowed was a commemoration of 1939: at that time the German occupiers had closed the Czech universities after the student **Jan Opletal** had died. But the demonstration also became a protest against the government. The police attacked the students brutally. After that, hundreds of thousands took to the streets every day.

On **19 November** civil rights campaigners in Prague founded **Civic Forum** (Občanské fórum). A similar movement was formed in Slovakia. Huge crowds gathered in **Wenceslas Square**. They jingled their **bunches of keys**. This meant: you can lock up now and go home. A general strike showed that the whole country was behind the protests.

The government had to negotiate with Civic Forum. On 10 December President **Gustáv Husák** swore in a new government and then resigned. On 28 December **Alexander Dubček** became chairman of the parliament. In 1968, in the **Prague Spring**, he had attempted “socialism with a human face”. On **29 December 1989** the playwright and civil rights campaigner **Václav Havel** was elected president.

**Velvet** is a soft, smooth fabric. The name shows that the change of power was gentle and happened without bloodshed. The end of the joint state was peaceful too. On **1 January 1993** Czechoslovakia became two countries: the **Czech Republic** and **Slovakia**. That is why people also speak of the “Velvet Divorce”.

gewusst: As a critic of the regime, Václav Havel had spent several years in prison before he became president.
Today 17 November is a public day of remembrance in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

teile.einleitung: The national strike (Landesstreik) of November 1918 was the largest strike in Swiss history. Around 250,000 workers stopped working. After three days it was called off, but many of its demands were later put into practice.
wichtigste: The national strike began on 12 November 1918.
It was led by the Olten Action Committee under Robert Grimm.
On the first day, around 250,000 people went on strike.
The Federal Council had large army units deployed.
In Grenchen, soldiers shot dead three young watch workers.
The 48-hour week came in 1919, but the AVS only in 1948.
Robert Grimm was sentenced to six months in prison.

abschnitte.titel: Hardship in the First World War
abschnitte.text: Switzerland stayed neutral in the **First World War**, but many families suffered hardship. Food became expensive and scarce, and wages were not enough. At the same time, some companies made a lot of money. The workers' movement became more and more dissatisfied. In **February 1918**, the Social Democrats and the trade unions founded the **Olten Action Committee**. Its president was the Bern Social Democrat **Robert Grimm**.

General **Ulrich Wille** had already been pressing for a large deployment of troops in the cities. In November 1918 the Federal Council sent soldiers to Zurich. The committee then called the **national strike**. On **12 November 1918**, around **250,000** people stopped working, especially in industry and on the railways. After an ultimatum from the Federal Council, the committee called off the strike on **14 November**.

On **14 November 1918**, soldiers in **Grenchen** in the canton of Solothurn shot at strikers. Three young **watch workers** aged 17 to 29 were killed. Nobody was convicted for this. In 1919 Robert Grimm, Fritz Platten and Friedrich Schneider were brought before a **military court**. They were each sentenced to **six months in prison**.

The committee put forward **nine demands**. They included the **48-hour week**, **women's right to vote**, the election of the National Council by **proportional representation** and **old-age and survivors' insurance**. Proportional representation came as early as 1919, and the 48-hour week came in 1919 through the Factory Act. The **AVS** only came into force on **1 January 1948**. Women had to wait until 1971 for the right to vote at federal level.

Robert Grimm was a well-known politician of the workers' movement. In **1915** he organised the **Zimmerwald Conference** in the canton of Bern. There, opponents of the war from the socialist movement in several countries met, including **Lenin**. Grimm is still regarded today as the face of the national strike. Later he even became president of the National Council.

gewusst: During the national strike, the Spanish flu was also raging, and many soldiers fell ill with it.
The Olten Action Committee got its name from the town of Olten, where it first met.

teile.einleitung: The Yalta Conference was a meeting of the three most important Allies in February 1945. Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin discussed what should happen after the victory over Germany. Their decisions shaped Europe for decades.
wichtigste: The conference took place from 4 to 11 February 1945.
Yalta is on the Crimean peninsula on the Black Sea.
Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin are called the “Big Three”.
Germany was to be divided into occupation zones.
Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan.
The founding of the United Nations was prepared.
The Potsdam Conference followed in the summer of 1945.

abschnitte.text: Yalta is a resort on the southern coast of the **Crimean** peninsula on the **Black Sea**. The conference met in the **Livadia Palace** from **4 to 11 February 1945**. The Second World War in Europe was almost over at that time. The Allied troops were advancing on Germany from the west and the east.

At Yalta **Franklin D. Roosevelt** met for the USA, **Winston Churchill** for Great Britain and **Joseph Stalin** for the Soviet Union. They are called the **“Big Three”**. Although they were fighting Germany together, they had different aims. The Western states wanted democracy, while Stalin wanted to secure the Soviet Union's influence in Eastern Europe.

The Allies decided to divide Germany into **occupation zones** after the victory. **France** was also to receive its own zone. **Poland's** borders were to be moved **westwards**. The Soviet Union kept eastern Poland. In compensation, Poland was to receive territory in the west at Germany's expense.

**Stalin** promised to fight against **Japan** three months after the end of the war in Europe. In **August 1945** the Soviet Union did indeed declare war on Japan. The three powers also prepared the **United Nations**. They agreed on a founding conference in **San Francisco**, where the UN Charter was signed in June 1945.

Roosevelt died in April 1945. So at the **Potsdam Conference** near Berlin in July and August 1945, **Harry S. Truman** represented the USA. Many people see Yalta as a beginning of the division of Europe into East and West. This division lasted throughout the **Cold War**.

gewusst: The Livadia Palace used to be a summer residence of the Russian tsars.
Roosevelt was already seriously ill at the conference and died two months later.

teile.einleitung: The Moscow Kremlin is an old fortress in the middle of Moscow, the capital of Russia. Behind its red walls stand palaces, churches and government buildings. Today it is the official seat of the Russian president.
wichtigste: The Kremlin is a fortress with palaces, churches and government buildings.
The Russian word “kreml” means castle or fortress.
The red brick wall is more than two kilometres long and has many towers.
The Kremlin lies on the Moskva, the river that gave Moscow its name.
Since 1918 Russia, at that time the Soviet Union, has been governed from the Kremlin.
Today the Russian president works here.

abschnitte.titel: A castle in the heart of the city
abschnitte.text: A **kremlin** is a fortified castle in the centre of an old Russian town. Novgorod, Kazan and other cities also have a kremlin, but the one in Moscow is the best known. It stands on a hill on the bank of the **Moskva**. Right next to the wall lies **Red Square**. Together, the Kremlin and Red Square are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The **Kremlin wall** is made of red bricks and is more than two kilometres long. Many towers rise up from it. On top of five towers sit large **stars made of red glass**, which glow from inside at night. The best-known tower is the **Spasskaya Tower** with its large clock and chimes. Its bells ring in the New Year in Russia.

abschnitte.titel: Churches, palaces and a giant bell
abschnitte.text: Inside stand several old **cathedrals** with golden domes. This is where the tsars used to be crowned. There are also large palaces and government buildings. Particularly famous is the **Tsar Bell**, the largest bell in the world. A large piece has broken off, so it has never rung.

In March 1918 **Lenin** moved the seat of the Soviet government from Petrograd to the Kremlin in Moscow. Lenin lived and worked in the **Senate Palace**. After that, all Soviet leaders governed from the Kremlin. Today it is the official seat of the **Russian president**. That is why people often say “the Kremlin” when they mean the Russian government.

gewusst: The Tsar Bell is so heavy that it could never be hung up. It stands on a plinth on the ground.
The red stars on the towers glow at night because lamps burn inside them.

teile.einleitung: Solidarność is Polish and means “solidarity”. It was the name of the first free trade union in the communist Eastern Bloc, which was formed in Poland in 1980. With its leader Lech Wałęsa it played a decisive part in the peaceful end of communism in Poland and across Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: Solidarność was founded in the summer of 1980 after big strikes at the shipyard in Gdańsk.
Its leader was the electrician Lech Wałęsa.
Soon the trade union had about ten million members.
In December 1981 martial law was declared and Solidarność was banned.
Lech Wałęsa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983.
In 1989 Solidarność won the first partly free elections in Poland.
Lech Wałęsa was president of Poland from 1990 to 1995.

abschnitte.text: **Solidarność** is a **trade union**, in other words an association of employees that stands up for their rights. In communist Poland the party controlled all trade unions, and there was no real say. Solidarność was the first independent trade union in an Eastern Bloc country. It quickly became a big movement for freedom and democracy.

In August 1980 the workers at the **Lenin Shipyard** in Gdańsk, in German Danzig, went on strike. The triggers were rising food prices and the dismissal of a woman crane operator. The strikers drew up 21 demands, including free trade unions and freedom of speech. On 31 August 1980 the government had to accept many of the demands in the **Gdańsk Agreement**.

**Lech Wałęsa** was an electrician at the shipyard and became the leader of the strikers. He was a courageous speaker who could inspire many people. The movement was also supported by the Catholic Church and by the Polish Pope John Paul II. In 1983 Wałęsa was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

On 13 December 1981 General **Wojciech Jaruzelski** declared martial law in Poland. Tanks stood in the streets, and thousands of Solidarność members were arrested. The trade union was banned, but carried on working secretly **underground**. It printed banned newspapers and organised protests.

abschnitte.titel: The Round Table and the change
abschnitte.text: In 1989 the government negotiated reforms with Solidarność at the **Round Table**. In the elections on 4 June 1989, Solidarność candidates won almost all the seats they were allowed to stand for. With Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a man from the movement became the first non-communist head of government in the Eastern Bloc. This encouraged people in the GDR, Czechoslovakia and other countries to stand up for freedom too.

begriffe.erklaerung: An association of employees that fights for good wages and working conditions.
Sticking together and helping one another.
When employees stop working together in order to achieve something.
A state of emergency in which the army gains a lot of power in the country.

gewusst: The red Solidarność logo with its wobbly letters was designed by a graphic artist in 1980 and is still known around the world today.
Lech Wałęsa could not collect the Nobel Prize himself in 1983; his wife received it in Oslo.
Gdańsk airport is named after Lech Wałęsa today.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Stalingrad was one of the biggest battles of the Second World War. It lasted from 1942 until early 1943 and ended with a heavy defeat for the German Wehrmacht. It is regarded as the turning point of the war.
wichtigste: Stalingrad lies on the Volga and is called Volgograd today.
The German Sixth Army was led by Friedrich Paulus.
With Operation Uranus the Red Army encircled the Germans in November 1942.
At the end of January and beginning of February 1943 the German troops surrendered.
About 90,000 German soldiers were taken prisoner.
The statue “The Motherland Calls” commemorates the battle.

abschnitte.text: The city stretches a long way along the west bank of the **Volga**. Until 1925 it was called Tsaritsyn; then it was named after the Soviet dictator **Stalin**. Since 1961 it has been called **Volgograd**. The Volga was an important transport route, especially for oil from the south. That is why the German Wehrmacht wanted to capture the city in 1942.

In the summer of 1942 the German **Sixth Army** under **Friedrich Paulus** reached the city. Months of fighting followed, often over individual streets and houses. The city was almost completely destroyed. But the Soviet troops held on to a narrow strip on the bank of the Volga. It was a terrible time for the civilian population too.

On **19 November 1942** the **Red Army** began **Operation Uranus**. It attacked to the north and south of the city. A few days later the ring around the Germans was closed; this is known as the **Stalingrad pocket**. In winter those trapped inside lacked food, ammunition and warm clothing. Shortly before the end, Paulus was promoted to field marshal. Even so, he was taken prisoner at the end of January 1943, and at the beginning of February the last troops surrendered.

About **90,000** German soldiers were taken prisoner. Only about 6,000 of them returned home years later. A great many people died on both sides. After Stalingrad Germany lost the **initiative** in the East, in other words the ability to attack on its own terms. After that the Red Army pushed the Wehrmacht back step by step. That is why the battle is regarded as the **turning point** of the Second World War.

On **Mamayev Kurgan** (Mamayev Hill) in Volgograd there is a huge memorial. At its centre is the statue “**The Motherland Calls**”. It shows a woman with a raised sword and was unveiled in 1967. Including the sword, it measures about 85 metres. In Russia the memory of Stalingrad is still very important today.

gewusst: When it was unveiled, the statue “The Motherland Calls” was one of the tallest statues in the world.
Mamayev Kurgan was fiercely fought over during the battle because it gave a view over the city.

teile.einleitung: The Việt Minh was an alliance that fought for the independence of Vietnam. Hồ Chí Minh founded it in 1941. It fought first against the Japanese occupiers and then against the colonial power, France.
wichtigste: Hồ Chí Minh founded the Việt Minh in 1941.
The full name means “League for the Independence of Vietnam”.
The communists led the alliance, but it also brought together other nationalists.
On 2 September 1945 Hồ Chí Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.
From 1946 to 1954 the Việt Minh fought against France in the Indochina War.

abschnitte.text: In 1941, after many years abroad, **Hồ Chí Minh** returned to Vietnam and founded the **Việt Minh**. The full form is **Việt Nam Độc Lập Đồng Minh Hội**, meaning **League for the Independence of Vietnam**. The name stressed the national goal and not communism. The alliance was led by the communists. But it also brought together non-communist **nationalists**.

At that time Vietnam belonged to **French Indochina**. In the Second World War **Japan** occupied Indochina from 1940. In March 1945 the Japanese took full control. The Việt Minh fought against the occupiers. When Japan surrendered in August 1945, it seized the opportunity to **take power**.

On **2 September 1945** in **Hanoi**, Hồ Chí Minh read out the declaration of independence of the **Democratic Republic of Vietnam**. France did not recognise it and wanted its colony back. So in 1946 the **Indochina War**, also called the First Indochina War, began. It lasted until 1954 and ended with France’s withdrawal. In 1954 the states negotiated the end of the war at the **Indochina Conference in Geneva**.

gewusst: The name Việt Minh is a short form of the much longer Vietnamese name.
The negotiations to end the Indochina War took place in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1954.

teile.einleitung: Socialism is a political idea according to which wealth should be shared out more fairly and important factories, land and businesses should belong to the community. It came about in the 19th century, when many workers lived in poverty. For Karl Marx, socialism was a transitional stage on the way to classless communism.
wichtigste: Socialism comes from the Latin word socius, which means companion or comrade.
The idea came about during industrialisation in the 19th century.
Under socialism, factories and raw materials are supposed to belong to the community and not to a few rich individuals.
Karl Marx saw socialism as an intermediate stage before communism.
There are very different strands, from democratic socialism to communist dictatorship.
The states of the Eastern Bloc called themselves socialist.
In Switzerland the Social Democratic Party is one of the big parties.

abschnitte.text: Under **socialism** the **means of production**, in other words factories, machines, land and raw materials, are supposed to belong to everyone together. Profits are not supposed to go to a few owners, but to benefit everyone. Important goals are social equality, fair wages and security for all. Socialists have been arguing for more than 150 years about exactly how this is to be achieved.

During **industrialisation**, men, women and even children often worked twelve hours a day in factories. They earned little and lived in cramped, dirty homes. Thinkers such as Robert Owen in Great Britain looked for fairer ways of living together. In 1848 **Karl Marx** and Friedrich Engels published the Communist Manifesto.

abschnitte.titel: Socialism and communism according to Marx
abschnitte.text: Marx believed that the workers would take power and own the factories together. In this first stage, socialism, there would still be a state and wages according to performance. After that **communism** was to follow, a classless society without a state, in which everyone receives according to their needs. This final stage was never reached anywhere in the world.

Communist parties wanted to achieve socialism through a **revolution**, for example in the Soviet Union from 1917. The states of the Eastern Bloc called themselves socialist, but they were dictatorships with planned economies. **Democratic socialism** and social democracy, on the other hand, want to create more justice step by step through elections and reforms. Many achievements, such as unemployment insurance or paid holidays, go back to this movement.

In 1888 the **Social Democratic Party of Switzerland** was founded. In the general strike of 1918 the workers demanded, among other things, a 48-hour week, votes for women and an old-age insurance scheme. Many of these demands were met later, the AVS (old-age insurance), for example, in 1948. Today the SP is represented in the government and works within the framework of democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything you need to make goods, for example factories and machines.
A society without differences between rich and poor, masters and workers.
A movement that wants to achieve social justice through democracy and elections.
The period when machines and factories replaced work by hand.

gewusst: From 1849 until his death Karl Marx lived in London, where he wrote his main work, “Capital”.
Before the Russian Revolution, Lenin lived in Switzerland for several years, last of all in Zurich, before returning to Russia in 1917.
Some countries still call themselves socialist today, for example Vietnam and Cuba in their official names or their constitutions.

teile.einleitung: The Pan-European Picnic was a celebration on the border between Hungary and Austria on 19 August 1989. During it a border gate was briefly opened, and hundreds of GDR citizens fled to the West. The event is regarded as an important step towards the fall of the Iron Curtain.
wichtigste: The picnic took place near Sopron on 19 August 1989.
A border gate was to be opened symbolically for three hours.
Between 600 and 700 GDR citizens fled to Austria during it.
Its patrons were Otto von Habsburg and Imre Pozsgay.
It was organised by the Paneuropean Union and the Hungarian Democratic Forum.
On 11 September 1989 Hungary opened the border completely for GDR citizens.

abschnitte.text: In May 1989 Hungary began to dismantle its border installations with Austria. On **27 June 1989** the foreign ministers **Gyula Horn** of Hungary and **Alois Mock** of Austria cut through a piece of the border fence in front of the cameras. The pictures went round the world. Many GDR citizens spent their summer holidays in Hungary. They hoped to get to the West from there.

The picnic took place near **Sopron**, in German **Ödenburg**, in the far west of Hungary. It was organised by the **Paneuropean Union** and the **Hungarian Democratic Forum**, an opposition movement. Its patrons were **Otto von Habsburg**, the president of the Paneuropean Union, and the Hungarian politician **Imre Pozsgay**. An old border gate to Burgenland in Austria was to be opened symbolically for **three hours**. It was meant to be a sign of a Europe without borders.

Many GDR citizens had heard about the picnic. On 19 August 1989 between **600 and 700** of them ran through the open gate into Austria in several groups. The Hungarian border guards did not intervene. It was the largest mass escape from the GDR since the Wall had been built in 1961. From Austria the refugees travelled on to the Federal Republic of Germany.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the fall of the Wall
abschnitte.text: During the night of 10 to **11 September 1989** Hungary officially opened its border for GDR citizens. Tens of thousands then travelled to the West via Austria. As a result the GDR lost more and more people and came under heavy pressure. On **9 November 1989** the Berlin Wall fell. Today a memorial near Sopron commemorates the picnic.

gewusst: Otto von Habsburg was the eldest son of the last emperor of Austria-Hungary.
A picnic became one of the most important events on the way to ending the division of Europe.

teile.einleitung: On 13 December 1981 Poland's communist leadership under General Wojciech Jaruzelski imposed martial law. Its main aim was to crush the independent trade union Solidarność. Martial law officially lasted until 1983.
wichtigste: Martial law was declared during the night of 12 to 13 December 1981.
Power was held by the Military Council of National Salvation under Jaruzelski.
The trade union Solidarność was suspended and banned in 1982.
Lech Wałęsa was interned for about eleven months.
At the Wujek coal mine, nine striking miners were shot dead.
On 22 July 1983 martial law was formally lifted.

abschnitte.text: During the night of **13 December 1981** the Polish leadership imposed **martial law**. Tanks appeared in the streets, telephone lines were cut and there was a curfew. **Thousands of opposition members** were arrested and **interned**, that is, locked up without trial. Power was held by the **Military Council of National Salvation**, **WRON** in Polish. It was made up of senior officers under General **Wojciech Jaruzelski**.

Martial law was directed above all against the trade union **Solidarność**. It was independent of the state and had around **ten million** members. With martial law it was suspended and officially banned in **1982**. Its leader **Lech Wałęsa** was arrested on the very first night. He remained interned until **14 November 1982**.

Many workers went on strike against martial law. On **16 December 1981** special police units opened fire on striking miners at the **Wujek mine** in **Katowice**. **Nine people** died. It was the bloodiest incident during martial law. Today a large cross there commemorates the victims.

At Christmas 1981 US President **Ronald Reagan** called on people to put a **candle in the window** as a sign of solidarity with Poland. The USA also imposed **sanctions**. At the end of 1982 martial law was suspended, and on **22 July 1983** it was formally lifted. Jaruzelski later said it had been a **“lesser evil”**, because it had prevented an invasion by the Soviet Union. Whether this danger really existed is **disputed** among historians.

gewusst: On the morning of 13 December 1981, Polish television showed a speech by Jaruzelski instead of its usual programmes.
Many restrictions from the time of martial law remained in the laws even after 1983.

teile.einleitung: After the Second World War the Soviet Union wanted to build its own atomic bomb as quickly as possible. On 29 August 1949 it carried out its first successful test. This ended the USA’s monopoly on nuclear weapons, and the arms race of the Cold War began.
wichtigste: The first Soviet atomic bomb was detonated on 29 August 1949.
The test took place at the Semipalatinsk site in Kazakhstan.
The scientific director was the physicist Igor Kurchatov.
The secret police chief Lavrentiy Beria organised the project.
The spy Klaus Fuchs passed on secrets from the US atomic bomb project.
The Soviets called the bomb RDS-1, and the Americans called it Joe-1.

abschnitte.text: In 1945 the **USA** became the first and only country to use atomic bombs in war. Until 1949 it was the only country to have such weapons. The Soviet Union under **Joseph Stalin** wanted to catch up quickly. The scientific director of the project was the physicist **Igor Kurchatov**. He is often called the **father of the Soviet atomic bomb**. The Kurchatov Institute in Moscow is named after him.

From 1945 the secret police chief **Lavrentiy Beria** was in charge of organising the project. He put the researchers under heavy pressure and had **prisoners** work on the building sites. Important help came through **espionage**. The German-born physicist **Klaus Fuchs** worked at **Los Alamos** in the USA and passed on construction plans. In 1950 he was convicted in Great Britain.

Thanks to espionage, the Soviets knew how the American plutonium bomb **Fat Man**, which had been dropped on Nagasaki, was built. Their first bomb, the **RDS-1**, was very similar to it. On **29 August 1949** it was detonated at the test site of **Semipalatinsk** in the steppe of Kazakhstan. The Americans called it **Joe-1**. The name was a reference to Stalin, who was also known as “Uncle Joe” in the West.

With this test the Soviet Union became the world’s **second nuclear power**. Now an **arms race** began between the two superpowers in the **Cold War**. Both sides built more and more, and ever more powerful, weapons. The physicist **Andrei Sakharov** later helped to develop the Soviet **hydrogen bomb**. After that he campaigned for human rights and against nuclear tests, and was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1975.

gewusst: More than 400 nuclear tests took place at the Semipalatinsk test site up to 1989.
The researchers jokingly interpreted the abbreviation RDS-1 as “Russia does it itself”.

teile.einleitung: The Vietnam War was a long and bloody war in South-East Asia that raged mainly in the 1960s and 1970s. Communist North Vietnam fought against South Vietnam, which was supported by the USA. In the end the North won, and Vietnam was united under communist leadership in 1976.
wichtigste: After 1954 Vietnam was divided into a communist North and a South.
North Vietnam was led by Ho Chi Minh and supported by the Soviet Union and China.
From 1965 the USA sent combat troops, at times more than half a million soldiers.
In the South the communist Vietcong guerrillas fought against the government.
In 1973 the USA withdrew its troops.
On 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese troops captured Saigon.
Millions of people died in the war, most of them Vietnamese.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Vietnam was a French **colony**. After a war against France, the country was provisionally divided in 1954 at the **Geneva Indochina Conference** in Switzerland. In the North the communists under **Ho Chi Minh** ruled, and in the South an anti-communist government. The planned elections for reunification never took place.

In the **Cold War** the USA feared that one country after another could become communist, like dominoes. That is why it first supported South Vietnam with money, weapons and advisers. After an incident in the Gulf of Tonkin in 1964 it greatly expanded the war. In 1968 there were more than 500,000 American soldiers in Vietnam.

The **Vietcong** fought as guerrillas from the jungle and from tunnel systems. The USA used bombs, **napalm** and the poisonous defoliant Agent Orange, whose effects still make people ill today. In 1968 the North took everyone by surprise with the Tet Offensive, an attack on many cities at once. Serious crimes were also committed against civilians, for example in the My Lai massacre.

The Vietnam War was one of the first wars whose pictures were shown on television every day. In the USA, in Europe and in Switzerland too, mainly young people took to the streets against the war. Many young Americans did not want to be called up and burned their draft cards. The resistance helped to bring about the US agreement to withdraw in the **Paris Peace Accords** of 1973.

On 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese troops took **Saigon**, the capital of the South. In 1976 the country was united as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, and since then Saigon has been called Ho Chi Minh City. Estimates put the number of Vietnamese dead at two to three million; in addition about 58,000 US soldiers died. Afterwards hundreds of thousands fled across the sea in small boats as so-called **boat people**, and some were also taken in by Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fighters who attack in small groups from hiding.
An area that is ruled by a foreign country.
The communist fighters in South Vietnam.
People who fled from Vietnam in small boats after the war.

gewusst: Near Cu Chi the Vietcong dug a tunnel system more than 200 kilometres long, with sleeping quarters and hospitals underground.
Today Vietnam and the USA are trading partners again and have good relations.
The Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington is a black wall bearing the names of more than 58,000 US soldiers who died.

teile.einleitung: War communism is the name for the economic policy of the Bolsheviks in Russia during the civil war, from about 1918 to 1921. The state took over industry and forced the peasants to hand over grain. The results were hunger and a lot of unrest.
wichtigste: War communism lasted from about 1918 to 1921.
From June 1918 large-scale industry was nationalised.
Peasants had to hand over grain by force; this was called prodrazvyorstka.
Armed food detachments seized grain in the countryside.
Because of inflation, workers were often paid in food instead of money.
Private trade was banned; black marketeers were called meshochniki.
In 1921 war communism was replaced by the New Economic Policy.

abschnitte.text: After the October Revolution of 1917, **civil war** broke out in Russia. The Bolsheviks wanted to run the economy entirely from the state. With a decree of **28 June 1918** the large industrial enterprises were **nationalised**. By 1920 many small enterprises had also come into state hands. The state banned **private trade**.

The cities and the army needed food. Under **prodrazvyorstka** the state set how much grain each region had to hand over. Armed **food detachments** made up of workers went into the villages and took the grain by force. Often they even took the peasants' **seed grain**. From June 1918 **Committees of the Village Poor** were meant to mobilise poor peasants against better-off ones. Because they divided the villages, they were dissolved at the end of 1918.

Because of **inflation**, paper money lost almost all its value. So workers were increasingly paid **in kind**, for example in food rations. Many town dwellers went hungry. The **meshochniki** illegally brought food in sacks from the countryside to the towns. Their name comes from the Russian word for sack.

In 1920 **Leon Trotsky** proposed militarising labour and forming **labour armies** from troops that were no longer needed. But discontent grew: peasants rose up, and in 1921 the **Kronstadt sailors' rebellion** broke out. The party under **Lenin** then decided on the **New Economic Policy** in 1921. It allowed some trade again and replaced the compulsory handing over of grain with a tax.

gewusst: The New Economic Policy is often abbreviated to NEP.
Because of the hunger, many people moved from the towns back to the countryside.

teile.einleitung: Alexei Navalny was Russia’s best-known opposition politician. He exposed corruption and criticised President Vladimir Putin. After being poisoned and spending several years in prison, he died in a prison camp in February 2024.
wichtigste: For years Navalny was the best-known critic of President Putin.
In 2011 he founded the Anti-Corruption Foundation, FBK for short.
In August 2020 he was poisoned with the nerve agent Novichok.
He was treated in Berlin and returned to Russia in January 2021.
There he was arrested straight away at the airport and later sentenced to long prison terms.
He died on 16 February 2024 in a prison camp in the Arctic.

abschnitte.text: **Alexei Navalny** was a lawyer and became known through his blog. In 2011 he founded the **Anti-Corruption Foundation**, **FBK** for short. It published videos and investigations into the wealth of senior officials. Many of the videos were watched millions of times, especially by young people. In 2021 the foundation was banned in Russia as “extremist”.

In August 2020 Navalny suddenly became seriously ill on a flight in Siberia. The pilot made an unscheduled landing in **Omsk**, where Navalny was taken to hospital. This quick landing probably helped him to survive. After that he was flown to the **Charité** hospital in **Berlin**, where he recovered. Laboratories in Germany, France and Sweden found a nerve agent of the **Novichok** group.

In January 2021 Navalny voluntarily returned to Russia. Straight after landing in Moscow he was **arrested at the airport**. Shortly afterwards the video “**Putin’s Palace**” appeared, about a huge estate on the **Black Sea**. Within a few days it had been viewed tens of millions of times and sparked protests. Navalny was sentenced to long **prison terms** in several trials.

On **16 February 2024** Navalny died in a **penal colony** north of the Arctic Circle. Many Western governments held the Russian leadership responsible for his death. Thousands of people laid flowers in Russia and abroad. His widow, **Yulia Navalnaya**, announced that she would continue his political work from abroad.

gewusst: A documentary called “Navalny” was made about his life, and it won an Oscar in 2023.
After his death many people came to his funeral in Moscow, despite the risk of being arrested.

teile.einleitung: Mikhail Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union. From 1985 he introduced reforms such as “glasnost” and “perestroika”, which brought more openness and freedom. He played a major part in the peaceful end of the Cold War and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for it.
wichtigste: Mikhail Gorbachev was born in 1931 and died in 2022.
In 1985 he became General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
With “glasnost” he brought more openness, and with “perestroika” a restructuring of the economy.
In 1985 he met the US President Ronald Reagan in Geneva for the first time.
He allowed the countries of Eastern Europe to go their own way in 1989.
In 1990 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
On 25 December 1991 he resigned, and shortly afterwards the Soviet Union came to an end.

abschnitte.text: Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in the village of Privolnoye in southern Russia. His family were farmers, and as a teenager he helped out on the combine harvester. He studied law in Moscow, where he met his wife **Raisa**. After that he quickly rose through the ranks of the Communist Party.

In March 1985, at the age of 54, he became **General Secretary** and so the most powerful man in the Soviet Union. He realised that the economy was no longer working. With **glasnost**, which means openness, people and newspapers were allowed to voice more criticism. With **perestroika**, the restructuring, he wanted to modernise the economy and politics.

In November 1985 Gorbachev met US President **Ronald Reagan** for a summit in Geneva. The two got on better than expected. In 1987 they signed a treaty under which all nuclear intermediate-range missiles were destroyed. In 1989 Gorbachev withdrew the Soviet soldiers from Afghanistan.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Eastern Bloc
abschnitte.text: Unlike earlier party leaders, Gorbachev did not send in tanks when people in Eastern Europe protested in 1989. This allowed the Berlin Wall to fall and the communist governments to be replaced peacefully. In 1990 he agreed to the reunification of Germany. In the same year he was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

In August 1991 opponents of his reforms attempted a coup, but it failed. After that, more and more of the Soviet republics declared their independence. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the **Soviet Union** broke apart. In the West he is highly respected, while in Russia many people blame him for the collapse of the country. He died in Moscow on 30 August 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: Russian for “openness”: more freedom of speech in the Soviet Union.
Russian for “restructuring”: reforms of the economy and politics.
A meeting of the most important politicians of different countries.
A famous prize for people who work for peace.

gewusst: Gorbachev was easy to recognise by a striking birthmark on his forehead.
Gorbachev was the first and only president of the Soviet Union.

teile.einleitung: In a market economy, it is mainly companies and customers who decide what is produced and bought. Prices are set by supply and demand. Switzerland also has a market economy, but the state makes rules.
wichtigste: Switzerland has a market economy.
The price is set mainly by supply and demand.
If there is a lot of a product, the price usually falls.
If lots of people want a product, the price usually rises.
Companies decide for themselves what they produce.
In competition, companies try to be better or cheaper.
The state makes rules, for example to protect workers.

abschnitte.text: A **market** is any place where things are bought and sold. It can be a **weekly market**, a shop or an **online shop**. **Buyers** and **sellers** meet there. That is where the market economy gets its name. In a market economy, companies decide for themselves what they produce. A bakery, for example, bakes what its customers like to buy.

**Supply** tells you how much of a product there is. **Demand** tells you how many people want to buy it. If there are a lot of **strawberries** in summer, their price usually falls so that everything gets sold. If suddenly all children want the same **toy**, demand is high. Then the price often rises. In this way prices help to distribute goods.

When several shops offer similar goods, they compete for the same customers. This is called **competition**. Every company tries to be **better** or **cheaper** than the others. Customers benefit from this. In Switzerland, the **Competition Commission** makes sure that companies do not make secret agreements.

Even in a market economy there are **laws**. The state protects **workers** and the environment, for example. Through insurance schemes such as the **AVS**, it looks after people in old age. But the state does not set most prices. When the state has a bigger say in order to give people social security, this is called a **social market economy**.

The opposite of a market economy is a **planned economy**. There the **state** decides what is produced and how much it costs. That was the case, for example, in the **Soviet Union** and the **GDR**. Goods were often in short supply there, and people had to queue for a long time. Many countries today have a mixture in which the market decides most things.

gewusst: Switzerland has a Price Supervisor who can examine prices that are too high.
Even in the Middle Ages, many Swiss towns had regular weekly markets.

teile.einleitung: Nicholas II was the last tsar of Russia. He reigned from 1894 to 1917 and belonged to the Romanov family. During his reign Russia went through wars, revolutions and finally the end of the monarchy.
wichtigste: Nicholas II became tsar in 1894 after the death of his father, Alexander III.
He was the last ruler from the Romanov family.
After Bloody Sunday in 1905 he had to allow a parliament, the Duma.
In 1915 he took supreme command of the army himself.
In March 1917 he abdicated.
In July 1918 the tsar’s family was murdered in Yekaterinburg.

abschnitte.text: The **Romanovs** had ruled Russia since 1613. Nicholas II became tsar in 1894 after the death of his father, **Alexander III**. He was married to **Alexandra**, a princess from Germany. The couple had four daughters and a son, **Alexei**. The heir to the throne suffered from **haemophilia**: even small injuries could make him bleed dangerously.

In January 1905 thousands of workers in St Petersburg marched to the **Winter Palace** with a petition. Soldiers fired on the peaceful crowd. This **Bloody Sunday** destroyed many people’s trust in the tsar, and the Revolution of 1905 began. In the **October Manifesto** Nicholas promised basic rights and an elected parliament, the **State Duma**. However, its power remained limited.

In the First World War Russia suffered heavy defeats. In 1915 Nicholas took **supreme command** of the army himself and went to the front. As a result, many people held him personally responsible for the defeats. In the capital the tsarina gained more influence, and with her the wandering preacher **Grigori Rasputin**. He seemed able to calm Alexei’s bleeding, but he damaged the family’s reputation and was murdered in 1916.

In February 1917 a revolution broke out in Petrograd. In March **Nicholas abdicated**, for himself and for his sick son. He handed the throne to his brother **Michael**, who refused it the next day. That was the end of the monarchy. Later the Bolsheviks held the family prisoner in **Yekaterinburg** in the Urals, where the tsar, his wife and their five children were killed in July 1918.

gewusst: The Romanov family ruled Russia for more than 300 years.
Tsarina Alexandra was a granddaughter of the British Queen Victoria.

teile.einleitung: The Round Table in Poland was a meeting between the government and the opposition in 1989. The communists and the trade union Solidarność negotiated reforms there. The talks opened the way to the peaceful end of communism in Poland.
wichtigste: The Round Table met in Warsaw from 6 February to 5 April 1989.
As a result Solidarność became legal again.
In the election in June 1989, 35 per cent of the seats in the Sejm could be freely elected.
The Senate was newly created and freely elected in full.
Solidarność won 99 of the 100 Senate seats.
Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist head of government in the Eastern Bloc.

abschnitte.text: In the 1980s Poland was doing badly economically. The independent trade union **Solidarność** under **Lech Wałęsa** had been banned since 1981. In 1988 there were big strikes again. The communist government under General **Wojciech Jaruzelski** realised that it had to talk to the opposition. This is how the idea of a **Round Table** came about, at which everyone was to sit as equals.

The talks began on **6 February 1989** in Warsaw and ended on **5 April 1989**. On the government side the negotiator was the interior minister **Czesław Kiszczak**, a close confidant of Jaruzelski. Opposite him sat Lech Wałęsa. The most important result for the opposition: in April Solidarność was **legalised again**. In addition, they agreed on a partly free election.

In the **Sejm**, the parliament, 65 per cent of the seats were reserved for the communists and their allies. Only **35 per cent** could be freely contested. The **Senate**, with 100 seats, was newly created and was freely elected in full. On **4 June 1989** Poland voted. Solidarność won all 161 freely contested seats in the Sejm and 99 of the 100 Senate seats.

After the opposition’s clear election victory, the communists could no longer govern alone. In August 1989 the Sejm elected the Catholic journalist **Tadeusz Mazowiecki** as prime minister. He was the first non-communist head of government in the whole of the **Eastern Bloc**. Poland’s example encouraged people in other countries such as Hungary, the GDR and Czechoslovakia.

gewusst: Alongside the main round, many smaller working groups negotiated on subjects such as the economy, politics and trade unions.
On the same day as the Polish election, the Chinese government crushed the protests in Tiananmen Square.

teile.einleitung: In an Olympic boycott, countries stay away from the Olympic Games in protest. The best-known boycotts took place during the Cold War: in 1980 many Western countries stayed away from the Games in Moscow, and in 1984 the Eastern Bloc responded with a boycott of the Games in Los Angeles.
wichtigste: In 1980 more than 60 countries boycotted the Summer Games in Moscow.
The reason was the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan at the end of 1979.
US President Jimmy Carter called for the boycott.
Switzerland took part in 1980, but under the Olympic flag.
In 1984 the Soviet Union and almost all the Eastern Bloc states boycotted Los Angeles.
Romania took part in 1984 all the same.

abschnitte.text: At the end of 1979 the Soviet Union invaded **Afghanistan**. US President **Jimmy Carter** demanded that the troops be withdrawn. In January 1980 he announced that otherwise the USA would stay away from the Summer Games in **Moscow**. Many allies joined in, for example the Federal Republic of Germany and Japan. In total, more than 60 countries stayed away from the Games.

Not all Western countries took part in the boycott. **Switzerland** sent a team to Moscow, but marched in at the opening ceremony under the **Olympic flag**. In this way it showed that it did not approve of the invasion. The cyclist **Robert Dill-Bundi** won gold in the individual pursuit on the track. The mascot of the Games was the bear **Misha**.

In May 1984 the Soviet Union cancelled its participation in the Games in **Los Angeles**. Almost all the Eastern Bloc states followed its example. Officially it was said that the athletes would not be safe in the USA. However, many saw it as a response to the boycott of 1980. Only **Romania** refused to go along and sent a team, which was celebrated in the West for doing so.

The boycotts show how strongly the **Cold War** also shaped sport. Those who suffered most were the athletes who had trained for years. Some of them missed their only chance of an Olympic medal as a result. At other times, too, countries have stayed away from the Olympic Games in protest. Since 1988 the big countries of East and West have once again taken part together.

gewusst: At the closing ceremony in Moscow in 1980, a huge picture of Misha the bear shed a tear.
Because many strong teams were missing, the hosts won a particularly large number of medals at both Games.

teile.einleitung: The Cultural Revolution was a campaign in China from 1966 to 1976, started by Mao Zedong. It was directed against supposed enemies of communism and brought great violence and chaos. Millions of people were persecuted, and many cultural treasures were destroyed.
wichtigste: The Cultural Revolution lasted from 1966 to 1976.
Mao Zedong wanted to use it to secure his power and eliminate supposed enemies.
Young Red Guards attacked teachers, officials and artists.
Old temples, books and works of art were destroyed.
Millions of young people were sent to the countryside.
It came to an end with Mao's death and the arrest of the “Gang of Four” in 1976.
The party later called the Cultural Revolution a catastrophe.

abschnitte.text: With the “Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution”, Mao wanted to turn China upside down again from 1966. He said that there were still enemies in the country and in the party who wanted to bring back capitalism. In truth, he also wanted to get rid of rivals who had gained influence after the failed “Great Leap Forward”. Mao was revered like a hero, and a **personality cult** developed.

Mao called on schoolchildren and students to rebel against authority. They formed the **Red Guards** and carried the little red book of Mao quotations, the **“Little Red Book”**, with them. They publicly humiliated teachers, professors and officials and beat many of them. Schools and universities were closed for years.

The Red Guards were to fight the “Four Olds”: old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits. In doing so they destroyed temples, monasteries, books and valuable works of art. Many monasteries in Tibet were also damaged. Anyone who belonged to a “wrong” family, for example of landowners, was often persecuted.

When the violence between groups got out of control, Mao sent in the army from 1968. Millions of young people from the cities were sent to the countryside to learn from the peasants. Senior politicians such as the head of state **Liu Shaoqi** were also overthrown; he died in custody in 1969. **Deng Xiaoping** was also removed from power, but later came back.

After Mao's death in September 1976, the so-called **Gang of Four** around Mao's widow Jiang Qing was arrested. That ended the Cultural Revolution. Exactly how many people died is not known; estimates range from hundreds of thousands to millions. In 1981 the party officially declared the Cultural Revolution a serious mistake, but it can still hardly be talked about openly in China today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Groups of schoolchildren and students who fought for Mao against supposed enemies.
When a leader is excessively revered like a hero or a god.
Four powerful supporters of Mao who were arrested after his death.
The small red book of sayings by Mao Zedong.

gewusst: The Little Red Book of Mao quotations was printed in hundreds of millions of copies and is one of the most printed books ever.
The later head of state Xi Jinping was himself sent to a village in the countryside as a teenager during the Cultural Revolution.

teile.einleitung: In 1990 the Two Plus Four Treaty settled the external questions of German unity. The two German states and the four victorious powers of the Second World War signed it in Moscow. This cleared the way for reunification, and Germany became fully independent again.
wichtigste: “Two” stands for the FRG and the GDR.
“Four” stands for the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France.
The treaty was signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990.
It made German reunification on 3 October 1990 possible.
The Oder-Neisse border with Poland was confirmed as final.
Germany limited its armed forces to a maximum of 370,000 soldiers.
The treaty came into force on 15 March 1991.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the four **victorious powers** still had special rights in Germany and Berlin. They were the **USA**, the **Soviet Union**, **Great Britain** and **France**. When the Wall fell in 1989, the Germans wanted a single state again. The two German states, the **FRG** and the **GDR**, negotiated about this together with the four powers. This is how the name **Two Plus Four** came about.

The **foreign ministers** of the six states signed the treaty on **12 September 1990** in **Moscow**, the capital of the Soviet Union. It settled the external questions of German unity. A few weeks later, on **3 October 1990**, the GDR joined the Federal Republic. Germany has celebrated this day ever since as the **Day of German Unity**. The four powers gave up their rights in Germany.

In the treaty Germany confirmed that the **Oder-Neisse border** with **Poland** is final. In doing so it gave up former eastern territories. The united Germany also undertook to reduce its armed forces to a maximum of **370,000 soldiers**. It also reaffirmed that it would not have **nuclear, biological and chemical weapons**, NBC weapons for short. Conventional weapons remained allowed.

Many Soviet soldiers were stationed in the GDR. The treaty provided for them to withdraw **by the end of 1994**. The last Russian soldiers in fact left Germany in **August 1994**. By then the Soviet Union no longer existed, so they were Russian troops. After that, no foreign NATO troops were allowed to be permanently stationed in eastern Germany.

The treaty only came into force once all the states had **ratified** it, in other words officially confirmed it. The last to do so was the Soviet Union. Since **15 March 1991** Germany has been fully **sovereign**, in other words completely independent. The Two Plus Four Treaty is therefore regarded as a kind of final settlement after the Second World War.

gewusst: The treaty’s official name is the “Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany”.
Less than eleven months passed between the fall of the Wall and the signing of the treaty.

teile.einleitung: Utopian socialists is the name for thinkers of the early 19th century who imagined a fairer society. They wanted to achieve it through good examples and model settlements. The best known are Robert Owen and Charles Fourier.
wichtigste: The word “utopia” goes back to the book “Utopia” by Thomas More from 1516.
Robert Owen came from Wales and ran the factory settlement of New Lanark in Scotland.
Owen shortened the working day to ten and a half hours and founded a school.
In 1825 he founded the settlement of New Harmony in the USA.
Charles Fourier planned large communal buildings called “phalanstères”.
Marx and Engels called these thinkers “utopian”.

abschnitte.text: In 1516 the Englishman **Thomas More** wrote the book “**Utopia**”. In it he described an imaginary island with an ideal society without **private property**. The name means roughly “no place”, in other words a place that does not exist. Since then an imagined ideal state has been called a **utopia**. In the 19th century several thinkers designed such societies for the industrial age.

**Robert Owen** was born in Newtown in **Wales** in 1771. From about 1800 he ran the cotton mill at **New Lanark** in Scotland, which had belonged to his father-in-law, David Dale. At that time 13 to 14 hours’ work a day was normal. Owen shortened the working day to **ten and a half hours**, improved the housing and restricted child labour. He founded a **school** for the children, because he believed that upbringing shapes people.

In 1825 Owen bought a settlement in the US state of **Indiana** and called it **New Harmony**. There people were to live together without private property and work together. The project failed after a few years. But Owen’s ideas lived on. He is regarded as the founder of the **cooperative movement**, in which people run businesses together and share the profits.

The Frenchman **Charles Fourier** dreamed of large communal buildings, the **phalanstères**. About 1,600 people were to live and work together in each one. Work was to be shared out in such a way that everyone enjoyed it. Like Owen, Fourier is one of the **utopian socialists**. The Frenchman **Henri de Saint-Simon** is also often counted as part of this group.

The term **utopian socialism** was coined by **Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels**. They regarded their own teaching as “**scientific**”. In their opinion the older socialists were based on wishful thinking rather than on an analysis of society. In **Switzerland** cooperatives still play a big role today, for example in housing and in retail.

gewusst: New Lanark is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Robert Owen died in 1858 in Newtown, the same town where he had been born.

teile.einleitung: The New Economic Policy, NEP for short, was an economic programme in Soviet Russia from 1921. With it, Lenin allowed some private business again so that the country could recover after the civil war. Stalin ended the NEP at the end of the 1920s.
wichtigste: The NEP was adopted in March 1921 at the 10th Party Congress.
It replaced the harsh system of War Communism.
Farmers paid a fixed tax in kind and were allowed to sell their surplus.
Small businesses and trade were allowed to be private.
Heavy industry, banks and foreign trade remained in the hands of the state.
Around 1928 Stalin replaced the NEP with a strict planned economy.

abschnitte.text: During the civil war **War Communism** was in force. The state took grain from the farmers by force and banned free trade. Afterwards the country was impoverished and many people went hungry. There were uprisings, for example by the sailors in **Kronstadt** in March 1921. Lenin realised that he had to give way.
