In March 1921 the **10th Party Congress** adopted the New Economic Policy. Instead of handing over all their grain, the farmers now paid a fixed **tax in kind**, in other words a share of their harvest. They were allowed to sell the rest at market. Small shops, workshops and businesses were also allowed to be private again. The **“commanding heights”** of the economy, meaning heavy industry, banks and foreign trade, remained under state control.

Traders and business owners who became rich during this time were called **Nepmen**. Many communists viewed them with suspicion as new capitalists. From 1922 the state bank issued a new currency partly backed by gold, the **chervonets**. One chervonets was worth ten roubles in gold. The new currency helped to overcome the severe inflation.

Farming, trade and crafts recovered quickly, and the shops filled up again. By the mid-1920s production had almost returned to its pre-war level. After Lenin’s death in 1924, **Joseph Stalin** won the struggle for the top. Around 1928 he replaced the NEP with **five-year plans** and the **forced collectivisation** of agriculture. Private traders were pushed out once more.

gewusst: Lenin himself called the NEP a temporary step backwards in order to move forward again afterwards.
The name chervonets goes back to old Russian gold coins.

teile.einleitung: Social democracy is a political movement that wants to achieve more social justice. It relies on democracy, elections and reforms rather than on revolution. In Switzerland it is represented mainly by the SP.
wichtigste: Social Democrats want to change society through reforms within a democracy.
The SP of Switzerland was founded on 21 October 1888.
In 1918 the SP and the trade unions organised the general strike.
In 1943 Ernst Nobs became the first Social Democratic federal councillor.
Since the magic formula of 1959 the SP has had two seats in the Federal Council.
In Germany Ferdinand Lassalle was an important founder of the labour movement.

abschnitte.text: Social democracy grew out of the **labour movement** in the 19th century. It wants better wages, social security and equal opportunities for everyone. Unlike revolutionary **communists**, Social Democrats rely on **elections, parliament and laws**. Around 1900 the German **Eduard Bernstein** put forward the idea of achieving socialism through gradual reforms. His ideas are called **revisionism**.

In 1863 **Ferdinand Lassalle** founded the **General German Workers’ Association** in Leipzig. It is regarded as the forerunner of today’s **SPD**. Lassalle wanted to improve the situation of the workers through **universal suffrage**. Today the SPD is one of the oldest parties in Germany. In 1959, with the Godesberg Programme, it abandoned Marxism as its foundation.

The **Social Democratic Party of Switzerland** was founded on **21 October 1888**. It grew out of various workers’ associations. In November 1918 the SP and the trade unions organised the **general strike**. About 250,000 people stopped work. The Federal Council sent in the army, and the strike was called off after a few days. But one demand was soon met: in 1919 the National Council was elected for the first time by **proportional representation**, in other words in proportion to the votes.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the Federal Council
abschnitte.text: Thanks to proportional representation, the SP won many seats in the National Council in 1919. In 1943 **Ernst Nobs** from Zurich became the first Social Democratic **federal councillor**. He remained in office until 1951. Since the **magic formula** of 1959 the SP has had two seats in the national government. The magic formula shares out the seven seats on the Federal Council according to the strength of the parties.

In 1983 the SP nominated **Lilian Uchtenhagen** as the first woman candidate for the Federal Council. However, the Federal Assembly elected the Social Democrat **Otto Stich** instead. This caused a great deal of debate at the time. Then in 1984 Elisabeth Kopp of the FDP was elected as the first woman on the Federal Council. The SP still campaigns strongly for equality today.

gewusst: In many countries the red rose is a symbol of social democracy.
The general strike of 1918 is the biggest strike in Swiss history.

teile.einleitung: Leninism is the name for the political ideas of Lenin, the leader of the Russian Revolution of 1917. He built on the teachings of Karl Marx but stressed the role of a tightly led party. Under Stalin it became “Marxism-Leninism”.
wichtigste: In 1902, in “What Is to Be Done?”, Lenin called for a party of professional revolutionaries.
As a vanguard, the party was to lead the workers to revolution.
“Bolsheviks” means “members of the majority”.
Under democratic centralism, the leadership's decisions are binding on everyone.
In 1917 Lenin demanded “All power to the Soviets”.
In 1919 the Bolsheviks founded the Communist International.
Under Stalin, Marxism-Leninism became the state ideology.

abschnitte.text: In his work **“What Is to Be Done?”** of **1902**, Lenin called for a party of **professional revolutionaries**. It was to be tightly organised and disciplined and, as the **vanguard**, lead the working class to revolution. Lenin believed that, left to themselves, workers would only develop a **trade union consciousness**. They would then only fight for wages and working hours. Socialist consciousness, he said, had to come from outside, through the party.

At the congress of the Russian Social Democrats in **1903**, Lenin's wing won an important vote. After that, his supporters were called **Bolsheviks**, which means **“members of the majority”**. Their opponents were called **Mensheviks**, meaning “members of the minority”. The party followed the principle of **democratic centralism**: before a decision you could discuss, but afterwards strict discipline applied. In practice this led to rule by the party leadership.

After his return to **Petrograd**, in April 1917 Lenin presented the **April Theses**. Their most important slogan was **“All power to the Soviets”**. The Soviets were councils of workers and soldiers. Lenin did not want to support the Provisional Government. In the **October Revolution** of 1917, the Bolsheviks took power.

In **1919** the Bolsheviks founded the **Communist International**, **Comintern** for short, in Moscow. Its member parties had to submit to strict instructions from Moscow. In **1920** Lenin wrote a work criticising left-wing communists who wanted to boycott parliaments and trade unions. After Lenin's death in **1924**, **Joseph Stalin** summed up his teachings. **Marxism-Leninism** became the official ideology of the Soviet Union and of all the Eastern Bloc parties.

gewusst: Lenin's real name was Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov; “Lenin” was a pseudonym.
The 1920 work is titled “‘Left-Wing’ Communism: An Infantile Disorder”.

teile.einleitung: The People’s Socialist Republic of Albania was a communist state in south-eastern Europe. Under the dictator Enver Hoxha the small country cut itself off from the world more than almost any other.
wichtigste: Enver Hoxha ruled Albania from 1944 until his death in 1985.
One after another, Albania broke with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China.
In 1967 Albania declared itself the world’s first atheist state.
Out of fear of an attack, more than 170,000 bunkers were built.
Until 1991 private individuals were not allowed to own a car.
After Hoxha’s death Ramiz Alia took over, and from 1990 the country slowly opened up.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the communists under **Enver Hoxha** took power. The only party allowed was the **Party of Labour of Albania**. Hoxha ruled with **Stalinist methods**: anyone who disagreed was sent to prison or to a labour camp. A feared secret police kept watch on the people. With the constitution of 1976 the country was given the name People’s Socialist Republic of Albania.

Albania looked for powerful allies and then broke with them. In 1948 it split from **Yugoslavia**, in 1961 from the **Soviet Union** and in 1978 from **China** too. After that the country was almost completely **isolated**. The constitution of 1976 even banned taking out loans from abroad. Albania wanted to produce everything itself; this is called **autarky**.

Hoxha feared an invasion from outside. That is why the regime had more than **170,000 bunkers** built between 1967 and 1986. Many are small, round concrete domes that stick out of the landscape like mushrooms. They stand on beaches, in fields and in towns. Many of these bunkers can still be seen today.

In 1967 all **churches and mosques** were closed. Albania called itself the world’s **first atheist state**. Atheist means without belief in a god. Many places of worship were demolished or turned into warehouses and sports halls. Only towards the end of communism were people allowed to practise their faith openly again.

After Hoxha’s death in 1985 **Ramiz Alia** took over the leadership. From 1990 a cautious opening began, and other parties were allowed. In 1991 the country was renamed the **Republic of Albania**. In 1988 the **Pyramid** opened in Tirana as a museum for Hoxha. After the end of communism the building was used for other purposes.

gewusst: Until 1991 there were almost only lorries, buses and state vehicles on Albania’s roads.
The Pyramid of Tirana was designed with the help of Hoxha’s daughter Pranvera.

teile.einleitung: With industrialisation in the 19th century, many factories were built. Working-class families often lived in great poverty, worked very long hours and lived in cramped conditions. The plight of these people and the search for solutions is called the social question.
wichtigste: The social question refers to the hardship of workers in the 19th century and the search for solutions.
In many factories a working day lasted 12 to 16 hours.
Many children worked because their families needed the wages.
Cholera spread in the crowded working-class districts.
In 1864 Glarus passed a factory law with a maximum of 12 working hours.
The federal Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14.

abschnitte.text: With the new machines, large **factories** were built in the 19th century. Many people moved from the countryside to the towns to work there. But there were hardly any laws to protect them. Working days of **12 to 16 hours**, six days a week, were common. Wages were low, and anyone who fell ill or had an accident often lost their job. The debate about these problems was called the **social question**.

Many **children** worked in factories. Their parents’ wages were often not enough to live on, so families needed every bit of extra money. Factory owners liked to employ children because they could pay them less. There was hardly any time left for school and play. Only gradually did laws ban child labour.

There was a shortage of housing in the growing towns. In cities such as Berlin, **tenement blocks** were built, large buildings with dark back courtyards. Many families lived there in very little space. Light, fresh air and toilets were often lacking. Without **sewers**, germs got into the drinking water. This is how **cholera** spread and claimed many lives.

Some people fought back against the new machines and the misery. In 1832, in the **Uster Fire** in the canton of Zurich, home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill. They feared that they would lose their work because of the weaving machines. In 1844 the starving weavers of Silesia rose up in the **Weavers’ Uprising**. The army crushed it. The writer **Gerhart Hauptmann** later wrote the play “The Weavers” about it.

Switzerland was one of the pioneers in protecting workers. In 1864 the **Landsgemeinde of Glarus** (open-air assembly) passed a factory law with a maximum of 12 working hours a day. It also banned night work and was even pushed through against the wishes of the cantonal government. In 1877 the **federal Factory Act** followed. It banned children under 14 from factory work and was one of the most progressive laws in Europe. Trade unions, churches and parties also looked for solutions.

gewusst: The Swiss people voted on the federal Factory Act of 1877 in a referendum and narrowly approved it.
In the 19th century the canton of Glarus was one of the most heavily industrialised cantons in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Stalinism is the name for the rule of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union and the way he governed. Its features were a huge personality cult, political purges and mass terror against supposed enemies. Millions of people were arrested, sent to camps or killed.
wichtigste: Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union from about the end of the 1920s until his death in 1953.
He was worshipped like a hero; this is called a personality cult.
In the purges he also had former party comrades arrested and killed.
In the Great Terror of 1937 and 1938 about 700,000 people were shot.
Millions of people had to do forced labour in prison camps, the Gulag.
In famines at the beginning of the 1930s millions died, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
After Stalin’s death, Nikita Khrushchev publicly criticised his crimes in 1956.

abschnitte.text: **Joseph Stalin** was born in Georgia in 1878; his real name was Ioseb Jughashvili. The name Stalin means something like “man of steel”. After Lenin’s death in 1924 he gradually pushed aside all his rivals, such as Leon Trotsky. From about 1929 he was the undisputed ruler of the Soviet Union.

In a **personality cult** a ruler is worshipped like a faultless hero or almost like a god. Pictures of Stalin hung and statues of him stood everywhere, and towns were named after him. Children learned poems and songs about the “Father of Nations”. Anyone who criticised Stalin risked prison or death.

In the **purges** Stalin had supposed enemies in the party, the army and society eliminated. In so-called **show trials** the accused had to confess to invented crimes, often after torture. In the Great Terror of 1937 to 1938 about 1.5 million people were arrested, and about half of them were shot. Many officers of the Red Army were also killed.

The **Gulag** was a huge network of prison camps, often in Siberia or the far north. The prisoners had to build canals, railway lines and mines in terrible conditions. Stalin also forced the farmers to give up their land to collective farms, the **kolkhozes**. The result was the famines of 1932 and 1933; in Ukraine they are called the Holodomor.

With five-year plans the Soviet Union became an industrial state in a short time. In the Second World War Stalin led the country to victory over Hitler’s Germany, and afterwards he extended his power over Eastern Europe. After his death in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev gave a **secret speech** in 1956 in which he denounced Stalin’s crimes. The organisation Memorial later researched the fates of the victims and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: Excessive worship of a ruler.
Removing and persecuting people who are regarded as opponents.
The system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union.
A court case in which the verdict has been decided in advance and which serves propaganda.
A large farm that was supposed to belong to the farmers jointly.

gewusst: From 1925 to 1961 the city of Volgograd was called Stalingrad.
After his death Stalin’s body lay next to Lenin’s in the mausoleum on Red Square for some years, before it was removed in 1961.
Stalin had people who had fallen out of favour retouched out of old photos, so that it looked as if they had been erased from history.

teile.einleitung: Pathet Lao was a communist-led movement in Laos, a country in South-East Asia. For decades it fought against the royal government with the support of North Vietnam. In 1975 it took power and abolished the monarchy.
wichtigste: Pathet Lao means “Land of the Lao”.
Its best-known leader was Prince Souphanouvong, the “Red Prince”.
The movement was closely linked with North Vietnam.
In 1975 it came to power, and Laos became a people’s republic.
Since then the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party has ruled as the only party.

abschnitte.text: **Pathet Lao** literally means “Land of the Lao”. That was the name of the communist-led movement in Laos. Its best-known face was **Prince Souphanouvong**, a member of the royal family. He was called the **“Red Prince”**. His half-brother **Souvanna Phouma**, on the other hand, was several times a neutralist prime minister. The political core of the movement was the **Lao People’s Revolutionary Party**, founded in 1955.

The Pathet Lao was formed with the help of the Vietnamese Việt Minh and was later supported by **North Vietnam**. The **Ho Chi Minh Trail**, an important supply route for North Vietnam, ran through the areas under its control. That is why the USA bombed Laos very heavily. Measured against its population, it is regarded as the most heavily bombed country. Many **Hmong** fought against the Pathet Lao under General Vang Pao with the support of the CIA.

In December 1975 King **Savang Vatthana** abdicated, and the **Lao People’s Democratic Republic** was proclaimed. In the same year the communists also won in Vietnam and Cambodia. **Kaysone Phomvihane** became the first prime minister, and Souphanouvong became president. After 1975 tens of thousands of Hmong fled abroad. The Lao People’s Revolutionary Party is still the only permitted party today (as of 2026).

gewusst: Even today, many unexploded bombs from the war lie in the ground in Laos and are dangerous when people work in the fields.

teile.einleitung: The East-West conflict was the great rivalry between the West, led by the USA, and the East, led by the Soviet Union. It lasted from the end of the Second World War until about 1990. Because the two powers never fought each other directly, it is also called the Cold War.
wichtigste: The USA led the West, and the Soviet Union led the East.
The communist countries of Eastern Europe were called the Eastern Bloc.
In the West there were free elections with several parties.
The military alliances NATO and the Warsaw Pact faced each other.
Non-aligned states did not want to belong to either camp.
The conflict ended with the fall of the Wall and the end of the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** were the most powerful countries. The countries of Western Europe, such as France, were on the side of the USA. The communist countries of Eastern Europe, such as **Poland**, Hungary, Bulgaria and Romania, formed the **Eastern Bloc** together with the Soviet Union. The border between the two camps running right across Europe was called the **Iron Curtain**. Germany was divided into two states.

In the West there were **free elections** with several parties, freedom of the press and a market economy. In the East usually only the **communist party** decided. The economy there was planned by the state. Each side thought its own system was better. The military alliances **NATO** in the West and the **Warsaw Pact** in the East faced each other.

Both sides built many **nuclear weapons**. This is known as an **arms race**. Things became dangerous, for example, in 1962 during the **Cuban Missile Crisis**, when the world was on the brink of nuclear war. East and West also competed against each other in space and in sport. In 1980 many Western countries boycotted the Olympic Games in **Moscow**, and in 1984 the Eastern Bloc stayed away from the Games in **Los Angeles**.

Some countries, such as India or Egypt, did not want to belong to either camp. In 1961 they founded the **Non-Aligned Movement**. Switzerland remained neutral, but with its democracy and economy it belonged to the West. At the end of the 1980s people in the Eastern Bloc demanded freedom. In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell, and in 1991 the Soviet Union broke apart.

gewusst: The expression “Iron Curtain” was made famous in 1946 by the British politician Winston Churchill.
After the Cuban Missile Crisis the USA and the Soviet Union set up a direct line between their governments, the “red telephone”.

teile.einleitung: Perestroika is a Russian word meaning “restructuring”. From 1986 Mikhail Gorbachev used this name for his reforms, with which he wanted to renew the stagnant economy of the Soviet Union. The reforms changed the world more than Gorbachev himself had expected.
wichtigste: Perestroika means “restructuring” or “reshaping”.
Mikhail Gorbachev started the reforms after he had become head of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in 1985.
Businesses were to be given more freedom and allowed to decide more for themselves.
Perestroika included glasnost, meaning more openness and less censorship.
Even so, the economy did not recover, and many goods were missing from the shops.
The reforms helped to end the Cold War and contributed to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

abschnitte.text: **Perestroika** was a reform programme in the Soviet Union from 1986 onwards. The economy worked on the principle of a **planned economy**, in which the state laid down everything. Many factories were out of date and produced goods that nobody wanted. Gorbachev did not want to abolish the system, but to improve it and make it more modern.

In 1985, at the age of 54, **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary of the Communist Party. He was much younger than his predecessors, who had often been old and ill. He wanted people to believe in socialism again and to work harder. For his role in ending the Cold War he was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1990.

A law of 1987 gave state-owned businesses more independence. They were allowed to make some of their decisions themselves and were supposed to make a profit. From 1988 people were also allowed to set up small private firms, known as **cooperatives**. These led, for example, to private restaurants, workshops and shops.

Perestroika included **glasnost**, which means “openness”. Suddenly newspapers were allowed to report on problems, government mistakes and crimes from Stalin’s time. After the nuclear accident at **Chernobyl** in 1986, it became clear how dangerous secrecy can be. Many people now openly criticised the system.

The economy fell into a severe crisis, and long queues outside empty shops became part of everyday life. At the same time the peoples in the Soviet republics demanded more **independence**. In Eastern Europe Gorbachev allowed the revolutions of 1989 to happen without sending tanks. In December 1991 the Soviet Union broke up into 15 independent states.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned change that is meant to improve something.
Russian for openness: people were allowed to say and write more freely what they thought.
A small business that belongs to several people together.
The most powerful post in the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

gewusst: Gorbachev met the US President Ronald Reagan for the first time in Geneva in 1985.
In Russia Gorbachev is still controversial today, because many blame him for the collapse of the Soviet Union.
In the 1980s the word perestroika also became a buzzword in German-language newspapers.

teile.einleitung: “Socialism with Chinese characteristics” is the official guiding idea of the Communist Party of China. It combines the rule of the party with elements of the market economy. The term comes from Deng Xiaoping and was developed further by his successors.
wichtigste: Deng Xiaoping coined the term in 1982 at the 12th Party Congress.
In 1992 the 14th Party Congress set the socialist market economy as the goal.
According to the party, China is in the primary stage of socialism.
The Four Cardinal Principles set political limits to the reforms.
With Jiang Zemin’s Three Represents, entrepreneurs were allowed to become party members from 2001.
In 2021 the party leadership declared that the goal of a “moderately prosperous society” had been achieved.

abschnitte.text: After Mao Zedong’s death in 1976, **Deng Xiaoping** became China’s most important politician. He wanted to modernise the economy without giving up the power of the **Communist Party** (CPC). In his speech to the **12th Party Congress in 1982** he spoke of “**socialism with Chinese characteristics**”. The formula justified **market-economy reforms** under the leadership of the party.

As early as 1979 Deng laid down the **Four Cardinal Principles**. They set clear political limits to the reform. They are the socialist road, the people’s democratic dictatorship, the **leadership of the party**, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. A **multi-party system** on the Western model is expressly not part of it. The economy was to open up, but politics was not.

At the **13th Party Congress in 1987** the theory of the **primary stage of socialism** was set out. It says that China must first develop its economy, which is why market elements are necessary for the time being. The **14th Party Congress in 1992** set the **socialist market economy** as the goal. The market was to distribute goods, while the party and state-owned companies controlled important sectors. In 1993 the goal was written into the constitution.

Each party leader added ideas of his own. **Jiang Zemin** coined the theory of the **Three Represents**. According to it, the party represents the advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the interests of the majority. As a result, **private entrepreneurs** were allowed to become members from 2001. **Hu Jintao** coined the **Scientific Outlook on Development** for balanced and sustainable development. It was written into the party statutes in 2007.

An old Chinese goal is **xiaokang**, a society of modest prosperity. On the **100th anniversary of the party** in 2021, **Xi Jinping** announced that this goal had been achieved. Supporters point out that hundreds of millions of people have escaped poverty. Critics stress that political freedoms are still severely restricted.

gewusst: The term xiaokang comes from very old Chinese writings and is more than 2,000 years old.
A well-known saying is attributed to Deng Xiaoping: it does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.

teile.einleitung: Václav Havel was a Czech writer and civil rights campaigner. He fought against the communist dictatorship and was put in prison for it. After the change of regime he became president.
wichtigste: Havel first became known as a playwright.
In 1977 he was one of the founders of the civil rights movement Charter 77.
In 1978 he wrote the essay “The Power of the Powerless”.
Because he stood up for persecuted people, he was sentenced to prison in 1979.
From 1993 to 2003 he was the first president of the Czech Republic.

abschnitte.text: Václav Havel was born in **Prague** in 1936. He became known as a **playwright**, in other words a writer of plays for the theatre. He wrote **absurd** plays such as “**The Garden Party**” and “**Audience**”. In them he showed how meaningless and dishonest the language of those in power can be. Because of his criticism of the regime, his plays could for a long time only be performed abroad.

In 1977 Havel was one of the founders of **Charter 77**. This group demanded that the state respect **human rights**. In 1978 he founded the **Committee for the Defence of the Unjustly Prosecuted**, in Czech **VONS**. It collected cases of political persecution. Because of this, Havel was sentenced in 1979 to a **prison sentence** of several years.

In 1978 Havel wrote the essay “**The Power of the Powerless**”. In it he describes a **greengrocer** who puts a party slogan in his shop window even though he does not believe in it. In this way everyone goes along with it, and the system stays stable. Havel called on people to “**live in truth**”. According to Havel, anyone who stops playing along has a quiet power of their own.

In 1989 the **Velvet Revolution** led peacefully to the end of communism in Czechoslovakia. Havel became president of the country in December 1989. After Czechoslovakia split, he became the first president of the **Czech Republic** in **1993**. He served two terms, until **2003**. Havel died in 2011.

gewusst: Prague airport is named after Václav Havel today.
In 1989 Havel was awarded the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade, but could not collect it in person.

teile.einleitung: In the spring of 1989 hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Tiananmen Square (the Square of Heavenly Peace) in Beijing, China. They demanded more democracy, freedom of speech and an end to corruption. During the night of 3 to 4 June 1989 the army crushed the protests with bloodshed.
wichtigste: The Square of Heavenly Peace is called Tiananmen Square in Chinese and lies in the middle of Beijing.
The protests began in April 1989 after the death of the popular politician Hu Yaobang.
Mainly students took part, but workers did too.
During the night of 3 to 4 June 1989 soldiers and tanks cleared the square and the streets.
How many people died is still unknown today; estimates range from several hundred to a few thousand.
In China the subject is still strictly censored today.

abschnitte.text: **Tiananmen Square** is one of the largest city squares in the world. It lies in front of the Gate of Heavenly Peace, which leads to the Forbidden City. A huge picture of **Mao Zedong**, the founder of the People’s Republic of China, hangs there. For China’s government the square is an important place for parades and celebrations.

On 15 April 1989 the reformist politician **Hu Yaobang**, whom many young people admired, died. Students gathered to honour him and soon made political demands. They wanted **freedom of the press**, talks with the government and an end to corruption. In May thousands went on hunger strike, and there were protests in many other cities too.

In mid-May the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev visited Beijing, and journalists from all over the world also reported on the protests. On 20 May the government declared **martial law**. Students put up a white statue that they called the “Goddess of Democracy”. Within the party leadership there was disagreement about how to react.

During the night of 3 to 4 June soldiers with tanks advanced into Beijing and fired on people. Most of the victims died in the streets around the square. On 5 June an unknown man stood in the way of a column of tanks, and the photo of **Tank Man** became famous around the world. Afterwards many of those involved were arrested, and some fled abroad.

The party leader **Zhao Ziyang**, who had shown sympathy for the students, lost his post and was under house arrest until his death. The Communist Party under Deng Xiaoping continued to pursue economic reforms, but not political freedom. On the internet in China, terms relating to 4 June are blocked. In Hong Kong tens of thousands remembered the victims with candles every year, until these commemorations were banned from 2020.

begriffe.erklaerung: When many people gather to show their opinion together.
An emergency rule under which the army takes power in its own country.
When people deliberately do not eat in order to draw attention to their demands.
When the state bans reporting on certain things.

gewusst: Who the man in front of the tanks was and what became of him is still unknown today.
In the same year, 1989, the Berlin Wall fell in Europe, while in China the Communist Party stayed in power.
Because of censorship, many young people in China know hardly anything about the events of 1989.

teile.einleitung: In March 1921 the sailors of the fortress of Kronstadt rose up against Bolshevik rule. They demanded free elections to the soviets and more freedoms. The Red Army crushed the uprising after a few weeks.
wichtigste: Kronstadt is on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland, off St Petersburg.
In 1917 the Kronstadt sailors were seen as especially revolutionary.
They adopted their resolution on the battleship Petropavlovsk.
They demanded new elections to the soviets by secret ballot.
Stepan Petrichenko led the rebels' Revolutionary Committee.
Mikhail Tukhachevsky led the assault across the ice.
Kronstadt fell on 18 March 1921.

abschnitte.text: Kronstadt is on **Kotlin** Island in the **Gulf of Finland**, off **St Petersburg**. **Peter the Great** had the island fortified as a naval base. During the revolution of **1917**, the Kronstadt sailors were seen as especially revolutionary. At that time **Leon Trotsky** praised them as the **“pride and glory of the revolution”**.

After the civil war there was hunger and great hardship in Russia. At the end of **February 1921** the sailors on the battleship **Petropavlovsk** adopted a **resolution**. They demanded **new elections to the soviets by secret ballot**, as well as freedom of speech and of the press for left-wing parties. They wanted to free the councils from the rule of the party. The resolution became the programme of the uprising.

The rebels formed a **Provisional Revolutionary Committee**. It was led by **Stepan Petrichenko**, a clerk on the Petropavlovsk. The Bolsheviks saw the uprising as a threat to their power. The fact that it was the Kronstadt sailors of all people who rose up hit them especially hard.

In March the sea around Kronstadt was still **frozen**. Soldiers of the **Red Army** in white camouflage capes stormed **across the open ice**. The attack was led by **Mikhail Tukhachevsky** with the 7th Army. After heavy losses on both sides, Kronstadt fell on **18 March 1921**. Petrichenko fled abroad, and many other rebels were harshly punished.

gewusst: At the same time as the uprising, the party decided on the New Economic Policy and relaxed its control of the economy.
Today Kronstadt is part of the city of St Petersburg.

teile.einleitung: A people’s own enterprise, VEB for short, was the most common form of business in the GDR. Officially it belonged to the whole people, but in fact it was run by the state. Almost everyone in the GDR worked in a VEB.
wichtigste: VEB stands for “Volkseigener Betrieb”, meaning people’s own enterprise.
Officially a VEB belonged to the people, but in fact the state decided.
In 1989 about 80 per cent of all employees in the GDR worked in a VEB.
Several VEBs in the same industry together formed a combine.
In 1972 almost all the remaining private firms were nationalised.
After 1990 the Treuhandanstalt privatised the businesses.

abschnitte.text: In the GDR most businesses officially belonged to the **whole people**. They were called **people’s own enterprises**, or **VEB** for short. In fact, however, the state decided what happened to them. A **works manager** ran the business together with the **SED** party organisation. A well-known example is VEB Sachsenring in Zwickau, which built the **Trabant**.

The GDR had a **planned economy**. The **State Planning Commission** laid down what the businesses were to produce and how much. The state also set the prices. Anyone who **exceeded** the plan, in other words achieved more than required, was praised and given awards. Several VEBs in the same industry were grouped together to form a **combine**. The combines came under the industry ministries.

Many businesses had previously belonged to private families. Little by little they were **expropriated**. In the nationalisation of **1972** about **11,000** new VEBs were created once again. After that the share of state-owned businesses in industry was over 99 per cent. In 1989 **79.9 per cent** of all employees worked in a VEB. GDR citizens jokingly interpreted the abbreviation as “**Vaters ehemaliger Betrieb**” (father’s former business).

After the end of the GDR the **Treuhandanstalt** took over the people’s own enterprises. It sold them to private owners, restructured them or closed them. Many businesses were out of date and could not survive competition. That is why many people in eastern Germany lost their jobs. Some former VEBs still exist today under new names.

gewusst: The joke “Vaters ehemaliger Betrieb” (father’s former business) was a reminder of the expropriations.
By 1989 there were almost no private businesses left in the GDR.

teile.einleitung: The McCarthy era was a period in the USA around 1950 when people suspected communists everywhere. It is named after Senator Joseph McCarthy. Many people lost their jobs, often without any evidence.
wichtigste: Joseph McCarthy was a senator for the state of Wisconsin.
In February 1950 he claimed to know of many communists in the State Department.
From 1947 the HUAC committee questioned artists from Hollywood.
The Hollywood Ten refused to testify and were convicted.
Hundreds of people were on the blacklist.
In December 1954 the Senate formally censured McCarthy.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, the **Cold War** began between the USA and the **Soviet Union**. In the USA, fear of **spies** and communists grew. The Republican **Joseph McCarthy** was senator for **Wisconsin** from 1947 until his death in 1957. In **February 1950**, in a speech in **Wheeling**, he claimed to have a list of the names of communists in the **State Department**. He never produced any evidence.

From as early as **1947**, the **House Un-American Activities Committee**, **HUAC** for short, questioned artists about supposed communist links. It asked the witnesses: “Are you now or have you ever been a member of the Communist Party?” Ten screenwriters and directors refused to answer. They appealed to **freedom of expression**. These **Hollywood Ten** were sentenced to prison.

Suspected artists were put on a **blacklist**. After that, hundreds of people no longer got any work. Some carried on working under **false names**. The Rosenbergs were also caught up in this period: **Julius and Ethel Rosenberg** were convicted of **atomic spying** for the Soviet Union and executed in 1953. The verdict was controversial even at the time.

In **March 1954**, the television journalist **Edward R. Murrow** showed McCarthy's own statements and contradictions on his programme **“See It Now”**. This was followed by televised hearings about the **army**. In **December 1954**, the Senate passed a **formal censure** against McCarthy by a large majority. After that, he quickly lost influence.

In **1953** the writer **Arthur Miller** wrote the play **“The Crucible”**. It is set during the witch trials of **Salem** in the 17th century. But it is regarded as an allegory of the McCarthy era. Miller shows how fear and suspicion destroy a community. Later he himself had to testify before HUAC.

gewusst: The word “McCarthyism” today generally means making accusations without evidence.
HUAC existed until the 1970s, at the end under a different name.

teile.einleitung: Reform and opening-up is a change of course in the People’s Republic of China that began at the end of 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. China introduced elements of the market economy and opened up to foreign companies. In the process the Communist Party kept political power.
wichtigste: The policy began in December 1978 with the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee.
Deng Xiaoping put economic development at the centre.
The “Four Modernisations” were the most important goal.
Farming families were allowed to sell their surplus themselves.
In the village of Xiaogang the agricultural reform began secretly in 1978.
In 2001 China joined the World Trade Organization (WTO).

abschnitte.text: After Mao Zedong’s death in 1976, **Deng Xiaoping** won the struggle for the top. In December 1978 the **Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee** took place. There the party put **economic development** at the centre instead of class struggle. At the heart of the policy were the **Four Modernisations**: agriculture, industry, national defence, and science and technology. Zhou Enlai had already formulated this goal.

In 1978 farmers in the village of **Xiaogang** in Anhui province secretly divided the collective land among themselves. Their success became a model for the whole of China. Under the **household responsibility system**, farming families leased land from the state. They handed over a fixed amount and were allowed to sell the rest themselves. After that, harvests rose considerably.

Deng said, roughly, that it did not matter whether a **cat** was black or white, as long as it caught mice. By this he meant that what matters is what works, not pure doctrine. Another guiding principle was **“Let some get rich first”**. Others were to follow later. At first it was mainly the **coastal regions** that benefited, where special economic zones were set up for foreign companies.

abschnitte.titel: China opens up to the world
abschnitte.text: China became an important location for factories from all over the world. On 11 December 2001, after years of negotiations, the country joined the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**. This speeded up its rise to become an **export power**. Politically, the rule of the **Communist Party** remained in place. Critics point out that along with prosperity, the gap between rich and poor has also grown.

gewusst: The farmers of Xiaogang signed their secret agreement with their fingerprints.
In 1980 Shenzhen was a smallish town; as a special economic zone it grew into a city of millions.

teile.einleitung: A superpower is a country with a great deal of power all over the world. In the Cold War there were two superpowers: the USA and the Soviet Union. They were rivals and had very different ideas about what a state should be like.
wichtigste: A superpower has a big military, a lot of money and great influence.
In the Cold War the USA and the Soviet Union were the two superpowers.
The capital of the USA is Washington.
The Soviet Union was the largest country on Earth by area.
In the Soviet Union only the Communist Party ruled.
The Soviet Union broke apart in 1991.

abschnitte.text: A **superpower** is stronger than an ordinary state. It has a big **army**, a strong **economy** and influence over many other countries. After the Second World War there were two such countries: the **USA** and the **Soviet Union**. Both had nuclear weapons. Their rivalry is called the **Cold War**, because they never fought each other directly.

The capital of the USA is **Washington**. That is where the president, the parliament (Congress) and the Supreme Court work. The president lives and works in the **White House**. The flag has 13 red and white stripes and 50 white stars, which is why it is called the “**Stars and Stripes**”. People pay with the **dollar**, one of the most important currencies in the world.

The **Soviet Union** stretched from Europe to the Pacific. It was bigger than any other country on Earth. Many peoples with their own languages lived there. But the common language was **Russian**, which everyone learned at school. The capital was **Moscow**.

The two superpowers were very different. In the Soviet Union only the **Communist Party** ruled, and the state decided on the economy. The USA was a **democracy** with several parties and a free economy. Each side wanted to win other countries over. **Switzerland** stayed **neutral** in this rivalry.

In 1991 the Soviet Union broke apart into 15 separate states. The largest of them is **Russia**. After that the USA was regarded for a long time as the only superpower. Today people often discuss whether **China** has also become a superpower. Experts do not agree about this.

gewusst: The 13 stripes on the US flag stand for the first 13 states of the USA.
New York is bigger than Washington, but it is not the capital.

teile.einleitung: The fall of the Berlin Wall was the opening of the wall on the night of 9 to 10 November 1989. After 28 years, the people of East Berlin could once again go freely to the West. The event became a symbol of the end of the Cold War and led to the reunification of Germany.
wichtigste: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989.
It had been built by the GDR in 1961.
The wall separated East Berlin and West Berlin for 28 years.
It was triggered by a misleading announcement by Günter Schabowski.
Before that, hundreds of thousands of GDR citizens had demonstrated peacefully for freedom.
On 3 October 1990 Germany was reunited.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided, and in the east the communist **GDR** was created. Because so many people were fleeing to the West, the GDR built the **Berlin Wall** from 13 August 1961. It enclosed West Berlin along around 155 kilometres. At least 140 people died at the wall while trying to escape or in accidents.

In 1989 dissatisfaction in the GDR grew; people wanted the freedom to travel and a say. Thousands fled via Hungary, where the border fence had been opened. In Leipzig, at the **Monday demonstrations** in the autumn, hundreds of thousands took to the streets. Their chant was “We are the people”, and the protests stayed peaceful.

On the evening of 9 November 1989, the Politburo member **Günter Schabowski** read out new travel rules at a press conference. When asked from when they applied, he said: “As far as I know, it takes effect immediately, without delay.” Thousands then streamed to the border crossings. At the **Bornholmer Strasse** crossing, the border guards were the first to open the gate, shortly before midnight.

People from East and West hugged each other, and many wept with happiness. They climbed onto the wall at the Brandenburg Gate and celebrated all night. In the following days, millions of GDR citizens visited West Berlin. With hammers and chisels, many people knocked pieces out of the wall as souvenirs; they were called “wall woodpeckers”.

In March 1990 the first free elections were held in the GDR. On 3 October 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic; that day is now the **Day of German Unity**. Soon afterwards, the other communist governments in Eastern Europe collapsed too, and in 1991 the Soviet Union. Remains of the wall can still be seen today, for example at the **East Side Gallery** and at the memorial on Bernauer Strasse.

begriffe.erklaerung: German Democratic Republic, the communist state in eastern Germany from 1949 to 1990.
Peaceful protests that took place every Monday in Leipzig in 1989.
The joining of the GDR and the Federal Republic into one Germany in 1990.
A place where you can cross a border under supervision.

gewusst: The opening of the wall was not actually planned like this; it happened because of a misunderstanding at the press conference.
Pieces of the wall now stand in many countries of the world, including Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In a proxy war, great powers do not fight each other themselves. Instead they support different sides in a war between other countries. There were many such wars during the Cold War.
wichtigste: The USA and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly during the Cold War.
But they helped different sides with weapons, money and advisers.
In the Korean War, Western troops fought under the command of the UN.
Since 1953 Switzerland has helped to monitor the ceasefire in Korea.
The Vietnam War ended in 1975 with the fall of Saigon.
In Angola, Cuban troops fought in the civil war.

abschnitte.text: In the **Cold War** the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** faced each other. Both had nuclear weapons, and a direct war would have been dangerous for the whole world. That is why each of them supported one side in other countries. They supplied **weapons**, **money** and advisers. Wars like these are called **proxy wars**.

After 1945 Korea was divided at the **38th parallel**: the North came under Soviet influence and the South under American influence. In 1950 North Korea attacked the South. The UN Security Council decided to help South Korea, because the Soviet Union was boycotting its meetings. That is why the troops led by the USA fought under the command of the **United Nations**. In 1953 the war ended with a **ceasefire**.

Since 1953 **Swiss officers** have been stationed at **Panmunjom** on the border between North and South Korea. They belong to the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission**. It monitors the ceasefire of the Korean War. Switzerland was chosen because it is **neutral**. To this day there is no peace treaty between the two Koreas.

In Vietnam the communist North under **Ho Chi Minh** fought against the South. The USA sent many soldiers to help South Vietnam. North Vietnam received help from the Soviet Union and China. After the Paris Peace Accords the last US combat troops withdrew in **1973**. On **30 April 1975** the North captured **Saigon**, which today is called Ho Chi Minh City.

There were proxy wars in Africa too. In the civil war in **Angola**, **Cuba** sent tens of thousands of soldiers in the 1970s. They supported the **MPLA**, which was backed by the Soviet Union. The other side received help from the USA and South Africa. Other examples from the Cold War are the wars in Afghanistan and in Central America.

gewusst: Ho Chi Minh died in 1969, before the end of the Vietnam War.
Today’s border between North and South Korea runs roughly along the 38th parallel.

teile.einleitung: The Axis powers is the name for the states that were allied with Nazi Germany in the Second World War. The most important were Germany, Italy and Japan. Their opponents were called the Allies.
wichtigste: In 1936 in Milan, Benito Mussolini spoke of a Berlin-Rome “axis”.
In 1936 Germany and Japan concluded the Anti-Comintern Pact.
In May 1939 Germany and Italy became allies in the Pact of Steel.
The Tripartite Pact of September 1940 joined Germany, Italy and Japan.
Hungary, Romania, Slovakia and Bulgaria joined the Tripartite Pact.
In September 1943 Italy agreed an armistice with the Allies.

abschnitte.text: In November 1936 the Italian dictator **Benito Mussolini** gave a speech in **Milan**. In it he spoke of a **Berlin-Rome axis** around which other European states could turn. This image gave rise to the name **Axis powers**. At that time both Germany under Adolf Hitler and Italy under Mussolini were **dictatorships**.

Italy and Germany moved closer together during the **Abyssinian War**. Because of the attack on Ethiopia, the League of Nations imposed sanctions on Italy in 1935 and 1936, but Germany supported it. In November 1936 Germany and Japan concluded the **Anti-Comintern Pact** against the Communist International, which was controlled from Moscow, and Italy joined in 1937. In May 1939 the **Pact of Steel** between Germany and Italy followed. On 27 September 1940 Germany, Italy and Japan signed the **Tripartite Pact** in Berlin.

In the **Tripartite Pact** the three states divided up spheres of influence in Europe and East Asia and promised to support one another. The first further country to join was **Hungary**, on 20 November 1940. Shortly afterwards **Romania** and **Slovakia** followed, and in March 1941 **Bulgaria** too. From 1940 **Switzerland** was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers and the areas they occupied.

On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the US base at **Pearl Harbor**. On **11 December 1941** Germany and Italy declared war on the USA, even though the Tripartite Pact did not oblige them to do so. With that the war finally became a **world war**. The USA now fought against the Axis powers in Europe and in the Pacific.

Italy only entered the war in June 1940 and suffered many defeats. On 8 September 1943 the **Armistice of Cassibile** with the Allies was announced. With it Italy left the Axis, and German troops occupied large parts of the country. Germany surrendered in **May 1945**, and Japan in **September 1945**. With that the Second World War was over.

gewusst: So the term “axis” came from Mussolini and not from Germany’s opponents.
Although Japan belonged to the Axis, its troops fought almost only in Asia and the Pacific, far away from Europe.

teile.einleitung: Todor Zhivkov was the communist ruler of Bulgaria. He led the Bulgarian Communist Party for 35 years, from 1954 to 1989, which made him one of the longest-serving rulers in the Eastern Bloc.
wichtigste: Zhivkov was at the head of the Bulgarian Communist Party from 1954.
He was a close ally of the Soviet Union.
From 1984 the Turkish minority was forced to change their names.
In the summer of 1989 more than 300,000 Bulgarians of Turkish origin left for Turkey.
On 10 November 1989 the Politburo removed Zhivkov from power.
His successor was Petar Mladenov.

abschnitte.text: Todor Zhivkov took over the leadership of the **Bulgarian Communist Party** in **1954**. His title was at first First Secretary and later **General Secretary**. He stayed in power for **35 years**. During this time Bulgaria was one of the Soviet Union’s most loyal countries. Zhivkov even offered Moscow several times to make Bulgaria the **16th republic** of the Soviet Union. Moscow declined.

From 1975 Zhivkov’s daughter **Lyudmila Zhivkova** headed the **Committee for Culture**. She promoted the arts and for many Bulgarians was a sign of a little more openness. She also organised the celebrations for the **1,300th anniversary of Bulgaria** in 1981. Her work shaped Bulgarian cultural policy.

From **1984** members of the **Turkish minority** had to change their names to Slavic names. The regime gave this the whitewashing name “**Revival Process**”. Anyone who resisted was persecuted. In the summer of **1989** the regime opened the border. More than **300,000** Bulgarians of Turkish origin left for **Turkey**. This greatly weakened the economy and Zhivkov’s reputation.

On **10 November 1989**, one day after the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Politburo removed Zhivkov from power. The change of power took place within the party. It had been organised by the long-serving foreign minister **Petar Mladenov**. He then took over Zhivkov’s posts. Shortly afterwards Bulgaria too set out on the road to free elections and several parties.

gewusst: Zhivkov was removed from power exactly one day after the fall of the Wall in Berlin.
The regime played down the exodus of 1989 by calling it the “Great Excursion”.

teile.einleitung: A Westpaket was a gift parcel that people in the Federal Republic sent to relatives and friends in the GDR. It contained things that were scarce or expensive in the East. The parcels kept the bond between families alive across the border.
wichtigste: Westpakete were presents from relatives in the Federal Republic to people in the GDR.
Real coffee was particularly popular.
On average about 25 million parcels were sent every year.
The parcels had to bear the label “Geschenksendung, keine Handelsware” (gift, not merchandise).
Money, tapes and war toys were not allowed inside.
Customs and the Stasi checked and opened some parcels.
As a thank-you, GDR families often sent back a Dresden Christmas stollen.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided into two states: the **Federal Republic** in the West and the **GDR** in the East. Many families suddenly lived in different countries. In the GDR goods that were perfectly normal in the West were often missing. That is why many West Germans regularly sent their relatives a **Westpaket**. Especially before Christmas, the post offices were full of these parcels.

The classic item in a Westpaket was **real coffee**. Real coffee was expensive and scarce in the GDR. Every year about **1,000 tonnes** of coffee were sent by parcel. On top of that there were chocolate, soap, spices and **clothes**: about five million items of clothing a year. Many people from the GDR still remember today the special smell when a Westpaket was opened.

Every parcel had to bear the words “**Geschenksendung, keine Handelsware**” (gift, not merchandise). This made it clear that the contents were not to be sold. In addition, a **list of the contents** had to be enclosed. Banned items included, for example, **cash**, **tapes**, war toys and certain publications. **Customs** and the **State Security**, Stasi for short, opened some parcels to check them. Banned items were confiscated.

The Federal Republic encouraged the parcels: senders could **deduct** the costs **from their taxes**. In this way the bond between families in East and West was meant to stay strong. Parcels also came back from the GDR. A popular present in return at Christmas was the **Dresden Christmas stollen**. Sometimes it was even baked with ingredients from the Westpaket.

gewusst: On average about 25 million Westpakete were sent to the GDR every year.
Each year the Westpakete together contained about five million items of clothing.

teile.einleitung: Raúl Castro is a Cuban politician and the younger brother of Fidel Castro. He fought alongside him in the revolution and was defence minister for almost 50 years. From 2008 to 2018 he was president of Cuba.
wichtigste: Raúl Castro was born in 1931 and is five years younger than Fidel.
From 1959 to 2008 he was defence minister.
In 2006 he took over the duties of office because of Fidel’s illness.
From 2008 to 2018 he was president of the state.
With Barack Obama he improved relations with the USA.
He led the Communist Party of Cuba until 2021.

abschnitte.text: Raúl Castro was born in 1931 and is five years younger than his brother **Fidel**. Together the brothers fought against the dictator Fulgencio Batista. After a failed attack in 1953 they were imprisoned and afterwards went into exile in Mexico. In 1956 they returned to Cuba on the boat **Granma**. From the mountains of the **Sierra Maestra** they led the fight until victory in 1959.

After the revolution, in 1959, Raúl Castro became **defence minister**. He held this office for almost 50 years, until 2008. He built up the Cuban **army**. For a long time he stood in his brother’s shadow. In 2006 Fidel had to undergo a serious operation, and Raúl temporarily took over the duties of office.

In 2008 Raúl Castro officially became **president of the state**. He allowed more **small private businesses**, such as restaurants or taxis. However, one-party rule remained in place. At the end of 2014 he and US President **Barack Obama** announced a rapprochement. In 2015 embassies reopened, and in 2016 Obama visited Havana.

In 2018 Raúl Castro gave up the office of president. This meant that for the first time since 1976 the head of state was not a Castro. His successor was **Miguel Díaz-Canel**, who was only born in 1960, after the revolution. Raúl had taken over the leadership of the **Communist Party** from Fidel in 2011. In April 2021 he also handed this office over to Díaz-Canel.

gewusst: Together, Fidel and Raúl Castro led Cuba for almost 60 years.
The boat Granma, on which the revolutionaries came to Cuba in 1956, is now in a museum in Havana.

teile.einleitung: Sputnik 1 was the world’s first artificial satellite. The Soviet Union launched it into space on 4 October 1957, and this marked the beginning of the space age.
wichtigste: Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 October 1957.
It was a metal sphere 58 centimetres in diameter.
It weighed about 83.6 kilograms.
It took about 96 minutes to go round the Earth once.
The launch caused the Sputnik shock in the West.
In response the USA founded NASA in 1958.

abschnitte.text: Sputnik 1 was a shiny **metal sphere** with a diameter of about **58 centimetres**. That is roughly the size of a large beach ball. It weighed about **83.6 kilograms**. Long **aerials** were attached to the sphere. With them Sputnik sent a simple beeping signal to Earth, which radio amateurs all over the world could also pick up.

On **4 October 1957** Sputnik 1 was launched on an **R-7 rocket** from the **Baikonur** cosmodrome. A cosmodrome is a launch site for rockets. The R-7 was actually a military rocket. The name Sputnik is Russian and means roughly “companion” or “fellow traveller”. A satellite, after all, accompanies the Earth on its path.

Sputnik 1 circled the Earth in about **96 minutes**, so in about an hour and a half. This meant it flew over the same countries several times a day. This path is called an **orbit**. After a few weeks the batteries ran out, and the beeping stopped. Later Sputnik sank lower and lower and burned up in the Earth’s atmosphere.

In the USA and Western Europe people were alarmed. This fright is called the **Sputnik shock**. Anyone who can put a satellite into space can also fire **nuclear missiles** a very long way. That is why in 1958 the USA founded the space agency **NASA**. On 31 January 1958 the first US satellite, **Explorer 1**, was launched. It discovered the radiation belts around the Earth.

As early as November 1957 **Sputnik 2** followed. On board was the dog **Laika**. She was the first living creature to go into orbit around the Earth. There was no plan for a return to Earth, and Laika did not survive the flight. These flights marked the beginning of the **space race** between the USA and the Soviet Union.

gewusst: Explorer 1 was launched almost four months after Sputnik 1.
Sputnik’s beeping could be heard with an ordinary radio receiver.

teile.einleitung: The “Manifesto of the Communist Party” is a short work by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels from 1848. It explains the ideas of communism and calls on workers to make a revolution. It became one of the most influential political texts in world history.
wichtigste: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote the manifesto in 1848.
It was published in German in London in February 1848.
It was commissioned by a small secret society, the Communist League.
The manifesto describes history as a struggle between classes.
It ends with the call “Workers of all countries, unite!”.
It has been translated into more than 100 languages.
Since 2013 it has been part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.

abschnitte.text: A **manifesto** is a public declaration in which someone sets out their aims. The Communist Manifesto is only about 23 pages long. At the end of 1847, the Communist League had asked Marx and Engels to write a programme. It begins with the famous sentence “A spectre is haunting Europe, the spectre of communism.”

**Karl Marx** came from Trier, and **Friedrich Engels** from Barmen, today's Wuppertal. Engels was the son of a factory owner and knew the hard life of factory workers in England. The two worked closely together for decades. Marx later also wrote the great work “Das Kapital”.

The manifesto says that the history of all societies is a history of **class struggles**. In their time, it says, the owners of the factories, the **bourgeoisie**, faced the workers, the **proletariat**. The workers were exploited, but would one day take power. Then private ownership of factories and land was to be abolished.

The manifesto appeared in a year full of unrest in Europe, the **revolutions of 1848**. In many countries people demanded more freedom and rights. At the same time, industrialisation was greatly changing life; many people, including children, worked in factories in terrible conditions. At first the manifesto remained little known; it only became famous decades later.

The manifesto influenced workers' movements, trade unions and socialist parties around the world. Communist leaders such as Lenin and Mao appealed to it. But in their states it turned into dictatorships that oppressed many people. Today the manifesto is read and discussed in schools and universities as an important historical document.

begriffe.erklaerung: A public declaration of aims and demands.
The class of factory owners and rich citizens.
The class of workers who own nothing but their labour.
The conflict between rich and poor over power and property.

gewusst: The manifesto was first printed in German, even though it was published in London.
Marx was only 29 years old when he wrote the manifesto, and Engels just 27.

teile.einleitung: Xi Jinping is a Chinese politician and the most powerful man in the People’s Republic of China. Since 2012 he has led the Communist Party as General Secretary, and since 2013 he has also been president. Under him China has become even more influential economically and politically.
wichtigste: Xi Jinping was born in Beijing on 15 June 1953.
His father, Xi Zhongxun, was a senior party official and vice-premier.
During the Cultural Revolution Xi lived in a village in the countryside for several years.
He has been General Secretary of the Communist Party of China since 2012 and president since 2013.
In 2018 the limit of two terms as president was abolished.
In 2013 he announced the New Silk Road project.
His ideas are written into the party and state constitutions as “Xi Jinping Thought”.

abschnitte.text: Xi Jinping was born in **Beijing** on **15 June 1953**. His father, **Xi Zhongxun**, had fought for the communists before 1949 and later became **vice-premier**. In 1962 his father was removed from power and was only rehabilitated after Mao’s death. During the **Cultural Revolution** the young Xi, like millions of other young people, was sent to the countryside. From 1969 he lived and worked in a **village** in **Shaanxi** province.

From 1975 Xi studied **chemical engineering** at **Tsinghua University** in Beijing. After that he rose step by step through the party. He worked in various provinces, among them **Fujian** and **Zhejiang**, and briefly in **Shanghai**. In 2008 he became vice-president of China. In this way the party prepared him for the highest offices.

In November **2012** Xi became **General Secretary** of the Communist Party. This is the most powerful post in China. In March **2013** he also became **president**, succeeding Hu Jintao. In 2018 the limit of **two terms** was removed from the constitution. This allowed Xi to begin a third term as president in 2023. His political ideas are officially called “**Xi Jinping Thought**” and have been in the party constitution since 2017.

One of Xi’s best-known campaigns is the **fight against corruption**. Since 2012 hundreds of thousands of officials have been punished in it. Critics say that it has also been used to remove political opponents. In 2013 Xi announced the **New Silk Road**. It is meant to create trade routes to Asia, Africa and Europe with ports, railways and roads. Human rights organisations and many Western governments criticise China’s treatment of minorities and people who think differently. The Chinese government rejects this criticism.

Switzerland and China have a **free trade agreement**, which has been in force since **2014**. In January **2017** Xi Jinping came to Switzerland on a **state visit**. During it he also spoke at the **World Economic Forum** in Davos. He was the first Chinese president to give a speech there.

gewusst: Since Mao Zedong, no Chinese party leader has been honoured so strongly in the constitution during his lifetime as Xi Jinping.
Xi was admitted to university as a “worker-peasant-soldier student”, without the usual entrance examination.

teile.einleitung: After the October Revolution of 1917, the Bolsheviks in Russia fought against their many opponents. This Russian Civil War lasted mainly from 1918 to 1921. In the end the Reds won, and millions of people had lost their lives or their homes.
wichtigste: The Bolsheviks were called the Reds, and their opponents the Whites.
The war lasted mainly from 1918 to 1921, and in the Far East until 1922.
The Reds won the civil war.
Admiral Alexander Kolchak led the Whites in Siberia.
Several foreign powers sent troops to Russia.
After the war there was a great famine along the Volga.

abschnitte.text: In October 1917 the **Bolsheviks** under Lenin took power. Many people did not agree with this. This led to **civil war**. The Bolsheviks were called the **Reds**, and their opponents the **Whites**. The Whites included supporters of the tsar, officers and liberals. There were also peasant armies and groups fighting for the independence of their regions.

In May 1918 the **Czechoslovak Legion** set off major fighting. This force of former prisoners of war was to be taken to France via Vladivostok. When the Bolsheviks tried to disarm it, it occupied large parts of the **Trans-Siberian Railway**. In Siberia, in 1918, Admiral **Alexander Kolchak** had himself proclaimed “Supreme Ruler” in Omsk. His troops were defeated, and he was executed in 1920.

Other countries also intervened, among them **Great Britain, France, the USA and Japan**. They landed troops in Russia and partly supported the Whites. However, their involvement remained limited, and they withdrew again. The Reds controlled the heartland with **Moscow** and **Petrograd** and had a tightly led force in the **Red Army**. The Whites, on the other hand, were divided and scattered across a vast area.

In December 1917 the Bolsheviks founded the secret police, the **Cheka**, under Felix Dzerzhinsky. It persecuted political opponents with great harshness, and people spoke of the **Red Terror**. The Whites also used violence against their opponents. In the economy **War Communism** was in force: businesses were nationalised and grain was taken from the farmers by force. This led to hunger and uprisings.

In 1921 and 1922 a severe **famine** struck the regions along the Volga. War, forced requisitions and drought were the causes. Millions of people died, and aid organisations from abroad also tried to help. About one to two million people left Russia. Many then lived in exile, for example in **Paris, Berlin or Prague**. At the end of 1922 the **Soviet Union** was founded.

gewusst: The Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen organised help for the starving and created a passport for stateless refugees, the “Nansen passport”.
At times the Czechoslovak Legion travelled along the Trans-Siberian Railway in armoured trains of its own.

teile.einleitung: The Paris Commune was a city government that rose up against the French government in Paris in the spring of 1871. It lasted only about 72 days, from 18 March to 28 May 1871. For the later labour movement and for Karl Marx it became an important model.
wichtigste: The Commune came about after France’s defeat in the Franco-Prussian War.
It was triggered by the dispute over the cannons on Montmartre on 18 March 1871.
The government under Adolphe Thiers was based in Versailles.
The Commune decided on the separation of church and state.
It ended in the “Bloody Week” from 21 to 28 May 1871.
Louise Michel is one of its best-known fighters.

abschnitte.text: In 1870/71 France lost the **Franco-Prussian War** against Prussia and its allies. Paris had been besieged for months, and many people had gone hungry. Many Parisians were outraged by the peace and by the new government. The **National Guard**, a citizens’ militia, had paid for cannons with money from the people. On **18 March 1871** the government wanted to have these cannons removed from **Montmartre**.

The soldiers fraternised with the crowd, and the plan failed. The government under **Adolphe Thiers** withdrew to **Versailles**. In Paris the people elected a council, the **Commune**. Its supporters were called **Communards**. From Versailles, Thiers sent troops against the rebellious city.

The Commune wanted a fairer society for workers and craftspeople. It decided on the **separation of church and state**: the state was not to favour any religion. In France as a whole this was only introduced in 1905. The Communards toppled the **Vendôme Column**, which commemorated Napoleon’s victories. For them it was a symbol of war and imperial rule.

From 21 to 28 May 1871 government troops won back Paris barricade by barricade. This period is called the **Bloody Week**, and thousands of Communards lost their lives. On 28 May the last fighters were shot against a wall in the **Père Lachaise** cemetery. This **Mur des Fédérés** (Communards’ Wall) is today a place of remembrance for the labour movement. The teacher **Louise Michel**, who had fought on the barricades, was exiled to New Caledonia.

gewusst: In 1871 Karl Marx wrote a work about the Commune entitled “The Civil War in France”.
Shortly before the Commune, the German Empire had been proclaimed in the Palace of Versailles.
